45,000 runners. 45 years of the Midnight Run.

And among them? Two of us.

My 13-year-old son and me. 

Our third official race together. Undoubtedly our best yet.

At kilometer 8, he looked over, breathing hard but grinning: "Dad, you don’t need to hold back for me!"

And oh my, is he getting faster!

Every race, every stride, I see it. 

I am spending more and more of every run cheering him along. 

Looking back, I realize the finish line isn't the real victory.

Watching him grow into his stride is.

The clock is ticking.

In a couple of more years, he'll slowly start beating my times. 

Not yet, but soon enough. And honestly? 

I can't wait.

That’s the gift of coaching; whether in running or in leadership. 

You guide, you push, you cheer from the sidelines. 

And one day, the people you’ve invested in outrun you. 

That’s not a loss. 

That’s the ultimate win.

We crossed the line among 44,998 others and celebrated the only way that made sense: midnight ice cream under the Stockholm sky.

Because the best successes aren't just about your own time on the clock; they're about who you share the finish line with.

Here's to passing the baton, celebrating the journey, and many more races together! 🏃‍♂️‍➡️🏃‍♂️‍➡️🍦

#Midnattsloppet #Running #Mentorship #Leadership #FatherSon #Growth

posts.text:
Take your initial guess, double it, and then double it again. - Kent Beck

Two years ago, I sat in the main SEB auditorium, watching one of the absolute legends in software engineering. 

Right there and then, Kent Beck wasn't talking about TDD or XP. 

He was talking about estimation. 

His rule of thumb? 

Whatever time you think it'll take; double it, then double it again.

2 weeks → 2 months.

At first, it felt cynical. 

After years of watching "quick fixes" become week-long rabbit holes and "simple features" turn into quarter-long epics? 

I realised that it is not cynicism. 

It's pattern recognition.

Here's what I've learned applying this rule:

The gap isn't about skill. 

It's about unknowns. 

Every estimate assumes a path.

Software development is a maze where you don't know the dead ends until you hit them.

The gap isn't about effort. It's about everything around the effort. 

Code reviews. 

Deployment issues. 

That one integration that looked simple. 

The meeting that wasn't on the calendar.

The gap isn't about pessimism. 

It's about honesty. 

The question isn't "how long should this take?" 

It's "how long will this take, given reality?"

Does the rule hold up? 

The "doubling" heuristic is widely cited in software circles. 

Beck himself has also voiced a more nuanced view; estimates make sense when you've done similar work before, not when you're exploring something new. 

He's also been known to say: 

"You don't have to estimate. 
You just have to not die."

But for most of us who can't just ignore that question about time estimates? 

Double it. 

Then double it again.

You'll still be wrong. 

Just less wrong.

#SoftwareEngineering #Estimation #KentBeck #ExtremeProgramming #TDD #XP

Recently I spent some time tidying up my posts archive and links site, cloudcloud.dev. 

What started as a quick housekeeping session turned into a refresher on performance, security, and migration safety.

Here’s the twist: the heavy lifting wasn't done by me manually. 

I leaned heavily on AI code generators to assist with the refactoring, and I have to say that I was genuinely impressed. 

The context understanding was spot on, and the deep domain knowledge in security hardening saved me hours of research.

A few highlights from the cleanup:

- Tamed page weight: One page was lugging around 672 posts (~1 MB). After splitting things up by year and engagement bucket, the largest page is down to 409 KB.

- Fixed hidden content: Unpacked 398 daily notes that were crammed inside a single 141 KB Markdown file with no individual URLs or active RSS feed. They’re all standalone, dated posts now.

- Verified, didn't guess: Validated the entire migration byte-for-byte before trusting it in production.

Hardened the site & pipeline:

- Sanitized third-party reposts, locked down external links, added SRI hashes for CDN stylesheets, and pinned GitHub Actions to commit SHAs to protect against supply chain risks. Also stripped --location from curl calls so API keys won't leak on redirects.

Smoother publishing: 

Now I just throw thoughts into a scratch file and commit. A GitHub Action dates it, publishes it, and clears the file automatically.

The lesson I relearned: Generating a change is the easy part, especially when you have AI doing the heavy lifting. 

Proving you didn't lose anything along the way, and ensuring the changes are secure and performant, is the actual job.

Big props to the AI tools that helped me move faster without cutting corners on security. 

The future of development isn’t about replacing the engineer, it’s truly about supercharging them.

Yes, coding has accelerated, but that's mostly the tail-end of the cycle. 

We still need to:

👉 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽 𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆  — which opportunities we're pursuing, in which market segments.

👉 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮𝘀 (𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻) — based on impact, cost, and supporting evidence. 

👉 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝗿 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 (𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆)

👉 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹𝘀 

AI does not eliminate the need for any of these. In fact they are more important than before.   

You still need an outcomes-based roadmap, a metrics tree, a GIST board, even if your engineers use Claude Code. 

🙋‍♀️  See courses that teach all of the methods shown in the diagram, with AI, in the comments.

The logic "we used to do these things because coding was expensive, but now we don't have to" doesn't hold water. 

We used these methods because launching bad products and features is a deadly anti-pattern. AI lets us sink ourselves in the quicksand of waste and bloat faster and deeper than before. 

AI may create a new PDLC paradigm in the future, when it is better understood and more widely used beyond coding. But we're not there yet. 

For now, "classic" product skills are as crucial for product peoples' and product leaders' success as they always were. 

If you disagree — let me know why in the comments.

posts.text:
I just finished Eric Ries’s latest book, ”Incorruptible”. 

While you may know Ries for the "Lean Startup" methodology, what he delivers in ”Incorruptible” is a masterclass in corporate governance and long-term value creation. 

He dismantles the tired dogma of short-term profit maximization and presents a compelling argument that the "financialization" of business is not just bad for society, it’s also bad for business.

Here is why this book resonates so well:

Ries moves beyond theory. 

He takes us inside companies that have successfully rejected the "squeeze every drop" mentality and have instead embraced a mission-first approach. 

The result? 

These organizations aren't just surviving; they are outperforming their peers, creating generational wealth, and building enterprises that last.

One of the fascinating aspects of the book is the prevalence of European case studies. 

Ries highlights companies like Maersk, IKEA, and Novo Nordisk as prime examples of this "incorruptible" model.

Why Europe? It speaks to a cultural and structural difference in how we define success. 

In the US, the quarterly earnings report seem the ultimate metric. 

In Europe, we probably rely on an older tradition of stakeholder capitalism, considering employees, communities, and the environment as integral to the P&L, not external to it.

These companies have navigated world wars, economic depressions, and industry disruptions. 

They survived not by being the fastest, but by being the most resilient and principles-driven.

Key Takeaways:

1. Profit is a Byproduct, Not the Goal: When you focus on solving a real problem for society, profit follows. When you focus only on profit, you eventually run out of road.

2. Managing for "The Long Now": Ries provides a framework for convincing skeptics and board members that long-term investment in R&D, culture, and sustainability isn't a cost, rather it's the only insurance policy against irrelevance.

3. Governance Matters: The book is particularly insightful on how family-owned and foundation-owned enterprises (like many in the book) have a natural advantage. 

They are insulated from the hysteria of the public markets, allowing them to make decisions that pay off over decades, not quarters.

We are living in a time of massive distrust. 

”Incorruptible” offers a practical, actionable antidote. 

It isn't naive idealism; it’s hard-nosed realism. 

Ries argues that the "classical capitalist" approach of beating last quarter’s earnings without considering global implications is a bug, not a feature. 

And the market is beginning to price that in.

If you are a founder, an executive, or an investor tired of the hamster wheel of quarterly earnings, this book will give you the ammunition and the roadmap to build something that matters.

Nobody has ever seen a single pane of glass.

It's been sold for twenty years. Observability vendors. ITSM vendors. Cloud vendors. Every one of them promising the pane. Every one of them becoming pane number seven.

Here's the part nobody says out loud: the panes aren't the problem. The panes are evidence.

Twelve dashboards means twelve teams answering twelve different questions with twelve different definitions of "healthy." You didn't buy too many tools. You never agreed on what you were looking at.

So the next platform won't consolidate anything. It can't. Consolidation isn't a feature. It's a decision, about which metrics matter, who owns them, and what everyone is allowed to stop maintaining.

Two options. Make that decision, then pick tooling that reflects it. Or buy pane thirteen and schedule the rationalization workshop for next year.

Most companies pick the workshop.

The vendors know this. It's why the demo always looks like your environment, and the invoice always looks like your last three invoices. Combined.

Buy the decision first. The glass is optional.

Over the years, I've worked alongside engineers at every level: junior and senior, novices and virtuosos. 

I've learned to adapt, to find common ground, and to build productive relationships across the spectrum of experience and skill. 

But there's one archetype I still find problematic; the engineer who is exceptionally skilled at identifying and articulating problems, yet remarkably absent when it comes to solutions.

At first glance, these individuals appear deeply knowledgeable. 

They voice concerns that no one else has considered, dissect risks with surgical precision, and frame challenges with apparent authority. 

But the depth is deceptive. 

When asked "What do we do about this?" they often go quiet. 

And when pressed to propose a path forward, they tend to problematise their own suggestions, dismantling any solution before it can gain traction.

This isn't just frustrating; it's costly.

Research in team dynamics offers some explanation. 

A study published in Group & Organization Management analyzed over 43,000 utterances from problem-solving teams and found that problem-focused behavior actually reduces the likelihood of subsequent positivity within teams. 

In other words, sustained problem-talk doesn't clarify; it only drains. 

It shifts the emotional tone of collaboration from constructive to cautious, from forward-looking to stuck.

The distinction between "problem talk" and "solution talk" has been explored in organisational coaching literature, where shifting the focus from problems to solutions is seen as essential for progress. 

Conversations dominated by solution talk tend to be future-oriented, resource-focused, and marked by mutual respect. 

Problem talk, by contrast, keeps teams anchored in the past and in blame.

What makes the problem-only engineer so difficult is that they're not wrong; they're just incomplete. 

Problem identification is valuable. 

But value creation happens at the intersection of problem awareness and solution generation.

The most effective engineers I've worked with don't spend less time on problems; they spend different time. 

They diagnose, then design. 

They critique, then construct. 

They understand that identifying a flaw without offering a fix isn't rigour; it's inertia.

If you recognise yourself in this description, consider this: your problem-finding skills are a gift. 

But gifts are meant to be given. 

Pair every problem you surface with at least one possible solution. 

Frame every challenge with a "what if we tried..." 

Your team doesn't need more problems named. 

They need more problems solved.

#EngineeringManagement #Leadership #ProblemSolving #TeamDynamics #TechLeadership

Over the years, I've swung between two extremes in Jira and other task tools:

📄 Overdocumenting – writing so much detail that the task drowned in its own clarity.

✏️ Underdocumenting – writing so little that even I couldn't remember the why a week later.

Then it hit me. 

A task is not a novel. 

It's more like an order ticket at a restaurant.

The waiter scribbles on an order ticket: medium well steak, fries, side salad. 

Clear. Concise. Actionable.

That ticket goes to the kitchen, gets executed, and the meal lands on the table.

At the end of the day? They tally the totals, log the details, and throw the ticket away.

But here's the key twist: Jira tickets are not the meal; they're the bread crumbs.

The actual work happens elsewhere: in the codebase, in designs, in conversations. 

The ticket is metadata, a trace that points to the real thing. 

It should be clear enough for anyone skilled to grasp the context, the purpose, and the tasks at a glance.

It should not be a checklist or a novel, because nobody reads that. 

And it should never be mistaken for the work itself (a confusion I've seen mostly among non‑technical folks).

So today I work like this:

- Write just enough for execution, not for posterity.

- Link to the work, don't try to become it.

The goal isn't to build a knowledge base. 

It's to get things done.

The real skill? Knowing what to write and what to leave out.

Let the order ticket be your guide and remember, it's just the trail, not the destination. 🎫🔥

#Productivity #TaskManagement #Jira #WorkSmarter #ExecutionMatters 

P.S. Adding a picture from the labyrinth at Ekolsunds Slott. In a labyrinth, you don't map every stone; you identify unique markers. That's how I see Jira now: tickets are the markers we leave behind, guiding skilled hands toward the real work. The meal is cooked in the codebase, not in the ticket. D.S.

posts.text:
In 2015, I met waterfall development of the worst kind.

I was two years into my role as Technical Service Manager, with dozens of integrations behind me, including some of our biggest customers. 

So when a new integration project kicked off, I assumed it would be routine.

It wasn't.

The customer’s project manager scheduled a “deep dive” with their architects. 

They combed through our documentation, asking questions I’d never heard before, like exactly how our responses would look if they sent a specific payload. 

I validated it in a test environment, sent it over, and the questions kept coming.

Architects finished writing requirements. 

Developers started coding, and had their own questions. 

Testers took over, and had even more. 

And whenever something didn’t match our docs or their assumptions, we circled back for another round of deep dives.

We eventually delivered. 

Successfully.

But it took much longer than a standard integration. 

And the quality? No better. 

Just more handoffs, more documentation, and more meetings.

That project succeeded despite the process, not because of it.

Waterfall doesn’t prevent errors, it just delays their discovery. 

It turns every ambiguity into a crisis, and every question into a month-long loop. 

Meanwhile, agile teams start building with the docs they have, surface gaps early, and adapt in days, not weeks.

This thought me that the real cost of waterfall isn’t time, it’s the illusion that you can design all the answers before you’ve asked the right questions.

Anyone who thinks software engineering is ‘going away’ doesn’t understand the job. Kent Beck, XP and TDD creator, on why Dario has it wrong: 

[Gergely: Dario said, I quote, ‘coding is going away first, then all of software engineering’. ]

“My response is, that's a statement by someone who doesn't understand software engineering. Coding is part of what you're doing, but it's only a small part of what you're doing, even if it takes up a fair amount of time. 

You're building confidence, you're building connections with other people, you’re building your own understanding. All those things are happening while you're coding. And coding's actually a great way to cement understanding. The more you program, the more you understand the domain that you're working in. And so to say, well, we're just going to pass all that off to a machine. Well, that's not all there is to it.

A couple of days ago I saw a phrase, and it really hit me, that we're accumulating code faster than we're accumulating trust now. And that sense of trust comes from me struggling to understand some domain concept, ah, I get it! I represented it in the code. I write tests that demonstrate that I really did understand it and now, I trust my program. If we're programming together, that act of programming together means that we trust each other more. 

And none of that can be automated. None of that occurs. If we prompt, we get the finger guns, the genie goes, yeah, it's all finished, boss. And it is like, well, hang on, finished. What's finished?”

Nothing beats trading laptops for the Stockholm archipelago! 🌊🛥️

Yesterday, one of my teams headed out from Strandvägen to Fjäderholmarna for an afternoon of connection, reflection, and great energy.

From 10s of thousands of people to under a thousand; what's the biggest difference?

Decision velocity.

In a large enterprise, in my experience, decisions were a marathon: committees, governance bodies, layers of approval, rinse and repeat. 

You knew speed was a fantasy, so you juggled multiple initiatives at once, hoping parallel processing would offset the glacial pace.

In the smaller company? 

It's a different game entirely:

- Fewer people at the table
- Faster calls
- Radical transparency on how and why decisions are made

The science backs this up:

- Decision delays compound significantly with each additional organizational layer (MIT CISR, 2023)

- Structural complexity in large firms systematically erodes decision effectiveness (Journal of Organizational Behavior, 2020)

- Pushing decision rights to frontline teams dramatically improves organizational responsiveness (Review of Managerial Science)

The result? 

Better outcomes with fewer, more focused and motivated people.

Scale can be an asset, or a liability. 

The real differentiator isn't headcount. 

It's how close decisions sit to the action.

Because while the suit traditionally signals the seriousness of a decision, the real signal is how swiftly you make it. D.S.

AI is making it easier to produce more code. But are we really more productive? 

For decades, companies have tried to measure developer productivity through visible activity: lines of code, commits, pull requests, story points, features shipped, and now even tokens spent.

These metrics are not meaningless. They can be useful in specific contexts. But they are weak proxies for the thing we actually care about: value creation.

The classic mistake was applying factory thinking to software. More units produced meant higher productivity. But in product development, this logic breaks down because we do not know in advance which ideas will work.

A team can ship many features and create little value. Another team can ship less, but solve a more important customer problem and move the business forward.

Worse, optimizing for output can generate very nasty effects: perverse incentives, misalignment, siloning, product bloat, high-work-in-progress.

Optimizing for output is a clear anti-pattern. We seem to be repeating it with AI. 

Instead of trying to measure dev productivity we should ask: “What outcomes are our teams accountable for, and how well are we progressing toward them?”

Development speed matters. Engineering health matters. Flow metrics, quality metrics, and delivery metrics can all help diagnose problems. But they should play a supporting role. 

The main character should be business and user value.

To learn how to bring the right dev metrics to your company, see my latest article: https://lnkd.in/egrkJ7F2

I can't help but read these ideas of software factories powered by "AI" as a remix of the existing software development lifecycle.

Today, most code is generated by a compiler, or abstracted away behind a library or framework. Low-code platforms take this to another level, but with far less flexibility. Nonetheless, you have the ability to describe an application at a very high level.

A mature software development team leverages CI/CD pipelines, which takes our syntax, and in the case of something like gRPC, a definition of our communication protocol, and generate a working application. Additional CI/CD steps provide guardrails to ensure the software meets our company standards, and in some cases takes care of the entire deployment and release process end to end. This can be done with a few configuration files depending on the target platform.

I’ll admit, it takes time to get this process dialed in, but once you do, it feels like you have a software factory that enables developers to focus on high level logic expressed in code or some other manifest, and get running software on the other side.

Maybe "AI" agents makes this process easier, but the fundamentals seem roughly the same, but with the added cost of burning tokens for parts of the process that should be easily reproducible, and executable on commodity hardware.

AI was supposed to be the great equalizer for product orgs. The data says the opposite.

In our State of AI in Product 2026 survey (Product Institute x Product Circle), this was the most uncomfortable finding for anyone hoping AI would help them catch up to the leaders.

Organizations with mature operating models are 1.7 times more likely to say AI is strengthening them, and three times less likely to say it is making things worse. The companies that were already well run are pulling further ahead, not closer.

Here is why. AI does not install judgment. It amplifies whatever system it lands in. Drop it into an org with clear decision rights, sharp metrics, and real prioritization, and all of that gets faster. Drop it into an org where nobody agrees on what matters, and it just helps you produce the wrong things at scale.

Whatever your operating model was before AI, AI just gave you more of it.

That is what the tooling conversation keeps missing. Buying another AI tool while your operating model is shaky is the most expensive mistake I see leaders make right now. You are paying to accelerate a system that was not ready to go faster.

Denise Tilles and I wrote Product Operations because that underlying system is the thing almost nobody invests in until it breaks. AI just moved up the timeline.

If your AI results are underwhelming, the problem is probably not the AI.

Where would more speed actually help your org, and where would it just help you make mistakes faster?

Many analysts are puzzled (if not shocked) by the apparent irrationality of the stock market: 

- A company with $18.7 billion in annual revenue and a net loss of $4.94 should not be worth $2.43 trillion dollars.  

- Markets should not be strongly rallying while a war that is hampering global energy supply and driving inflation is raging on. 

Still, here we are. 

The thing is, we are suckers for a good story:

- AI  is a magic technology that will 100x productivity 
- SpaceX is a sure thing because it’s both about AI and “becoming a space faring species”
- Elon Musk is a once-in-generation genius. Every company he runs is efficient and widely successful. 

You can see similar irrationality all around us. People are voting for leaders who are obviously bad for them. Companies are making decisions (like broad AI mandates) that hurt their bottom lines. Baseless conspiracy theories run rampant on social media, mainstream news, and even some parts of academia, NGOs, and government. 

We believe we are more rational than our parents and grandparents, but there are signs the trend runs in the opposite direction.

A 2021 study "The rise and fall of rationality in language" by Marten Scheffer and his colleagues (link in comments) analyzed millions of texts from 1850 to 2019 and identified a profound shift in how we communicate:
- For over a century, the use of rational, fact-based vocabulary steadily increased while emotion-laden language declined
- This pattern abruptly reversed in the 1980s. Since then, emotional and individualistic words (such as "I" rather than "we") have increasingly dominated written media
- The trend sharply accelerated around 2007—a phenomenon the researchers attribute to the explosion of social media and the dawn of the "post-truth" era. 

This may explain what we’re seeing today. What I feel is more important than what is true. Emotions such as FOMO govern decisions. 

Politicians, business leaders, and influencers (some people are all three) understand we can’t resist a good, emotional narrative. They use this to their advantage. Pushing our buttons, motivating us to do what they want. 

What’s the solution? I honestly don’t know. Leave a comment if you do.

X: You seems negative about using LLMs to code.

Me: Quite the contrary, I'm positive about using LLMs to code small deterministic tools that can be verified.

X: What about entire systems?

Me: Ah … as a replacement for software developers?

X: Yes.

Me: LLMs conflate output with judgment and coherence with truth. You're correct, it can produce code output. What it cannot reliably do is exercise the judgment about whether that output is correct, appropriate, safe, maintainable, or even solving the right problem. It does not have the ability to search for and find the right question to ask. All it can give you is a coherent answer to what is asked. 

In software development, the output is usually the easy part once the right question and visualisation is found. The judgment needed in the search for the right question is where the actual value is.  Alas, the more plausible and coherent these LLMs become, the more dangerous that chasm becomes.

So, the output might be impressive but what we're lacking is the judgment, accountability and accumulated expertise needed. Those companies that have been replacing engineers wholesale with AI tools are likely to discover this the hard way through epistemic debt. Again this won't happen immediately, there will be early successes, but when systems fail in subtle ways they will have none of the expertise or accumulated knowledge of the system required to diagnose the problem. 

X: But AIs are getting better!

Me: Alas, that's not the issue. The problem is the practices have not yet co-evolved to safely manage these environments. We don't even have the mechanisms to capture the accumulated knowledge that is required. Yes, there are single examples and claims of how to do it, but the practices are far from converging on a norm. That's not to say they won't in the future but that is a question of adaptation rather than adoption. 

X: Explain?

Me: Yes, you can adopt this technology but we're not in a position to adapt to it safely. 

X: When will that happen?

Me: As I said back around 2019 (see attached), it'll take years for the practices to co-evolve. At which point it can start to enter the mainstream of enterprises and become seen as the norm.

X: When?

Me: I have no reason to change my view from back then, so I'll stick with 2029 onwards. It could even be as late as 2038 for conversational programming (or vibe coding or agentic engineering or whatever half arsed term or acronym we come up with) to truly shine. A lot depends upon individual actors actions, hence the broad range.

X: What do you think about the Mythos 5, Fable 5 models being shutdown to non US customers? Will this change things?

Me: No. And the US move is completely irrelevant as far as I am concerned. It's only exciting for people who confuse sovereignty with the idea of owning the entire chain combined with the assumption that the most powerful models will win. It's a good message for marketing purposes and IPOs but that's about all.

Still today one can hear that "cloud is just someone else's data center." 

That statement couldn't be further from the truth, and it’s usually the first sign that the ops team is being left behind in the transformation.

In my experience, developers are the easier win. They normally don't care where the application runs; they just want it to deploy and run fast, scale seamlessly, and be secure. The cloud delivers on all these. 

But the ops and infrastructure side? That’s where the real friction lives.

Let’s call it what it is, it’s a job protection impulse. 

There is a genuine fear that skills such as racking servers, managing SANs, patching hypervisors are becoming obsolete. 

The narrative of "the cloud is taking our jobs" is persistent but flawed.

Yes, the cloud abstracts the hardware. 

Yes, it changes the virtualization layer. 

But for the last 20 years, there has been a consistent need for cloud infrastructure engineering. 

Developers can spin up resources, but they rarely want to own the networking, the policy-as-code, the cost optimization, or the disaster recovery architecture. 

When they do touch it, they quickly hand it over to a team better equipped and more engaged in the operational heavy lifting.

So, How Do We Move from On-Prem to Cloud-Native?

It’s not a lift-and-shift of skills; it’s a lift-and-shift of mindset.

1. Develop Programming Chops: If you don’t have them yet, start now. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the lingua franca of the cloud. Terraform, Pulumi, or CDK are no longer "nice-to-haves"; they are the new terminal.

2. Do It Deliberately: There is no substitute for reps. Write IaC, deploy it, break it, fix it, and improve it. Iterate on your code base the same way a dev iterates on an application.

3. Avoid the 'ClickOps' Trap: Sure, you can build a VPC via the console. But if your mindset is stuck in the GUI, you are using the cloud suboptimally. The true strength of the cloud is that everything is an API call. Treating the cloud like a physical data center is the fastest way to lose the value proposition.

I have seen this work. When you embed a strong cloud practitioner with a team that has zero cloud experience, something beautiful happens. 

Given management focus, the skeptics start to see the speed, the repeatability, and the safety nets (like automated rollbacks) that the cloud provides.

But here is the cautionary tale: 

When management focus falters, the transformation fizzles. 

I’ve watched ambitious migrations turn into a trail of "bright spots"; isolated pockets of success that never scaled because leadership stopped illuminating the path forward.

Transformation is not a project; it’s a cultural commitment. 

It requires consistent supervision, visible leadership, and a willingness to retool your best talent rather than replace them.

Final thought: The cloud doesn't make ops obsolete. It makes ops strategic. 

#CloudTransformation #DevOps #InfrastructureAsCode #CloudOps #DigitalTransformation

AI just made it possible to build twice as much in half the time. For most teams, that is the worst thing that could happen to them.

I wrote Escaping the Build Trap because I kept seeing the same pattern. Companies measuring success by how much they ship, not by the value any of it creates. Features go out the door, the roadmap looks busy, everyone is moving, and the business barely changes.

That is the build trap. Mistaking output for outcome. Confusing motion for progress.

For years, the one thing that slowed the trap down was effort. Building was expensive, so teams had to be at least a little selective about what they built.

AI just removed that brake.

When shipping a feature costs almost nothing, the discipline of asking "should we build this at all" gets quietly skipped. Why argue about value when you can just build it and find out? So teams produce more, faster, and call it progress.

Our recent survey put numbers to it: the measurable wins from AI are landing where engineers build, not where customers feel it. The work got faster without getting wiser.

The teams that win the next few years will not be the ones that build the most with AI. They will be the ones that still know how to say no to the wrong work, now that building it is no longer the bottleneck.

The build trap was always a discipline problem dressed up as a speed problem. AI just raised the stakes.

What is one feature your team shipped this year that you would take back if you could?

For years, I lived the one-phone life.

One number. One device.

Work and life, all tangled up in my pocket.

Most of the time, my employer provided it.

Often, I could even bring my old number along to the new job.

Same number, new device, different bill-payer.

Seamless.

Then I joined a company where that wasn’t an option.

No bringing your number. A device so locked down it was practically useless outside working hours.

So, reluctantly, I did the two-phone thing.

Work device. Work number.

Personal device. Personal number.

At first, I hated it.

Two near-identical iPhones.

Twice the pockets. Twice the weight.

It felt like clutter, not clarity.

But something shifted.

The work phone became exactly that: for work.

Emails. Chats. Documents.

The personal phone? For everything that actually matters when the laptop closes.

And here’s the part I didn’t expect: the physical separation became mental freedom.

The work device now stays on my home desk when I’m off.

I don’t carry it around the clock.

I don’t hear it buzz during dinner.

I rarely glance at it on weekends “just in case.”

What started as an annoying compromise became one of the healthiest boundaries I’ve ever set.

I’ve since moved into a new company and chosen, deliberately, to keep that separation.

Two phones isn’t a burden anymore.

It’s a boundary.

And that boundary protects my peace far better than one device ever did.

Sometimes the “inconvenience” you didn’t choose is the work-life upgrade you didn’t know you needed.

I've been coding with the genie for a while. Here’s what I see. I ask for something, it hands me code, I take it. An hour later I'm deleting it, because what I accepted wasn't what I needed.

There's a story going around that this part is solved. Machines write the code now; people just review it. It arrives as a confident headline, with the caveats in small print.

Faros, a leading engineering operations platform, recently put out a new study on AI's real impact on output, and I've partnered with them to dig into it. They went and measured the small print: two years of telemetry, 22,000 developers. Surprise, output is up. So is the rest of it: code churn up ~860%, incidents per change up ~245%, bugs per developer up ~55%. They call the pattern the Acceleration Whiplash, and it isn't a developer problem. It's a system one.

Set that beside the claim that AI code is now on par with a human's. It isn't, not yet. Code that's genuinely as good as a careful person's doesn't get deleted at ten times the rate, or leave more bugs the harder you lean on it. The volume is real. So is the share of it that has to be redone and the rework, not the typing, is where the speed quietly goes.

So here's how I've come to understand it. The genie is a brilliant junior intern — fast, tireless, occasionally inspired, and in constant need of supervision. You don't hand an intern the keys to production and walk away. You give them a system to work inside, guardrails, and someone accountable for what ships. 

Which means your senior engineers matter more now, not less. Someone has to be the architect to own design and correctness, to decide what "good" means and hold the line. You can't outsource that to an LLM. It writes the code; it doesn't own whether the code is right. That part is still ours.

So no, software isn't solved. The typing got faster. The thinking didn't move.

Read more on their report here: https://fandf.co/49RpvNS

“You are the most qualified and competent candidate for this role. But we’re going with someone who projects better optics and navigates internal politics easier.”

A few years ago, I sat across from a hiring manager for an internal promotion and received more or less that exact feedback.

I expected the usual corporate platitudes. 

Instead, I got radical, unfiltered honesty. 

He openly admitted that my track record and skills were unmatched, but the organization’s culture required a politician, not a builder.

The manager thought they were delivering a disappointing blow.

Instead, I walked out of that room with a profound sense of clarity. 

I wasn’t defeated; I was liberated. 

It made me realize I was playing the wrong game in the wrong stadium.

“When optics supersede outcomes, theater replaces performance.”

When an organization begins to prize political maneuvering over actual competence, two things inevitably happen:

High performers exit. 

People who drive real value refuse to spend 50% of their day managing perceptions and kissing the right rings.

The culture rots from the top. 

You eventually end up with a leadership team of actors who know how to look busy, rather than leaders who know how to execute.

As the saying goes: “Culture eats strategy for breakfast.” 

But a culture of optics eats everything: innovation, morale, and ultimately, bottom-line results.

That interview was the ultimate wake-up call. 

It forced me to ask myself: Am I at a company that values what I do, or just how I look doing it?

To the leaders out there: If you choose optics over outcomes, don’t be surprised when your best people leave to build things elsewhere.

To the professionals: Don’t waste your career trying to fit into a culture that values the shadow more than the object. 

Find a place where your results speak louder than your politics!

X: Why are you so negative about AI?

Me: I'm not, quite the opposite. But as I've said many times before, it will take years for the practices to co-evolve. The key to the changes (as with the industrialisation of any technology) is not whether organisations adopt AI but how they adapt to it. That's when it really heads toward mainstream in a productive manner, think DevOps and cloud.

X: How many years?

Me: Back around 2018/19, I had the date pegged for 2029 onwards. See the column on conversational programming or what you now call [prompt engineering | vibe coding | agentic engineering | harness engineering | spec driven development | ...].

The practices are still emerging, hence we are still coming up with names for it and have no consistent flag. I've seen no reason to change my predictions. We are still in the "myths" phase.

X: Myths?

Me: As I said in Jan 2023, the myths will be strong including ...

1) You’ll need fewer engineers. Nope. See Jevon’s paradox. You’ll need to retrain to a new world but you’ll end up doing more stuff. 

2) It’ll reduce IT budgets. Nope. See Jevon’s paradox again. You’ll end up doing more stuff, more cost efficiently.

3) You have choice. Nope. See Red Queen Effect. This is only a question of “when” not “if”.

4) It’s only for startups. Nope. Startups have less past success and hence lower inertia barriers to change. Large enterprises will resist the change due to the pre-installed capital. Eventually, they will have no choice. See Red Queen Effect.

5) We can build our own. Nope. Well, technically you can but you’ll regret it. Doesn’t mean that won’t stop hordes of self interested vendors trying to persuade you to do so for reasons of “security”, “lock-in” and “customisation to your needs”.

6) I can make a more efficient application by hand crafting the code. Nope. I’d also suggest reading into Centaur Chess if you think even the most gifted engineer will outcompete an average engineer with an average AI.

7) It’ll be the death of DevOps / FinOps etc. Nope. Well, technically it will be but that takes a very long time. 

There's actually a long list of these.

X: What about building for reasons of sovereignty?

Me: Ok, that can be an interesting space but outside of China most of the sovereignty discussion appears next to useless and little is based upon any situational awareness of the technological and economic landscape. At best, if you're very lucky, you might get some graphs based upon SBOMs (better than nothing but far removed from where we need to be) however most of the time you're in a world of stories.

Record profits troubled by a ticking clock on customer loyalty.

The McKinsey 2026 Global Banking Annual Review is out, and the message for the industry is clear: 

Record performance in 2025 won't save you from disruption!

Here are the key takeaways every banking leader needs to know:


🚀 The Profit Paradox

While global net income hit a record $1.3 trillion in 2025, investors remain skeptical. 

Banking continues to have the lowest price-to-book and price-to-equity ratios of any industry, signaling that the market isn't buying into a long-term vision of continued growth.


⚠️ The Battle for the Customer

Customer primacy is at a tipping point, threatened by four major forces:

1.  Mature Fintechs: Now claiming 17% of industry revenues, up from 10% in 2021.

2.  Breakout Neobanks: Players like Revolut and Nubank are shattering the traditional growth/performance frontier with ROEs of 30–35%.

3. AI & Stablecoins: A "two-headed technological revolution" making it easier to bank without traditional banks.

4.  Shifted Trust: For the first time, leading fintechs are recording higher customer satisfaction and trust scores than traditional high-street banks.


⏱️ No More "Grace Periods"

In the past, banks could afford to be "smart followers" because older, high-value customers were slow to adopt digital. AI has changed the math. AI adoption is happening 7x faster than digital banking did, with young and old users piling in at nearly the same rate.


⚙️ The Solution: Precision with Speed

The era of broad-brush strategies is over. To survive, banks must evolve into multispeed organizations managing three distinct innovation tracks:

- Fast (Business-as-Usual): Focusing on core modernization and AI-enhanced operations.

- Faster (Incubator): Testing strategic plays like embedded finance and AI-enabled advisory.

- Fastest (Seed/R&D): High-risk, high-reward bets on autonomous finance and quantum computing.


The Bottom Line: 

Slowness used to be a feature of bank resilience; now, it's a fatal bug. 

The winners will be those who can maintain risk discipline while operating at the speed of light.

#GlobalBanking #Fintech #AI #FutureOfFinance #McKinsey #BankingStrategy

Just finished Nexus by Yuval Noah Harari, and I quite enjoyed it.

What I appreciated most was its setup: not a narrow AI alarm, but a sweeping historical exposé of human information networks stretching from oral traditions and sacred texts to bureaucracies, print, and now algorithms. 

Harari walks us through how societies evolved with each new network, then uses those patterns to search for clues about how we might fare in a not-too-distant AI-dominated future.

One thread I found surprisingly hopeful, amid all the warnings, was the discussion about the inherent unpredictability of AI models. 

Even in totalitarian settings, the argument goes, that very unpredictability can become a vulnerability for oppressors, potentially accelerating their collapse over time. A small but real glimmer.

Looking at the broader reception, it’s clear the book has sparked the kind of debate Harari intended. 

Many reviewers praise his ability to connect dots across millennia, turning Nexus into a kind of intellectual thriller that reframes everything from mythology to machine learning. 

Others point out that his treatment of technology sacrifices nuance for narrative force, but for me, that big-picture synthesis is exactly the point. 

This is not an engineering manual; it’s a story about power, trust, and what happens when the networks that hold society together begin thinking for themselves.

If you work anywhere near information, governance, or tech, it’s a read that will leave you chewing on questions long after you put it down. 

#Nexus #YuvalNoahHarari #BookReview #InformationNetworks #AI #FutureOfSociety #HistoryMatters

posts.text:
In 1984, Steve Jobs told Newsweek Access:

“The next stage is going to be computers as ‘agents’… as if there’s a little person inside that box who starts to anticipate what you want.” 

He thought it would take 5–10 years. It took 40, and LLMs.

A decade later, Jobs explained object-oriented programming to Rolling Stone:

“Objects are like people… They have knowledge inside them about how to do things and have memory… We interact at a very high level of abstraction. That’s what objects are. They encapsulate complexity.”

His NeXT Computer (1985–1997) built an entire operating system, NeXTSTEP, around this metaphor; reusable, independent objects communicating through clean interfaces. 

Tim Berners-Lee used a NeXT machine to invent the web. 

Looking back, Jobs wasn’t just describing software objects. 

He was sketching the philosophical arc of our industry in a 40-year dialogue about how to encapsulate complexity, distribute intelligence, and interact at ever higher levels of abstraction.

That dialogue has a rhythm.

The monolith era embodied a kind of stoicism. All logic lived in-memory, interfaces were clean, and conversations were minimal. 

Then containers arrived, and we swung the other way. The monolith shattered into microservices. What was once a single, silent mind became a buzzing society of chatty specialists. We traded central control for distributed orchestration.

Now the pendulum is moving again. 

We’re decomposing microservices into autonomous agents; smaller, smarter, goal-directed. The pitch calls them “digital workers.” 

Developers see something more familiar: functions and classes with an LLM orchestrating them. 

The underlying question hasn’t changed since Jobs spoke it aloud: how small can a unit of intelligence be before the conversation becomes the cost?

This is where three of the best minds in software offer a framing that helps us understand the moment.

Martin Fowler gave us the vocabulary for microservices, but his deeper contribution is a law of distributed design: every boundary carries a price in latency, complexity, and failure modes. 

He’s not saying “don’t distribute”, he’s asking us to weigh whether the autonomy gained is worth the coordination tax. 

Agents take that question to its logical extreme. They’re not just distributed. They negotiate.

(Continued in comments.)

#AIAgents #Microservices #SoftwareArchitecture #SteveJobs #MartinFowler #SamNewman #KentBeck #AgenticAI

I’ve heard the same question for nearly a decade:

“Will we have to change how we work?”

It usually comes from the teams closest to traditional IT when there is strong push for going to cloud. 

I’ve always sympathised. 

But pretending things won’t change when you move to cloud is dishonest, hollow, and visible from a mile away.

The honest answer? 

Things will change. 

You should change with them.

- Storage becomes a SaaS with three or four nines SLA. No storage tech management. Just engineers setting lifecycle policies, defaults, and org guardrails.

- Networking moves from ClickOps and hardware switches to software, infrastructure as code, APIs, self-service, pull requests.

- VM fleets get patched through a control plane that actually lives in a cloud-native context; not a lift‑and‑shift illusion that realises zero benefits.

Plenty of work still exists for skilled on‑prem engineers. 

It just demands a mindset shift and a knowledge journey.

Proof? 

One of my former cloud engineers came in with deep sysadmin chops but zero IaC or CI/CD experience. 

Within months of focused and dedicated learning, he didn’t just catch up; he became the team’s go‑to in both old and new domains.

Where there’s a will, persistence, and management that actually supports and trusts its people, there’s a way. 

That’s not a platitude, it’s exactly how engineers move from on‑prem to cloud and thrive.

Bet on your people. Be honest about the change. They may very well surprise you.

posts.text:
In a previous company, I pondered over a particular metric:

The per-unit cost of a provisioned but unused sandbox project.

A provisioned but unused sandbox cost €3/month just standing there doing absolutely nothing, with all pre-provisioned resources idling. 

Nothing that breaks the bank, literally, but many drops make an ocean. 

So, we made sure to lifecycle the sandboxes  aggressively.

That €3 idle project is a micro-example of a massive macro-problem. 

When migrating applications to the cloud, most leadership teams obsess over one scary number: Total Monthly Spend. 

But total spend is a vanity metric without context. 

If you want a truly successful migration, you have to shift your focus to Cloud Unit Economics; breaking down your cloud bill into per-unit costs.

Moving to the cloud shifts IT from a fixed cost (CapEx) to a variable cost (OpEx). 

If you don't calculate your per-unit cost before and during a migration, you are essentially driving a car without a fuel gauge.

Here is why calculating per-unit cost is absolutely critical for your migration strategy:

- It Links Tech Spend to Business Value
Traditional IT looks at the aggregate infrastructure bill. Cloud Unit Economics looks at business outcomes. Instead of saying "Our cloud bill is €20,000," you want to be able to say "It costs us €0.05 per active user" or "€1.20 per processed order." If your total bill doubles but your user base triples, your per-unit cost actually went down. Without this metric, you might mistakenly view business growth as an IT failure.

- It Prevents "Sticker Shock"
The fastest way to blow the budget is the "lift-and-shift" trap. Directly copying over-provisioned, on-prem servers into cloud virtual machines results in massive, unexpected bills because idle resources still cost money. Knowing your unit costs early forces you to right-size your environment before cutting over.

- It Dictates Your Migration Strategy
Your per-unit cost estimate tells you how to migrate:

> High predicted unit cost? A simple rehosting won't work. You need to Refactor the application to use cloud-native services (like serverless or containers) to make it financially viable.

> Low predicted unit cost? A faster, cheaper migration method (like Rehosting or Replatforming) is justified.

How to Get Started:

- Define your "Unit": Identify the primary business driver (e.g., per "standard" app, per API call, per active user, per terabyte streamed).

- Tag Everything: Implement a strict cloud tagging strategy during migration so every resource is mapped to a specific feature, team, or application.

- Build a FinOps Culture: Get engineering, finance, and product teams talking to each other. When engineers understand that an idle sandbox costs €3/month, they build better automated cleanup habits.

Stop measuring just the cost of the cloud. 

Start measuring the cost of value.

#CloudMigration #FinOps #CloudEconomics #CloudComputing #TechLeadership #AWS #Azure #GoogleCloud

posts.text:
Remember the "throw it over the wall" era?

Devs shipped artefacts on a Friday, Ops prayed, and the first fix was always “try restarting it.”

When that didn’t work, a brave DBA would hotfix a stored procedure straight into production.

A network engineer would punch a new firewall rule.

Those temporary fixes became permanent; the technical debt many companies are still unpicking today.

And who can forget the Friday 5pm escalation?

A NOC technician, exhausted, trying to decode errors they never had the context or training to understand.

Hero culture was at its peak.

And yet, software reliability was rock bottom.

Then came “You build it, you run it.”

Ownership became clear. Dev teams welcome in production.

First responders in support and NOC triaging signals, armed with well-rehearsed playbooks for known issues, and for everything else, their job becomes pulling in the right people, unblocking, and communicating.

No more cowboy fixes born from desperation.

But here’s what I’ve learned over the years: getting to that ideal state is anything but simple.

Ops engineers often miss the adrenaline of fixing production live; the hero aura is addictive.

Devs, on the other hand, might lack sufficient infrastructure context to isolate a problem quickly.

The best outcomes I’ve seen firsthand?

When you put both perspectives in the same room – Ops and Dev complementing each other, playing to each other’s strengths.

Ops brings the systems thinking and battle scars.

Dev brings code-level mastery.

Together you move from firefighting to genuine resilience.

Modern practices make this even stronger:

- Blameless postmortems that treat every incident as a learning opportunity, not a witch hunt.

- Observability instead of guesswork – dashboards that give everyone the same context.

- Chaos engineering to test systems, not luck.

- Shift-left security and reliability so fixes happen in design, not in panic.

The old world celebrated the lone hero.

The new world celebrates the team that builds systems so boringly reliable, there’s no need for heroics.

But we still need the Ops instinct that knows when something’s off, married with the Dev’s ability to fix it for good.

#DevOps #YouBuildItYouRunIt #SRE #PlatformEngineering #TechCulture

Here's my new write-up on engineering ideas I use in the skills: https://lnkd.in/gF5JjA67

This is the reality of agentic coding right now: A senior engineer's job is mostly the parts that don't show up in the diff. Specs. Tests. Reviews. Scope discipline. Refusing to ship what can't be verified.

By default, AI coding agents skip all of those parts.

They take the shortest path to "done." Ask for a feature, and it writes the feature. It doesn't ask for a spec or write a failing test first. It produces code, declares victory, and moves on - the exact same failure mode every senior engineer has spent their career learning to avoid.

Agent Skills is my attempt to bolt that senior-engineer scaffolding back onto the AI. It's a system to make those invisible, critical steps non-negotiable.

I wrote a new post detailing the design choices behind the project, how it maps to Google's published engineering practices, and what you can steal from it for your own teams (even if you never install a single skill).

A few core principles:

1. Process over prose: Workflows are agent-actionable

2. Anti-rationalization tables: Pre-written rebuttals to the lies agents (and tired engineers) tell themselves to skip best practices ("I'll write tests later").

3. Verification is non-negotiable: Every task must terminate in concrete evidence. "Seems right" is never enough.

4. Scope discipline: The single biggest determinant of whether an agent's PR is mergeable. Touch only what you're asked to touch.

AI agents are extremely capable junior engineers with no instinct for the invisible parts of the job. The senior-engineer parts are no longer optional, even when the engineer is a model.

#ai #programming #softwareengineering

Everyone blames the developers when cloud migrations stall. But there's a quieter, more stubborn bottleneck.

It’s easy to think cloud transformations get delayed or fail due to developers’ inability or difficulty to rearchitect their applications. 

That’s surely one reason – but one that’s not spoken about nearly enough is delays and failures caused by platform and infra teams’ inability to change their tech stack and tooling.

In a way, it’s almost as if going to the cloud is like being sent to a deserted island, and everyone gets to bring along one item they think they’ll need. 

The island is a big unknown – none has been there before, so all bets are off. 

And yet, there will be those who bring items of no or limited value in the new environment.

The CI/CD team may want to bring Jenkins.

The observability team, whatever tool was hot in the Gartner quadrant a couple of years ago and is finally working as intended on-prem.

The WAF team, whatever tool they know inside out.

The Linux team, whatever distro and control plane they’ve successfully run on-prem.

The security team, whatever tool their SOC is comfortable with.

Etcetera.

The point being: if everyone gets to bring their favourite item, the implementation timelines for cloud transformation will stretch infinitely – making it incredibly difficult to even get started with application rearchitecting, as long as the supporting infrastructure remains a big unknown.

🛑 The fix? Be ruthless with the old.

One way to solve it is to be very restrictive in bringing along old ways, old tools, and old processes. 

Only allow them when all cloud-native options have been truly exhausted, and the feature set being asked for is an absolute must for the majority of consuming teams.

Lift-and-shift your thinking before you ever touch a workload. The island doesn’t need Jenkins.

#cloudtransformation #platformengineering #cloudinfrastructure #aws #azure #gcp #cloudnative

Something has been nagging at me lately, and I finally wrote it down.

AI coding tools are genuinely exciting — I love that building is getting faster and cheaper. But I've noticed a pattern: the easier it becomes to build something, the less time we seem to spend asking whether we should.

Marty Cagan recently wrote about the distinction between building to learn and building to earn — and how as delivery costs drop, discovery becomes the real competitive advantage. I think that's exactly right. But I'd add that the same dynamic is playing out inside product teams too, not just in how companies structure their process.

The four big risks Cagan defines — value, usability, viability, feasibility — didn't go away. It's just getting easier to ignore three of them.

I wrote up my thinking in a short article. Curious whether this resonates with others in product right now.

👉 https://lnkd.in/dxfVidJ8

Marty's piece if you haven't read it: https://lnkd.in/dV-sCeGU

Somehow I was reminded of Trello yesterday. Some may remember it.

The last time I worked with it was 2005-2006. We used it to organise work tasks in our integration team. It was simple, easy, and gloriously uncluttered.

Then came Jira.

At first, it was only slightly more difficult. 

But over the years, across multiple teams and companies, a pattern emerged: feeding the Jira beast with ever more fields, metadata, and assorted bits and bobs at times felt more important than the work itself.

I’ve always pushed back hard on this. 

My stance: less is more. 

If you genuinely need metadata, collect it automatically - don’t force humans to fill in endless manual fields just to satisfy some process fetish.

Here’s the ironic twist. 

All those years of customising the Jira Data Center version beyond recognition, straying far from Atlassian standards, have now made migrating to Atlassian Cloud an absolute nightmare. 

I’m seeing ads for “Jira migration projects”, probably spanning months, even years, with dedicated teams and hefty budgets. 

The very customisations that were meant to optimise work are now the reason organisations are stuck in expensive, drawn-out modernisation efforts. 

They effectively built their own cage and locked the door.

Moral of the story, one I live by: Keep it simple.

Tool bloat is a silent productivity killer. 

The moment your workflow tool demands more attention than the work itself, you’ve lost the plot. 

Process is there to serve people, not the other way around.

Before you add that next custom field, ask yourself: Are we helping the work, or are we just feeding the beast?

#Jira #Atlassian #KISS #process #tools #Trello

On Day One, your model is essentially pre-trained on a vast corpus of past experience: previous jobs, case studies, subject deep dives and learnings, and the ghost of every question you ever fielded. 

The architecture is solid, but the weights are frozen in a semi-generic configuration. 

You sit in that first stand-up like a freshly loaded checkpoint: plenty of parameters, zero domain-specific fine-tuning.

The first week is all unsupervised learning. 

You lurk in Slack channels, scanning for co-occurrence patterns. 

Your internal tokenizer starts chunking the company’s acronyms and system names into manageable embeddings, a whole sub-lexicon that no public dataset ever prepped you for. 

You inference like mad. 

Sometimes you’re dead right, other times you hallucinate, and most times you’re somewhere in the middle.

Then comes the reinforcement learning from human feedback. 

You adjust the temperature dial daily. 

By week three, the new neural pathways are physically forming. 

The office floor plan, once a blur of non-Euclidean horror, has become a navigable latent space. 

Slowly but surely, you’re not just auto-regressing through the day; you’re generating value.

And yet, the true art isn’t just in the accuracy, it’s also in understanding the biases of the new world. 

Your fresh perspective is an adversarial sample that the system needs, a perturbation that might just push the whole model toward a better local minimum.

Which brings me, finally, to the pivot. 

There comes a moment in this beautiful, chaotic process of retraining oneself when you glance at the date and realize that today, the day you’ve truly started to feel the architecture of your new life humming, is 

May the Fourth. 

And in that instant, the metaphor expands and collapses into something cosmic: you’re not just a language model learning a new subject space; you’re a young padawan feeling the Force flow through unfamiliar corridors. 

That gut instinct you’re building? 

It’s not just pattern recognition; it’s the Force awakening. 

The temperature setting is your balance between the calm of Obi-Wan and the wild leap of a Skywalker.

So here’s to new learnings and new beginnings. 

Your model is updating, your midi-chlorians are multiplying, and the Fourth is most definitely with you. 

May your loss function keep decreasing, your hyperparameters stay tuned, and may the Fourth be with you, always!

#maythefourth #starwarsday #newbeginnings

📊 The 4 Paradoxes of AI Developer Productivity

- The "More Code, Less Software" Paradox

🧠 What we think: More AI-generated code = more features shipped.

📉 What data shows: CircleCI analyzed 28M CI workflows and found average throughput surged 59% YoY, but median main-branch throughput dropped 7%. Almost none of the feature-branch explosion reached production. Recovery times hit a 5-year high (72+ min). 

Source: CircleCI 2026 State of Software Delivery Report

- The "Faster to Write, Longer to Review" Paradox

🧠 What we think: AI saves hours per week on coding tasks.

📉 What data shows: Faros AI found that for every PR merged with AI, code review time increased 91%. The time saved writing code is completely re-absorbed by auditing and verification. 

Source: Faros AI Engineering Report 2026 (10,000+ devs)

- The "47% More Workflows, Same Output" Paradox

🧠 What we think: More productivity activity = more business value delivered.

📉 What data shows: CircleCI found that even top-10% teams, ie running 47% more workflows, achieved essentially flat main-branch activity. Feature-branch throughput jumped 50%, but almost none translated into shipped changes. 

Source: CircleCI & Thoughtworks 2026

- The "84% Use It, 96% Don't Trust It" Paradox

🧠 What we think: Universal adoption means validated, reliable output.

📉 What data shows: Sonar's 2025 State of Code survey found 72% of developers use AI tools daily, estimating 42% of committed code is AI-generated, yet 96% don't fully trust AI output. DORA reports 30% explicitly distrust AI-generated code. 

Source: Sonar 2025 & Google DORA 2025


AI isn't the problem. 

Treating it as a coding shortcut instead of a systems challenge is.


Sources for further reading:

1. CircleCI 2026 State of Software Delivery - 28 million CI workflow analysis showing throughput-up-shipment-down paradox: https://lnkd.in/dQv3m-Rd

2. Thoughtworks' breakdown of the CircleCI report, Martin Fowler's team explains why the bottleneck moved and how to respond: https://lnkd.in/dVdWy_i2

3. Faros AI Engineering Report 2026 - 22,000+ engineers reveal review time up 91%, incidents more than double: https://lnkd.in/dW9E7CuB

4. Google DORA 2025 Report - AI amplifies both strengths and dysfunctions; throughput improves while stability deteriorates: https://lnkd.in/d-Kpx_U3

5. Sonar 2025 State of Code - 42% of committed code is AI-assisted, 96% of devs don't fully trust AI output: https://lnkd.in/dYYWZxY6

In spring 2022, a small group of us from SEB’s cloud transformation visited Spotify’s headquarters to learn how they do FinOps at scale. 

We came away impressed, inspired – and I left with one line I’ve never forgotten.

Our host, Anders Hagman, and his team showed us how they practiced FinOps across thousands of engineers, with all workloads in the cloud. 

One thing was particularly surprising though! 

They weren’t (only) counting stacks of dollars or euros saved. 

Instead, they translated their optimisations and savings into the number of new colleagues Spotify could hire as a direct consequence of their work.

I found that extremely human-centric, and deeply aspirational.

The reasoning was simple: 

Spotify’s primary growth constraint (at the time) wasn’t technology – it was an insufficient number of skilled, talented people, in turn limited by financial constraints. 

By reframing cloud savings into people they could now afford to bring on board, FinOps became instantly relatable. 

Not a spreadsheet exercise. 

A talent multiplier.

Fast forward to today. 

Our world is now dominated by AI models, tokens and prompts. 

Cost per 1k tokens, GPU utilisation, inference vs. training spend – the metrics have become less human centric. 

And I wonder:

Is there now a similar ambition to save in on unnecessary Cloud and AI costs voiced at Spotify, or anywhere else, so that more colleagues can be brought onboard? 

Or does that phrasing belong to a time that has gone by?

In an era obsessed with unit economics of intelligence, maybe the most powerful FinOps metric is still the one Anders left with me four years ago: 

How many more dreamers, builders and problem-solvers can we afford to hire because we optimise our Cloud and AI costs?

#FinOps #CloudOptimisation #AIOptimisation #HumanCentric #AI #Talent #EngineeringCulture

I’ve always been a fan of Uncle Bob’s teachings on what an architect should be, and I’ve always seen all my engineers as architects in their own right. 

An architect is not necessarily a job title but a state of mind and operation.

That mindset becomes even more crucial when you weave it into today’s AI developments. 

AI tools can churn out code at incredible speed, but the real architectural work, the thinking, the boundary drawing, the ownership of consequences, still belongs to the hands‑on developer. 

Here’s how that philosophy fits the AI era:

- AI amplifies the need for architectural judgement, it does not replace it. 

A developer who has stepped back from the code can’t tell whether an AI’s suggestion respects the system’s dependency rules or introduces hidden coupling. Only someone wiring in every day, feeling the friction, can sense when the design is drifting.

- The architect becomes the ultimate reviewer and integrity guard.
  
Bob Martin says architects must suffer the consequences of their choices. Now you have to suffer the AI’s choices too. That means reviewing, testing, and refactoring what the tool produces, so you don’t delegate understanding to a black box.

- Design intent must be expressed as living code.

The AI matches patterns; it doesn’t grasp the trade‑offs you’ve intentionally made. So you encode your architectural boundaries in tests, interfaces, and module structures that guide the tool’s output. That act of framing is pure architecture, and it demands hands‑on presence.

- The “architect as the strongest programmer” now includes AI literacy.

To lead by example, you must wield AI tools with the same discipline you’d apply to hand‑written code: prompt thoughtfully, reject anything you can’t explain, and never let generated code that you don’t understand into the codebase.

- The risk isn’t mediocre diagrams, it’s architectural erosion at machine speed.
  
Without a coding architect, a team leaning heavily on AI can fork from the intended design in days. Staying immersed means you spot the small divergences before they become a rewrite.

So if you already treat every engineer as an architect, then AI simply raises the stakes: the state of mind that insists on taking responsibility for the system’s structure is the only thing that stops the project from becoming a pile of plausible‑looking but incoherent pieces. 

That’s Uncle Bob’s philosophy in the AI age, the architect’s hands stay dirty, the whole team owns the design, and the tool stays a tool, never the decision‑maker.

#UncleBob #SoftwareArchitecture #CleanArchitecture #HandsOnArchitect #ArchitectsCode #AIandCoding #DeveloperMindset #ArchitectStateOfMind #CodeOwnership #AILiteracy #DesignIntegrity #EveryEngineerAnArchitect #CodingIsCraft #ResponsibleAI

posts.text:
X: SaaS is dead.

Me: Oh dear. I suppose your argument is it's quicker to build your own than use a SaaS?

X: Exactly. You disagree?

Me: There's a slight problem. 

X: ?

Me: SaaS was a marketing term.

X: Explain.

Me: Activities evolve from genesis to custom built to product to commodity. When we talk about services then they start to appear in custom built as timeshare, in product as rental and in commodity as utility services. SaaS was used as a catch all for all of these in the application space but timeshare, rental and utility are not the same. There are solid utility services out there. An easy example of this can be found in the infrastructure space with EC2 (compute as utility). In the software application space you have a mixed bag of some utility like services and then a whole bunch of things with providers who have not been industrialising and they've been exploiting ecosystems of consultants to customise. To be blunt, they've been pretending timeshare or rental models are utility models and they deserve to feel some pain. So, some SaaS is dead but that is not the same as all SaaS is dead.

X: How can I tell the difference?

Me: Try the cheat sheet, attached.

X: Why don't I just get an AI to build it all for me?

Me: There's no point in rebuilding highly industrialised utility services unless you are a glutton for punishment. Sure, there are lots of monstrous deathstar projects out there which are faking it by trying to be the platform for everything and are far from tightly defined utility services. Personally, I'd spend 30 minutes or so mapping out the space and then use that to determine what utility services you can use and where you might legitimately want to rebuild.

X: Seems easier to just get an AI to build it all for me.

Me: Well, I suppose the good news is that some LLM/GPTs have even been spontaneously providing Wardley Maps in PRDs they create. In any case your LLM/GPT will recommend using some services (which are utility like) and not others because they have a bias towards whatever is the most common, well documented path for a given problem (a useful but imperfect proxy). If this continues, they might start doing the "thinking" for you. That's not a bad thing given you seem so keen not to spend 30 minutes on this.

X: So, SaaS is dead?

Me: Timeshare and rental models faking it as a utility with large consultant ecosystems might face some trouble ... yes. 

X: So, SaaS is dead?

Me: Why do I feel I might have a better conversation talking with your LLM/GPT?

X: I'm not interested in mapping stuff, I just want an answer!

Me: It's not binary. Ask your LLM/GPT ... oh, actually, don't bother. Just ask your "AI" to build your stuff and let it deal with the nuance.

X: So, I'm right? Let AI build it all, SaaS is dead?

Me: FFS. Sure, just when your LLM/GPT recommends using Vercel, SendGrid, Stripe and S3, just go along with it.

Over the years I’ve been back and forth on the need for prescriptive and opinionated CI/CD toolchains. 

I’ve seen both highly centralized and decentralized implementations across different companies, and I’ve come to view this as one of the more consequential, yet under-discussed, architectural decisions in platform engineering.

In my experience, highly centralized implementations raise the floor for all feature teams. 

They ensure build and deployment consistency while enabling governance and security at a scale that is otherwise impossible. 

When all company deployments go through a centrally managed CI/CD toolchain, getting metrics, implementing guardrails, and ensuring SBOM compliance is considerably easier than a free-for-all, "pick your own adventure" approach.

The obvious drawback? 

The team in charge of this central toolchain inevitably becomes the bottleneck for the few teams that legitimately need to move faster or operate outside the standard mold. 

It creates a tension between platform stability and edge-case velocity.

Now, when you flip the switch to a "build it yourself," componentized toolchain, providing pipeline examples as a North Star but no hard limitations on what a pipeline should do, you get a broad spectrum of outcomes. 

You’ll see some teams investing incredible time into elaborate, bespoke toolchains serving their very specific (and often self-perceived) needs. 

Meanwhile, others remain in the Continuous Delivery Stone Age, with hardly any build or deployment automation to speak of.

I have landed on the belief that the centralized approach works very well in small to midsized companies. 

However, sheer organizational entropy forces the decentralized approach at most big companies. 

This is a shame, because it leaves these large enterprises without the critical levers to enforce a continuous flow of functional, secure, and compliant software. 

When every team invents their own deployment wheel, you don't just lose efficiency, you lose the ability to measure system-wide health and, more critically, to patch a zero-day vulnerability across the estate in a matter of hours.

What I'm observing now is the emergence of a necessary third path: 

Opinionated Platforms with Paved Road Escape Hatches.

We can't pretend that a single YAML schema will satisfy both the front-end SPA team and the legacy mainframe integration team. 

The future of this isn't "choose one or the other." 

It's about providing a golden path that handles 90% of use cases (security scanning, attestation, artifact promotion) but allows the 10% of complex teams to bring their own execution environment, provided they conform to a standardized contract for observability and artifact signing.

The goal shouldn't be to make every pipeline identical. 

The goal should be to make every pipeline verifiable.

#DevOps #PlatformEngineering #CICD #SoftwareDelivery #TechStrategy #DeveloperExperience

If you’ve ever been in a team with internal customers, such as a platform engineering or infrastructure team, you probably know more than well the flip side of having an open Teams or Slack channel where customers can chat with you about their problems.

While the ambition is honourable, the effects are far from it.

These channels quickly become the go-to places for customers with random thoughts, issues, problems, and everything in between. 

Why bother looking information up on a wiki when it’s much easier to fire off a question? 

Sometimes without sufficient context at the start, requiring the chat conversation to drag on while the clock ticks.

There are also no statistical tools in chat services that can collect:

- The number of interactions.
- The types of interactions.
- The number of resolutions.
- The time from initiation to resolution.

So to summarise: while using chat as a support channel for internal customers is honourable, it comes with its drawbacks.

Switching over to only responding to customer requests through tickets is neither optimal. 

Tickets are often impersonal, requiring a lot of context to be provided for resolution, and overall fairly inefficient. 

On the other hand, the statistics are easily collectible.

Is now the time we’ll see a continuation of the chat as a support channel, but with AI bots taking over first-line inquiries while being trained on the team’s knowledge base articles, internal documentation, run- and playbooks?

Has anyone witnessed / used a bot, that goes beyond regular key word and pattern recognition and actually provides working solutions to customer issues?
