👉 How do you objectively assess the operational maturity of an infrastructure team?❓

There’s no single metric that perfectly reflects a team’s efficiency, reliability, and alignment with business objectives. 

However, several key metrics can provide strong indications of maturity. Some are well-known classics, while others are less common yet equally valuable:

1️⃣ Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Adoption
	•	Measures the proportion of infrastructure managed through code.
	•	Why it matters: Higher adoption ensures consistency, scalability, and reduced manual errors.

2️⃣ Automated Testing Coverage
	•	Evaluates how much of the infrastructure is tested automatically.
	•	Why it matters: Greater coverage catches issues early, leading to more reliable deployments.

3️⃣ Deployment Frequency
	•	Tracks how often the team releases new updates or features.
	•	Why it matters: High frequency signals agility and streamlined processes.

4️⃣ Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR)
	•	Measures the average time to restore services after an incident.
	•	Why it matters: Lower MTTR reflects robust incident response and recovery mechanisms.

5️⃣ Change Failure Rate
	•	Calculates the percentage of changes that result in failures requiring remediation.
	•	Why it matters: A low rate reflects effective change management and deployment quality.

6️⃣ Service Level Objectives (SLOs) Compliance
	•	Monitors adherence to defined performance and reliability targets.
	•	Why it matters: Consistent compliance demonstrates strong service management practices.

7️⃣ Incident Frequency and Severity
	•	Tracks the number and impact of incidents over time.
	•	Why it matters: A declining trend indicates improved stability and proactive issue management.

8️⃣ Operational Documentation Quality
	•	Assesses the comprehensiveness and accessibility of documentation.
	•	Why it matters: High-quality docs support efficient onboarding, troubleshooting, and scalability.

9️⃣ On-Call Metrics
	•	Evaluates the health and effectiveness of on-call practices, including response times and workload balance.
	•	Why it matters: Healthy on-call practices foster resilience and avoid burnout.

🔟 Continuous Improvement Initiatives
	•	Monitors the implementation of lessons learned from post-incident reviews and proactive process enhancements.
	•	Why it matters: A commitment to continuous improvement shows operational excellence.

👉 Did I miss any important metrics, or do these provide a fairly comprehensive reflection of an infrastructure team’s operational maturity? Let me know your thoughts!

Good to Great: Lessons Beyond Business

I recently finished Jim Collins’ classic Good to Great, and it struck me how its principles extend far beyond business - they apply to #life, #leadership, and #personalgrowth.

The book explores why some companies transition from mediocrity to excellence while others fail to sustain greatness. 

Collins distills this into actionable principles, many of which resonate on a deeply personal level:

1. The #Hedgehog Concept
Great companies (and individuals) thrive at the intersection of three things: what they are deeply passionate about, what they can be the best at, and what drives their economic (or life) engine. This applies to personal purpose too - when we align our #skills, #passions, and #opportunities, we position ourselves for meaningful #growth.

2. Level 5 Leadership
#Humility combined with fierce #resolve defines great leaders. This principle isn’t just about leading companies - it’s about showing up in every aspect of life with a servant’s heart and a relentless commitment to #excellence.

3. First Who, Then What
Collins emphasizes getting the #rightpeople “on the bus” before deciding the #direction. In life, this means surrounding yourself with people who share your values and uplift you, whether professionally or personally.

4. The #Flywheel Effect
Momentum builds from #consistent, #disciplined #effort. Success isn’t about one big leap; it’s about pushing the flywheel forward, one disciplined turn at a time. This idea encourages #patience and #persistence in achieving goals.

5. #Confront the Brutal #Facts
Greatness requires an unflinching commitment to #reality. Whether in #relationships, #careers, or personal #goals, honesty about challenges is the foundation of growth.

The brilliance of ”Good to Great” lies in its simplicity and universality. 

It’s a roadmap not only for building great companies but for leading a life of purpose, discipline, and impact.

Empowerment beats control every time.

Recently, I had the chance to listen to the audiobook of ”Flow Engineering” by Steve Pereira and Andrew Davis. 

While the narrator lacked a bit of energy, the content itself was compelling and insightful - a must-read (or listen) for anyone passionate about improving work systems and optimizing value streams.

Key Concepts Addressed:

1. Value Stream Thinking
Central to the book is the idea of understanding value streams - how work moves from ideation to delivery and where value is added (or lost) along the way.

“You can’t fix what you can’t see; mapping the flow of work reveals opportunities for change.”

2. Constraint Management
Drawing on principles from the Theory of Constraints, the book emphasizes identifying and addressing bottlenecks.

“Flow accelerates when constraints are removed, but only if they’re truly understood.

3. Systemic Improvement
Flow engineering rejects isolated fixes, advocating for end-to-end solutions that align with organizational goals. 

“Every improvement in isolation risks creating new bottlenecks elsewhere in the system.”

4. Continuous Feedback Loops
The importance of feedback at every stage cannot be overstated. By shortening feedback loops, teams can respond quickly to challenges.

“The faster you learn, the faster you grow - feedback is the engine of progress.”

5. Collaboration Across Silos
True flow requires breaking down silos. Teams must align on shared goals and engage in transparent communication.
	
“Flow thrives in an ecosystem of trust and collaboration.”

6. Flow Metrics
The book highlights metrics like lead time, cycle time, flow efficiency, and throughput as critical indicators of system health.

“What gets measured gets improved - provided it’s tied to outcomes, not output.”

7. Cultural Shifts
Adopting flow engineering is as much about mindset as it is about tools and processes. Organizations must embrace a culture of experimentation, learning, and adaptability.

“Flow begins with people - it’s the mindset, not the method, that drives transformation.”

My Key Takeaway: 

- Understand work as a system - map, measure, and improve it holistically.

A few memorable quotes:

“The path to flow begins with understanding how work flows - or doesn’t - through your system.”

“Flow is not a destination; it’s a journey of continuous learning and adaptation.”

Despite the narration not matching the energy of the ideas, the book’s message shone through. 

If you’re looking to improve how your team delivers value, this book offers a structured yet flexible approach to making work truly flow.

Have you read it? What resonated with you the most?

👉 Identity is the New Perimeter

With the rise of cloud adoption, remote work, and digital transformation, our systems and users have leapt outside of on-premise environments and tightly controlled networks.

Today, identity is the new perimeter.

This shift is more than a buzzword - it’s a major change in how we approach security. 

🔒 Why is identity critical?

- Cloud-first environments: In the cloud, access control begins and ends with identity. Role-Based Access, Multifactor Authentication (MFA), and Least Privilege principles are non-negotiable.

- Remote work: Employees need access to corporate systems from anywhere, but that access must be secure, regardless of location or device.

- Zero Trust principles: A user’s identity and its verification become the foundation of trust, replacing assumptions based on physical or network location.

🔑 What does “identity as the perimeter” mean in practice?

1️⃣ Identity and Access Management (IAM) becomes the backbone of security, ensuring only the right people have the right access at the right time.

2️⃣ Continuous validation: Trust is no longer permanent. Access is continuously monitored, and trust is repeatedly earned, not given.

3️⃣ Unified policies: Centralized identity systems provide a single source of truth for permissions and access, reducing the risk of misconfigurations.

💡 How can organizations get this right?

- Invest in robust IAM solutions integrated across your ecosystem.

- Enforce MFA for all users - no exceptions.

- Regularly audit and refine access policies, ensuring alignment with the principle of least privilege.

- Educate your teams on why identity security is critical, making them part of the solution.

As businesses transform, so must our approach to security. 

By prioritizing identity, we’re not just protecting systems - we’re protecting the trust our customers, employees, and partners place in us.

How is your organization adapting to this new reality?

On-premise infrastructure engineer skillsets aren’t directly transferable to public cloud environments due to differences in technology, mindset, and operational approaches:

1. Shift from Physical to Abstracted Resources
- On-Premise: Focus on physical servers, storage, and networking hardware, with hardware dependency still prevalent.
- Cloud: Resources are fully abstracted and accessed as scalable services.

2. Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
- On-Premise: Configuration is manual or relies on tools like Ansible or Puppet.
-Cloud: Requires expertise in IaC tools (e.g., Terraform, CloudFormation) to manage modular, version-controlled infrastructure.

3. Networking Complexity
- On-Premise: Static, hardware-defined networks with VLANs, firewalls, and physical switches.
- Cloud: Virtualized and dynamic networking (e.g., VPCs, load balancers, peering), requiring multi-region and shared-responsibility expertise.

4. Scalability and Elasticity
- On-Premise: Hardware provisioned for peak loads leads to under-utilization.
- Cloud: Engineers leverage autoscaling, monitoring, and cost optimization to match resource allocation to usage.

5. Security and Compliance
- On-Premise: Perimeter-based security relying on firewalls and physical isolation.
- Cloud: Identity-based access controls (IAM), encryption, and shared responsibility models across multi-tenant environments.

6. Service Consumption vs. Management
- On-Premise: Direct management of servers, databases, and storage systems.
- Cloud: Focus on managed services (e.g., Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage) with an emphasis on SLAs, API integrations, and platform-specific configurations.

7. Monitoring and Observability
- On-Premise: Monitoring with custom tools tied to physical infrastructure.
- Cloud: Requires use of platform-native tools (e.g., CloudWatch, Stackdriver) and an understanding of distributed logging and ephemeral environments.

8. Cost Management
- On-Premise: Fixed, upfront CapEx costs with minimal focus on resource optimization.
- Cloud: Pay-as-you-go OpEx requires cost monitoring, tagging strategies, and optimization tools like GCP Cost Management.

9. Cultural and Operational Shift
- On-Premise: Siloed roles for servers, storage, and networking.
- Cloud: Cross-functional collaboration (DevOps, SRE), automation-first culture, and CI/CD familiarity are critical.

10. Continuous Learning Curve
- On-Premise: Slower technology evolution.
- Cloud: Rapid changes in services and best practices require ongoing learning to remain relevant.

While foundational skills like Linux, scripting, and networking basics transfer, successful cloud engineers must embrace a service-oriented, automated, and cost-aware approach to thrive. 

Transformation from on-premise infrastructure engineer to cloud engineer is not easy or fast, but definitely possible and worthwhile.

I’ve shouldered many roles over the years, but one role in particular has been really useful regardless of where I worked. 

#Projectmanagement is a universally useful role that on surface seems easy, but takes a (work)lifetime to master.

Having been involved in numerous projects in different capacities alongside project management itself; I think I’ve learnt what mistakes to stay away from. 

1.	Poor #Communication
• Not clearly conveying goals, priorities, or expectations.
• Not actively listening to team members or stakeholders.
• Neglecting to provide timely updates, leaving the team in the dark.

2.	#Micromanagement
• Focusing excessively on minor details, undermining team autonomy.
• Distrusting team members’ abilities, leading to frustration and disengagement.

3.	Inability to #Prioritize
• Lacking clarity on project priorities, causing confusion and inefficiency.
• Overloading the team with conflicting tasks or shifting focus frequently.

4.	Avoidance of #Accountability
• Shifting blame to others when things go wrong.
• Not taking responsibility for decisions or project outcomes.
	
5.	#Inflexibility
• Refusing to adapt to changing circumstances or new information.
• Enforcing rigid processes even when they hinder progress.
	
6.	Poor #TimeManagement
• Missing deadlines or failing to set realistic timelines.
• Wasting time in unproductive meetings or irrelevant tasks.
	
7.	Lack of Empathy
• Ignoring team morale or individual challenges.
• Failing to recognize or celebrate team efforts and achievements.
	
8.	Weak Decision-Making
• Hesitating to make decisions, delaying progress.
• Making rash decisions without consulting the team or stakeholders.
	
9.	Inadequate #Planning
• Not defining clear objectives, deliverables, or success criteria.
• Neglecting risk assessment, leading to avoidable problems.
	
10.	Ineffective Conflict Management
• Avoiding addressing conflicts, allowing them to escalate.
• Favouring certain team members, creating resentment and division.
	
11.	#Overpromising
• Making unrealistic commitments to stakeholders, causing undue pressure on the team.
• Failing to manage stakeholder expectations effectively.
	
12.	Lack of Technical Understanding 
• Misunderstanding technical aspects of the project, leading to poor decisions.
• Failing to seek input from experts when necessary.

Effective project management requires continuous self-awareness and improvement to avoid these pitfalls.

Do you recognise some of the pitfalls and how do you stay clear?

#FoodforThought

Sometimes I hear:

“Well, this or that expert we engaged told us this or that, so we are doing exactly this or that.”

Great - but have you stopped to consider why you are doing it?

The truth is, the #expert you hire will always be influenced by the frames of reference set by those hiring them. Consciously or unconsciously, they will seek to satisfy those references and asks.

Most experts are engaged for their #skills and #objectivity, but many end up being #subjective—shaped by the #dynamics and #dominant voices at their client.

“As you ask, so shall you receive.”

Next time you engage an expert, try being more #inquisitive and less #prescriptive.

Peter Senge’s ”The Fifth Discipline: The Art and Practice of the Learning Organization” is a guide to building organizations that thrive on #continuouslearning, #innovation, and #adaptability. 

It freely mixes #systemsthinking, #personalgrowth, and #organizationaleffectiveness. 

👉Systems Thinking: The Fifth Discipline
- Central to the book is systems thinking, a holistic approach that helps organizations to see patterns, interdependencies, and underlying structures, rather than just reacting to events.

Key principles include:
- Interconnectedness: Recognizing that changes in one part of a system affect others.
- Root Cause Focus: Addressing deeper, systemic issues rather than reacting to symptoms.
- Feedback Loops: Understanding how actions generate responses that influence future outcomes.
- Long-Term View: Considering the delayed effects of decisions and avoiding short-term fixes that may create long-term problems.

In essence, systems thinking helps identify sustainable solutions by seeing the “big picture” and understanding the dynamic interplay within complex systems.

👉 The Other Four Disciplines

- Personal Mastery: Encourages individuals to continuously learn and grow, and align their personal goals with organizational objectives.

- Mental Models: Highlights the importance of recognizing and challenging internal assumptions and biases that shape our decision-making.

- Shared Vision: A compelling shared vision fosters commitment rather than compliance. Senge argues that great organizations thrive when people are united by a shared purpose.

- Team Learning: Teams that engage in open dialogue and collaboration make better decisions and adapt more effectively to change.

The author stresses that creating a learning organization is not just a technical challenge but a deeply human one. 

Leaders must cultivate curiosity, humility, and empathy to empower their teams.

👉 The Learning Organization
- Embraces change as an opportunity.
- Encourages innovation through curiosity and collaboration.
- Cultivates a culture of trust and openness.

These insights are as relevant today as they were when the book was first published in 1990.

The book provides a rare blend of theoretical depth and practical application. 

The author’s call for organizations to embrace long-term thinking, collective intelligence, and continuous learning feels both timely and timeless.

What breaks #microsegmentation in the Cloud as seen from a #googlecloud perspective? 

Microsegmentation relies on strict boundaries and fine-grained network controls to secure #workloads. 

When GCP projects (or tenants if you will) are treated as #trustboundaries, certain practices, misconfigurations, or architectural choices can break or weaken microsegmentation. 

Here are key factors that break microsegmentation:

1. Cross-Project Communication Without Zero-Trust Controls
- Using broad network ranges or overly permissive firewall rules between projects.
- Lack of mutual TLS (mTLS) or similar authentication/encryption mechanisms for inter-project traffic.
- Hardcoding IPs instead of relying on service discovery or identity-based access.

2. Shared Resources Without Clear Isolation
- Sharing VPCs, subnets, or networking components across projects.
- Using shared services (e.g., logging, monitoring, or APIs) without enforcing project-level access control policies.

3. Overly Permissive #IAM Roles or Policies
- Granting broad permissions like Editor or Owner across projects.
- Failing to implement #leastprivilege principles for service accounts, users, or resources that span multiple projects.

4. Dependency on Centralized Control Planes
- Relying on a single #controlplane for identity, policy enforcement, or management that spans multiple projects without project-specific isolation.

5. Lack of Application Identity Awareness
- Failing to implement workload identity (e.g., Google Cloud’s #WorkloadIdentity).
- Allowing service-to-service communication without verifying the identity of the caller.

6. Weak Enforcement of Organizational Policies
- Neglecting to define or enforce organization-level policies (e.g., using Google Cloud’s Organizational Policy Service to restrict inter-project dependencies).
- Allowing deviation from network or IAM standards across projects.

7. Hybrid Networking with On-Prem or External Cloud Environments
- Using #flatnetwork designs that mix cloud projects with on-prem or other clouds.
- Inconsistent application of segmentation policies between cloud and on-prem networks.

8. #Mismanagement of API Gateways and Service Mesh
- Exposing APIs or services globally instead of restricting them to trusted projects.
- Misconfigured service meshes (e.g., Istio) that allow unrestricted traffic between workloads in different projects.

9. #ShadowIT and Unregistered Resources
- Teams deploying cloud resources outside of sanctioned projects, bypassing central policies and trust boundaries.

Microsegmentation in the cloud demands strict adherence to trust boundaries and continuous policy enforcement. 

Breaking these boundaries leads to significant risks, such as lateral movement or data exfiltration.

Recently I got thinking of how a public cloud offering can be viewed as “monolithic” when considered through the lens of it’s integrated and tightly coupled architecture. 

Here’s more on this perspective:

Centralized Control

- Public Cloud providers like #AWS, #Azure, or #GoogleCloud operate as single entities consisting of a vast array of services. 

These services - storage, compute, networking, AI, and more - are all deeply integrated into a unified ecosystem. 

Managing individual services on a standalone basis is often much easier said than done. 

While some services offer enterprise grade control planes that work across multiple tenants, such as #Kubernetes or #databases, such services are still quite rare.

In fact, the one single, scalable way to standardise and manage an organisation’s (hopefully many) cloud tenants is by proving one or two common landing zone setups that are continually developed, maintained and released to the consuming teams. 

The #landingzone thus governs key aspects of all cloud environments, and aligns all cloud environments to an organisation’s standards, policies and best practices.

Opinionated Ecosystem

- Public cloud providers impose a set of conventions, practices, and APIs that users must adhere to. This “opinionated” design streamlines workflows but can limit flexibility, akin to a monolith where the “rules of the game” are predefined and inflexible. Deviating from these standards often creates friction.

- Switching providers or integrating non-cloud-native components might feel like attempting to “break apart” a monolith - however this is challenging and time-consuming, and end results are questionable at best.

All-or-Nothing Adoption

- Adopting a #publiccloudprovider frequently necessitates adopting it’s integrated services to unlock full functionality and performance. Much like a monolithic application, where you can’t easily swap out a single module, in public cloud, using alternatives outside the ecosystem often leads to suboptimal results or added complexity.

Scaling and Resource Management

- While public clouds offer “infinite scalability” in theory, scaling often requires navigating the tightly coupled nature of their services. For instance, a simple performance optimization in one service may ripple across dependent services due to their integration - mirroring challenges in scaling monolithic applications.

Single Point of Failure

- Despite undisputed and robust #SLAs, public cloud ecosystems remain centralized. A major outage in a region or a critical service can impact multiple interdependent systems and users, highlighting their “monolithic” nature at a macro level.

Conclusion 

While cloud platforms may resemble monolithic systems in some aspects, their benefits far outweigh the drawbacks for most organizations. 

The cloud provides a foundation for #scalability, #innovation, and #resilience that no other option can match.

🚧 The “hidden in plain sight” Cost of Team Dependencies in Software Development 🚧

Have you ever thought why your teams aren’t moving as fast as they could? 

If it’s not a skills gap or lack of effort - it is probably dependencies.

Analysis by Troy Magennis highlights a stark reality: 

As dependencies between teams increase, delivery speed decreases and uncertainty skyrockets.

As an example, if your team has 3 dependencies (other teams needed, approvals, etc), there is only a 1 in 8 chance of delivery on time.

In the same example, AT LEAST one dependency being delayed is 7 times MORE likely. 

The maths is simple and straightforward.

For every step of building something (dependencies), that step can be on-time or delayed. 

If we want to know the chance of each dependency being on-time, it will be 1 chance in n power of 2, ie 2 multiplied by itself n times (where n = number of dependencies).

🔍 The takeaway? 

When multiple teams are involved, delays are inevitable - because aligning priorities, schedules, and deliverables is a huge challenge. 

And worse, small issues compound into major bottlenecks.

✅ The solution? 

Minimize inter-team dependencies:

• Empower autonomous teams that own their domains end-to-end.

• Align priorities and workflows across teams when dependencies are unavoidable

• Focus on decoupled architectures that enable parallel workstreams.

Remember that speed isn’t about how fast a team works.

👉 Speed is about how well teams can collaborate without blocking each other!

I was recently spurred to give a brief lay of the land on how I see team work in an agile team. Not an all encompassing one but one focused particularly on certain roles on an agile team. Here it is, written in 10-15 mins and shared over Teams:

Anyone in the team is free and encouraged to create tickets. Those can be just ideas or more well thought out and aligned user stories. Sub tasks, tasks, user stories, epics etc

The PO goes over the tickets regularly and assigns priority and when in time things ideally should be done.

The PO, Tech Lead, Architect, SM regularly review tickets and make updates to increase readability, context, so that there is a mutual understanding in the team on the work to be done.

The PO ensures that priority and delivery is aligned with stakeholders ambitions and expectations.

The team regularly meets to track progress, remove impediments and look ahead at things that should be done next.

The team is all previously mentioned roles and of course the engineers.

SM facilitates these meetings, keeps participants focused on the purpose and meeting objectives.

To me all these roles play an important role in team’s success.

The PO is ultimately in charge of what gets delivered, when.

The SM is in charge to ensure that the team has the best chances of delivering on priorities, through setting a structure for team’s work, removing distractions and barriers and helping the team continuously improve their ways, their skills and their collaboration.

The architect/tech lead is ultimately responsible for ensuring that what the team is building is viable, scalable and as per best practice.

Now, none of the roles is set in stone and normally all of us move slightly into adjacent areas, at times as and when needed. 

It’s all perfectly natural and good as it teaches us about what different roles entail.

This is what I think it’s all about.

Marty Cagan’s Transformed offers a compelling guide on what it takes to build a truly product-driven company. 

Known for his work in Inspired and Empowered, in this book Cagan tackles the challenges companies face in adapting to a product-focused mindset.

His insights come from years of experience in Silicon Valley and consulting with tech companies globally.

👉 Empowered #ProductTeams
High-performing product organizations are led by empowered, autonomous product teams. These teams are responsible not only for building products but also for defining the right products to build, based on customer needs and market opportunities. This empowerment enables faster innovation, as teams can make critical decisions without extensive managerial oversight.

👉 Outcome-Oriented Approach
Rather than focusing on outputs (features and deliverables), Cagan argues for an outcome-oriented approach where teams are driven by metrics that reflect customer and business value. By aligning product goals with desired outcomes, organizations can ensure that their efforts directly contribute to strategic objectives.

👉 Customer-Centricity
Cagan’s approach to transformation revolves around understanding and prioritizing customer needs. He discusses the importance of continuous user research, experimentation, and validation, which help product teams stay aligned with real-world problems and create solutions that deliver real value.

👉 Effective Cross-Functional Collaboration
Effective product teams thrive on #collaboration across functions, particularly with engineering, design, and business stakeholders. Cagan explains how this collaboration eliminates silos, allows for a seamless exchange of ideas, and fosters alignment toward shared goals.

👉 Transforming Leadership
Leadership in a product-driven company is less about top-down control and more about guiding teams toward #autonomy. Leaders must provide clear strategic #direction, remove obstacles, and #empower teams to solve problems. Cagan highlights the role of product leaders as coaches who help teams build the capabilities and mindsets necessary to succeed.

👉 Prioritizing Product Discovery
Product #discovery - the process of identifying and validating ideas before they are built - is critical. Cagan emphasizes the value of spending time in discovery to avoid wasting resources on features or products that don’t meet customer needs or business goals. Discovery enables teams to experiment, learn, and iterate, leading to more effective and efficient product development.

Transformed by Marty Cagan complements and expands on themes from his previous books, Inspired and Empowered, and resonates with other product management and transformation books. 

While Inspired focuses on the fundamentals of building great products, and Empowered discusses the empowerment of product teams, Transformed dives into how organizations as a whole can adopt a product-driven mentality.

All in all, a good addition to Cagan’s book suite.

While out running today I got reminded of Forrest Brazeal’s wisdom/cleverness curve.

I got thinking of a 3rd dimension alongside wisdom and cleverness.

The 3rd dimension I got thinking of was cost. 

Think about it for a moment! 

When you use the cloud as a datacenter, the cost goes up 1-2 notches. 

You’re more or less moving all your 3rd party systems and tools as they are on premise into the cloud.

All of these 3rd party systems and tools need a solid supply of compute and storage to run, and they normally utilise only a fraction of cloud’s benefits. 

Better yet, all of on premise drawbacks and limitations are still around: tight coupling, perimeter centric security, flat networks, long lead times for both dev and ops etc. 

On the positive side, you don’t need to invest much in people upskilling or reskilling, as you are not drawing much synergies from any of the cloud services. 

And as you probably need to keep both on premise and cloud running in parallel for a while, you probably need to hire additional staff to support both. 

Gradually, you may leave on premise altogether but as you are still running the cloud as just another data center, there probably won’t be many cost synergies. 

Going on to the 2nd option, building on trusted cloud native service, the cost initially goes up while running in parallell on premise and in cloud, and over time goes down, as migration completes. 

Here the main investment is on reskilling and upskilling your staff to take advantage of cloud’s capabilities and not to carry over on premise systems, tools and practices unless absolutely necessary.

Cost wise, this option over time is a zero sum game. If cloud migration is executed sensibly, you don’t have to hire additional staff but you need to be superfocused on reskilling and upskilling your current staff. 

And although the cost initially increases when migration commences, if cloud is used to it’s advantages by a skilled and competent staff, over time the cost goes down, even below previous on premise levels. 

And as of the 3rd option, this is probably the most expensive of all. 

You will need to hire highly skilled staff, normally the kind that don’t join any regular enterprise for less than a fortune and then you need to bankroll all the RnD needed in writing your own “cloud-agnostic” tooling. 

The benefits, scalability and long term sustainability are questionable at best.

To summarise, with a 3rd cost dimension, below curve becomes inverted with the cost being the cheapest when using the cloud native services, and that’s without mentioning all the other benefits of the #cloudnative approach!

What is the price premium you’re willing to spend on additional features in a system or a tool, that are only sparingly, if ever, used? 

Most would say that they’d focus on buying the most cost effective, most bang for the buck alternative, but reality is that features sell, regardless if they are used or not.

There are many different metrics in the IT field but in my experience, there are 2 key measurements of a modern infrastructure capable of running a modern application stack:


1️⃣ Percentage of production infrastructure defined as Infrastructure as Code (#IaC):

Goal: Strive for close to 100% of production infrastructure to be defined as IaC.

Rationale: Managing infrastructure as code allows for better version control, auditability, and repeatability, improving stability and reducing configuration drift.

Key Metrics: The percentage of infrastructure deployed and managed via IaC tools like #Terraform or Ansible, compared to manually configured or legacy infrastructure.


2️⃣ Percentage of applications delivered to production using CI/CD:

Goal: Target 100% of production applications being deployed through fully #automated CI/CD #pipelines.

Rationale: CI/CD ensures that applications are continuously #tested, #integrated, and #deployed, reducing manual intervention, speeding up #deployments, and lowering the risk of errors in production.

Key Metrics: The percentage of applications that are released to production via a standardized CI/CD pipeline versus those deployed manually or with ad hoc scripts.


These two success measurements not only drive operational efficiency but also ensure #scalability, #reliability, and faster time-to-market for applications in a modern infrastructure setup. 

They offer a clear path toward #automation, #stability, and overall system #integrity in both infrastructure management and software delivery.

And although they may seem very natural, I don’t know of many companies that actually measure these? Do you?

Tuesday food for thought:

If you are an “agile person” focused on output over outcomes, individual roles and responsibilities over working as a team, helping out where needed and just getting things done, strict process and framework adherence over having the process serve the team, can you then still call yourself “agile” at all?

#Agile, at its essence, prioritizes #collaboration, #adaptability, and responding to change over rigid structures and excessive focus on outputs.

True agility involves:

1.	#Outcomes over #Outputs: Agile values delivering real value to customers and stakeholders (outcomes), rather than simply producing a lot of work (outputs). The goal is to continuously improve and adapt toward better outcomes.

2.	#Team #Collaboration over Individual #Roles: Agile principles emphasize #crossfunctional collaboration, where teams work together to achieve a common goal. A focus on individual roles may inhibit this shared responsibility.

3.	#Adaptability over #Process #Rigidity: While frameworks and processes provide structure, they should serve the team and adapt to the team’s needs. Strict adherence to process for its own sake contradicts Agile’s principle of valuing “individuals and interactions over processes and tools.”

If your focus is on simply getting things done without flexibility or collaboration, you’re leaning more toward a rigid, task-oriented approach rather than embodying the true spirit of agility, which thrives on #continuousimprovement, #teamwork, and #responsiveness. 

So, while you may still call yourself “agile” in a technical sense, you are not embracing its core philosophy.

Something I hear now and then is the opinion that #DevOps doesn’t work. 

The folks putting out such statements generally think that #developers don’t care enough about #operations, #security etc of their applications and all they want is to churn out new features, as requested by the business. 

How these new features fare after they’ve been coded and released, they state, doesn’t concern the #dev folks a lot.

Having been mostly on the operations side of the proverbial development to operations wall, I can’t say I have any desire to go back to that modus operandi.

If you’re young or innocent enough, you may not know of the wall.

However, it’s a pretty horrible place to be, on either side of it.

On the operations side, because we would be deploying black boxes into production without much insight as to what changed versus the previous black box version. 

When things went south, as they sometimes do, we would apply much silver taping and MacGyver style heroics. Eventually, people would come to their senses and consult some from the development side. And, dear folks, this is how much of technical debt in production accumulated in those days. Through great many middleware fixes.

In development, things were not much better either. 

Sure, there was peace and calm as someone else normally was dealing with production. But there were release target dates, test environments that were all but same from those beefed up ones in production and occasional involvement into production issues, normally by the time operations had exhausted all the bells and whistles in their tools and systems. 

To anyone thinking that it used to be better, I’d rather say that you just haven’t done enough DevOps yet.

This is what I think. What do you think?

P.S. An interesting figure I heard the other day is that only 30% of all applications globally are delivered to production using automation and pipelines. Keeping that number in mind, I’d argue that there is still 70% of applications to go before we can truly assess the effectiveness of DevOps. D.S.

P.P.S. In other words, we’ve spent 50 plus years deploying applications manually and less than 15 years through #continuousdelivery. Ofcourse the change takes some time. D.D.S.

I have never told this story on LinkedIn in any shape or form but I think now it’s time. 

In a way it’s an origin story of my path to cloud.

7 years ago, in my previous company, I was managing a team of extremely skilled Continuous Delivery Engineers. Our realm of responsibility included all of our DevOps tooling, from BitBucket to Jenkins and everything in between. 

We were not merely managing these systems but we were putting in place all enablers for Continuous Integration,  Continuous Delivery and ultimately Continuous Deployment and these were being extensively used by our development and operations teams.

We had taken a big role in moving the company from yearly release cycles to monthly and weekly, for a 20 year old Java monolith as well as for all the games and supporting micro services. 

And ofcourse we were constantly dog fooding, so whatever CI/CD setup we were asking our developers to use, we were also using the same for our own systems and automation setup.

We were tracking in realtime the health status of all our systems and success or failure of running pipeline jobs.

In fact, we would frequently catch both intermittent and incipient infrastructure issues, before they were noticed by any other team, including our infrastructure teams.

And, as our systems were not running in production domain, the health of the underlying infrastructure was often down prioritised, in turn causing issues for both developers using our automations and us trying to operate highly available and reliable CI/CD systems.

One area where the problem was the most pressing was in backups, where we had repeatedly tried to automate back up and restore of our SVC (Software Version Control), BitBucket, but where our on premise systems and tools would not do the job. 

So, instead we went looking for a place that would meet those needs. 

The cloud was not really considered an option for any team at that time, but we realised quickly it was where we had to go, if we were to be able to take the next leap with our CI/CD offering. 

At the time, Atlassian had just published Terraform templates for operating Bitbucket on AWS with an HA setup, so after some internal discussion and persuasion, we got to work.

Six months, and some template tweaking afterwards as Atlassian’s templates didn’t work out of box 🤔, we were ready to flip the switch and start operating Bitbucket on AWS, but by that time the direction had changed and more teams had gotten on the Cloud bandwagon so we had to refocus our efforts on enabling application deployment on Google Cloud.

The moral of the story simply being that if a shoe doesn’t fit, don’t change the foot, but rather try a different pair!

P.S. #ChatGPT sometimes creates rather vivid imagery. D.S.

P.P.S. 1 year later we initiated a gradual migration to GitHub Enterprise Cloud from Bitbucket, as our ultimate value add wasn’t in operating the SVC system but enabling our developers to ship better, more secure code faster. D.D.S.

Empowering #Leadership: Creating Leaders, Not Followers 

On my journey through many facets of leadership, I’ve embraced three core tenets that I believe are essential for fostering a healthy and innovative team environment: 

1. Being Present and Available

One of the most valuable lessons I’ve learned in leadership is the importance of being present and available - not just for decisions, but for advice, coaching, and brainstorming. 

“As we look ahead into the next century, leaders will be those who empower others.” - Bill Gates

I truly believe that great leaders carve out time for their teams, encouraging them to think bigger and challenge the status quo. Regardless of how busy my calendar is or how many items I have to deal with right now, I always strive to be present and accessible to my team. 

I always finish our 1-2-1s with "If anything, I am only a ping away." By actively engaging with team members, we build trust and open channels for collaboration.

2. Decentralizing Decision-Making

An approach I hold close to my heart is moving decision-making closer to where the information is - often within the teams themselves rather than solely at the management level. 

This approach echoes Steve Jobs’ wisdom: “It doesn’t make sense to hire smart people and then tell them what to do; we hire smart people so they can tell us what to do.”

Empowering teams to make decisions puts their expertise to good use. 

This isn’t just about delegation; it’s about creating a culture where everyone feels ownership over their work. 

3. Leaders Create Leaders

At the core of my philosophy is the belief that leaders create leaders, while managers create followers. 

As Tom Peters said, “Leaders don’t create followers, they create more leaders.” 

True leadership is about inspiring others to step up, take ownership, and grow into their own leadership roles. 

By empowering others, we unlock their potential and cultivate a cycle of growth and innovation. 

As leaders, it’s not just about results - it’s about the people who make those results possible. 

By mentoring and developing future leaders, we ensure sustained growth and innovation within the organization. 

By embodying and living these principles every day, my goal is to cultivate a culture where every team member feels valued, empowered, and inspired to contribute their best. 

Would love to hear your thoughts on these leadership principles!

Recently, I finished listening Seth Godin’s “This Is Marketing.” 

The book offers insightful perspectives on modern marketing strategies, emphasizing the importance of empathy and building genuine connections with your audience. 

Godin reminds us that “Marketing is about the stories we tell,” highlighting the shift from traditional advertising to meaningful engagement. 

He stresses the value of understanding your target market deeply to create products and services that truly resonate. 

While the book provides solid fundamentals and thought-provoking concepts, I found that it didn’t leave a lasting impact on me. 

Perhaps it’s because many of the ideas are familiar territory for those already versed in contemporary marketing philosophies. 

Nonetheless, “This Is Marketing” serves as a good refresher and could be quite enlightening for newcomers to the field. 

It reinforces the notion that successful marketing isn’t just about selling - it’s about serving and connecting. 

Memorable takeaways: 

- Empathy is Essential: Understand the wants and needs of your audience to create meaningful solutions. 

- Focus on a Specific Audience: Aim to serve a specific group deeply rather than trying to please everyone. 

- Tell Authentic Stories: Use storytelling to connect with your audience on an emotional level. 

- Create Meaningful Change: Strive to make a positive impact through your marketing efforts

I was asked the other day to summarise key learnings from working with #cloudtransformation in #financialservices.

Here they are, in no particular order:

- Compliance in focus: It’s critical to have a tight and close dialogue with Control functions throughout the cloud journey, to ensure compliant technical implementations as well as shared and common understanding between Control functions, cloud platform and consuming teams.

- People at the center: Cloud transformation is more about people change management (both mindset & competences) than about technology itself. It’s critical to ensure that the path forward is clear to all, that the education about Cloud is abundantly available and that the message is consistently repeated.

- Change takes time: Embracing new technology, modifying operating models and employees’ mindsets while maintaining operations in the current environment is a difficult balancing act. Hence, transformation often takes longer than initially assumed or estimated, as hundreds of technical experts and developers need to adapt to possibilities and responsibilites of a new tech stack, ie Cloud.

- Transformation applies to all: Cloud adoption is not just a technology concern. It applies equally to Technology, Business, Control Functions, Finance and all others involved. All involved need to adapt their ways of both working and thinking. Eg Finance team needs to actively adopt and take lead in establishing FinOps (Financial Operations). Compliance can proactively assist in establishing a fair responsibility division between Platform and it’s consumers in relation to compliance obligations applying to all. Infrastructure teams need to embrace large scale automation and Infrastructure-as-Code. Development teams need to reconsider their dependencies and rearchitect their applications for the new tech stack. And so on. 

- Security is paramount: In financial services, security is a non-negotiable priority. Cloud transformation requires robust security controls, in particular around data protection, encryption, access management, and regulatory requirements. Security must be embedded into every layer of the transformation.

- Vendor and multi-cloud management: Financial institutions often adopt a multi-cloud strategy. Managing these relationships and balancing the risks of vendor lock-in versus optimally leveraging multiple providers is crucial for resilience and scalability.

- Legacy Systems Coexistence: In financial services, legacy systems and infrastructure continue to operate alongside new cloud-based solutions. Ensuring seamless integration, minimizing disruption, and gradually modernizing legacy applications is key to a successful long term transformation. 

- Regulatory and Audit Readiness: Beyond compliance, being prepared for audits and having clear documentation on how cloud services meet regulatory requirements is crucial. This involves building auditable processes around cloud governance, usage, and cost management.

Some pieces are eternal classics, such as the 1944 CIA manual on how to #sabotage an #organisation’s #productivity.

“The Simple Sabotage Field Manual” was distributed by the Allies in WWII to guide sympathetic citizens. 

It gave the rebellious ones instructions on how to weaken their occupied country by reducing productivity in the #workplace.

60 years later, some suggestions are equally applicable as during WWII, and stand probably even more unquestioned in a modern workplace:

- Insist on doing everything through “channels”. Never permit shortcuts to be taken in order to expedite decisions.

- When possible, refer all matters to #committees, for “further study and consideration”. Attempt to make committees as large as possible - never less than five.

- Talk as frequently as possible and at great length.

- Bring up irrelevant issues as frequently as possible.

- Haggle over precise wordings of communications, minutes, resolutions.

- Refer back to matters decided upon.

- Be worried about the propriety of any #decision.

Are you doing your developers a disservice, by adding #middleware "magic" in front of their applications, temporarily saving the day but long term creating a pile of tech debt, hard to get out of? 

I have seen this happen more than once over the course of my career. 

#DBAs saving the day by introducing stored procedures to the application database, to mitigate some application flaw that ideally should be fixed in the application code. 

#Network engineers saving the day by adding some network filtering rules to mitigate security and performance flaws in the application, that ideally should be fixed in the application code.

Short term, everyone gets to be a hero and save the day. 

Long term however, this silver taping, MacGyver style approach to #softwareengineering locks your company in unwanted dependencies and makes any modernization effort so much harder.

Have you got some other examples of similar practices?

#chatgpt had these additional examples of short-term fixes in software engineering that create long-term technical debt.

- #Caching Misuse - improper cache usage can lead to outdated data, cache invalidation problems, and hidden bugs that make the system harder to maintain in the long term.

- Hardcoding Configuration - this approach often leads to security vulnerabilities, difficulty in scaling, and complications when deploying to different environments (e.g., development vs. production).

- Overuse of Feature Flag - if they are left in place far too long, the #featureflags accumulate unnecessary complexity. 

- Using Cron Jobs to Fix Logic Issues - adding #cronjobs (scheduled tasks) to periodically run scripts that clean up or fix data issues caused by application bugs, may temporarily alleviate data inconsistencies, but it doesn't address the root cause in the application logic, and over time, it leads to a fragile system that depends on the cron jobs to stay operational.

- Relying on Deprecated Libraries - Sometimes, a library or framework may become outdated, but due to time pressures or fear of breaking things, the team continues using it instead of upgrading or refactoring. As the library continues to degrade and becomes unsupported, it creates compatibility issues with other parts of the system and makes future modernization much harder.

- Security as an Afterthought - bypassing proper #securitypractices (such as input validation, encryption, or access control) in the interest of speed, with the promise of “fixing it later" will result in a system that's prone to security breaches, forcing the company into a costly and difficult remediation process down the line.

All of these examples show how short-term thinking in #softwaredevelopment leads to #technicaldebt, ultimately slowing down progress and creating long-term difficulties for teams.

Sometimes there is this notion that you can “lift-and-shift” on premise ways of working, and responsibilities division straight into a #cloud environment.

Everything goes but that’s a recipe for inefficiency and ultimately disaster.

As the overly simplistic visual below shows, in a cloud environment, storage for example is no longer a #IaaS concern for the infrastructure team but rather a #SaaS offering. 

In fact storage buckets such as Amazon S3, or Google Cloud Storage are probably the world’s most used SaaS and trusted by millions of organisations to backup and store their data.

There is definitely some work to be done as goes for configuring, maintaining and scaling out a company common baseline for what to and not to do with different storage options in the cloud, but that’s still far from taking care of the whole stack from hardware, virtualisation, servers, OS, middleware, runtime, data and customer facing applications. 

Taking another example, #networking is no longer about cables, switches, routers etc. That responsibility has been handed over to the Cloud Service Provider. 

Networking is rather about writing a couple of lines of #IaC (Infrastructure as Code) using CSP’s cloud native offering, running it and seeing network magic come to life, on the back of #CSP’s high speed network. 

Another typical #antipattern when lift and shifting infra to cloud, is taking the main characteristics of one’s on premise offering and replicating them in a cloud context. 

Often this means running bloated and expensive third party systems on CSP’s IaaS tech stack, and barely utilising any of the native (vertically integrated) benefits of the cloud. 

This approach may work as a really short term #cloudmigration enabler, but for both the sake of infra and dev teams, there must be a sunsetting and modernisation plan. 

So when infra goes cloud, it needs to change into something else. 

It needs to change from little to no automation to full on IaC coding and start using CI/CD pipelines to be able to scale out it’s offering from a manageable few on premise environments to hundreds and thousands of cloud environments. 

It needs to think instant self service over slow order taking, if it is to scale out without significantly staffing up.

It needs to learn to deal with dependency management in an different way, eg in cloud being part of a common shared code base, necessitating a mutually shared understanding between infra teams, how they together make up a greater whole, for the benefit of their consumers. 

This is just a few items I figured out on the fly. Can you add a few more?

Someone jokingly said: 

“Tech is easy, people are hard.” 

Very true indeed. 

In a #cloudtransformation context, the difficult part is not the technology itself. 

Rather it’s the people #changemanagement.

Changing how people think, work and behave is key to having a successful transformation.

Having worked close to both traditional and #cloudinfrastructure, I’m struck by how difficult and slow transition from one to another sometimes can be.

Fairly often, #infrastructure teams working on premise assume that going to cloud is about carrying over what they do, into someone else’s data centre. 

Database hotels, multi-tenant single Kubernetes clusters, flat networks, third party services etc. 

Sure, that’s one way of doing it. Cloud service providers (#CSP) won’t mind. They will charge you for whatever you spend, and with this approach, you’re bound to spend plentiful. 

Operationally, this approach won’t work either. 

Each of the teams offering their lifted and shifted infrastructure services, becomes a bottleneck and one more dependency to take into account, on an application’s pathway from idea to production. 

Furthermore, as much of this won’t run on any of CSP’s managed services but rather on it’s #IaaS offering, there will be a maintenance burden to carry and care about for the infrastructure team.

There is however a better way for infrastructure teams to stay relevant when going to Cloud. 

It’s about assuming responsibilities within an infrastructure team’s current tech stack by having deep knowledge of the same within a CSP’s offering, example being databases, various compute options etc.

And as all of these offerings become all the more CSP managed, the unique USP of infrastructure team no longer lies in managing, patching, upgrading and that sort of upkeep activities, but rather programmatically managing a company common configuration baseline for CSP Managed services across microsegmented environments offered to individual development teams. 

The infrastructure team goes ideally from systems upkeep and management as done on premise to internal consultancy, best practises sharing and enforcement of a common configuration baseline in the #cloud.

In the process the tools need to change too. 

From #ClickOps and limited automation, to operating via #IaC (Infrastructure as Code) and code templates and libraries. 

This change is all about easy, but it’s also the most rewarding one for infrastructure teams as well as their companies. 

As more and more services in the cloud become CSP managed (examples being GKE Autopilot, Cloud SQL et al), the value add the infrastructure teams bring to the table in a cloud context needs to reflect this movement too.

I’ve written it before, and I’ll write it again. 

Good #recruiting is really hard. 

First spending hours and hours looking through hundreds of different CVs, all differently formatted, some reasonably well matched with asked for requirements, many totally off the chart, some under qualified, some over qualified, and then just a few hitting so slightly the sweet spot, necessitating one, two, three or more interviews, with oneself, team mates and other stakeholders. 

In the age of #genAI, the personal letters are also making a comeback. 

It’s easy enough to feed the #GPT with the job description and one’s CV, asking it to generate a personal letter weaving the two together. 

The results are interesting but not personal at all. 

Direct messaging also seems to be on revival. Either via LinkedIn, email, phone or by leaving voice call messages asking the recruiter to call back.

I guess it’s one way to get through, to get one’s CV on top of the stack, and hopefully be considered. 

Right now, I’m undecided if it’s a good or a bad thing. 

Being self confident, and a bit persistent is often a good idea, but it has to be done with a dose of self distance. 

In the end, what it all boils down to is: 

1) how well the recruiting team feels that the candidate is meeting the set criteria, or alternatively has potential to meet criteria within a reasonable time period. 

2) how much consensus there is in the recruiting team for offering the role to the candidate, dependent on how (consistently) the candidate has performed through different stages of the recruitment process. 

3) gut feeling - regardless of how scientific one wants to make the #recruitment, recruitment is very much about connections between real flesh and blood people. Has the candidate managed to establish a positive connection with the recruiting team, and equally so, has the recruiting team managed to do the same, as candidates may have several options themselves on the table.

A key ingredient thoughout the process is openness and transparency between the parties, ie setting the right expectations on job role, organisation, salary and benefits, as well as timelines for the recruitment process.

And last but not least, exercising the same transparency after having signed on one of the candidates, and having to turn down the remaining ones.

These are some of my reflections after being heavily engaged in recruitments in recent months. 

And even if good recruiting is hard, and takes long, it’s time well invested when one sees that the match is right and the team performs almost from the go together with the new hire.

”Give and Take: Why Helping Others Drives Our Success” by Adam Grant is a refreshing exploration of the dynamics in interpersonal relationships and how they influence individual and organizational success. 

Drawing from research in psychology and organizational behavior, the author divides people into three categories: ”givers”, ”takers” and ”matchers”.

- Givers are those who help others without expecting anything in return.

- Takers are the ones who seek to extract as much value as possible from others.

- Matchers attempt to balance giving and taking, ensuring fairness in relationships.

Grant argues that while givers may appear vulnerable to exploitation by takers, they often achieve the most success in the long run - provided they approach giving in a sustainable, strategic way. 

This observation goes against conventional wisdom, which assumes that takers or matchers would be more likely to succeed.

Grant explores how and why givers are frequently more successful than takers, despite the risk of burnout or being taken advantage of. 

He builds up the story with real-life examples from a variety of fields - medicine, business, sports, and entertainment - to show that givers, over time, build better relationships and networks, foster more collaborative environments, and ultimately find themselves with greater support from their peers. 

Their success comes not only from their hard work and intelligence but also from the goodwill they cultivate.

A key theme to me personally is that givers can achieve significant success if they give in a smart, sustainable way. 

Grant introduces the concept of being a "self-protective giver," suggesting that it’s crucial to set boundaries and avoid over-giving to the detriment of personal well-being. 

He emphasizes the importance of avoiding the "doormat" mentality, where givers allow themselves to be exploited.

The book also delves into the organisational impacts of fostering a culture of giving. 

Companies that encourage collaboration and generosity can spur innovation, improve employee satisfaction, and enjoy long-term financial success.

“Give and Take” is a thought-provoking, well-researched book that challenges traditional notions of success. 

Adam Grant's arguments provide a new framework for understanding interpersonal dynamics and personal fulfillment, emphasizing that generosity and kindness can be powerful drivers of success. 

Although the framework is a bit oversimplified, the book's lessons on fostering a culture of giving - both in personal and professional settings - are valuable and relevant.

I recall fondly how I back in 2008 started using Salesforce, while at Nokia.

It was a fundamental shift from working with on premise hosted systems, the interface was quick and fluid, access was easy och uninterrupted and flexibility and extensibility was miles away from many own hosted systems we had at the time.

In fact I liked it so much that when we partnered with another CRM (Customer Relationship Management) software provider a few years later, and I experienced the sharp contrast between the two CRM systems, both of which were cloud hosted, I truly started appreciating what Salesforce and Marc Benioff had created.

In essence, Salesforce, founded in 1999 by Marc Benioff, fundamentally changed the way businesses interact with software. 

By pioneering the Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) model, Salesforce challenged the traditional enterprise software paradigm, which relied on on-premises installations and licensing.

In the late 1990s, the enterprise software market was dominated by giants like Oracle and SAP. 

These companies offered complex, expensive software solutions that required significant upfront investments and ongoing maintenance. 

Salesforce, on the other hand, envisioned a future where software could be accessed and used over the internet, eliminating the need for costly hardware and IT infrastructure.

Salesforce's innovative approach to software delivery was met with skepticism and resistance from industry incumbents. 

Many questioned the viability of a cloud-based model for enterprise applications, citing concerns about security, reliability, and scalability. 

Undeterred, Benioff and his team forged ahead, building a platform that could deliver CRM functionality to businesses of all sizes.

One of the early challenges Salesforce faced was convincing potential customers to trust a cloud-based solution for their critical business needs. 

The company had to overcome the perception that cloud-based software was less secure and reliable than on-premises systems. 

To address these concerns, Salesforce invested heavily in security and infrastructure, ensuring that its platform met the highest industry standards.

While the road to success was all but easy, and doubters were many in numbers and big in size, today there is hardly anyone questioning the suitability of cloud and SaaS in the enterprise software market. 

Salesforce’s success has inspired countless others to challenge traditional business models and embrace the power of cloud computing.

What happens from time to time in technology organisations is unjustified, unreasonable and unsound requisition of general IT concepts, by select individuals or teams.

The thing is though that IT concepts that are fundamental to software development and delivery, can not possibly be sole possession of just a select few.

Such concepts are shared tools of the trade, not proprietary assets. 

Trying to claim ownership of general concepts within a single team is counterproductive for several reasons:

- Hindrance of Collaboration: It creates silos and prevents knowledge sharing across the organization.

- Limited Innovation: Isolating concepts restricts the potential for new ideas and approaches.

- Miscommunication: It leads to confusion and misunderstandings when communicating with other teams. 

- Difficulty in Attracting Talent: Limiting the use of common industry terms can make it harder to recruit skilled professionals.

Effective collaboration and innovation thrive on shared understanding of common concepts.

By openly using general IT concepts, teams can build upon each other's work, share knowledge, and ultimately achieve better results.

"The Infinite Game is not about winning or losing; it's about staying in the game. 

Infinite-minded leaders understand that 'best' is not a permanent state. 

Instead, they strive to be 'better.' 

'Better' suggests a journey of constant improvement..." - Simon Sinek 

This quote sums up “The Infinite Game” by Simon Sinek for me. 

The book takes inspiration from James P. Carse's concept of finite and infinite games. 

The core idea of finite vs. infinite games is pretty powerful. 

Finite games are played to win with clear goals and endings (think chess). 

Infinite games, on the other hand, have no finish line; it's about continuous adaptation and advancement (think business itself). 

This framework encourages readers to start thinking long-term and focus on building a lasting purpose-driven organization. 

Sinek provides practical tips on how to adopt an infinite mindset. This includes building a strong "Just Cause" (a higher purpose beyond profit), fostering trust within teams, and embracing a learning culture. 

Sinek's signature style is clear, concise, and engaging. He uses real-life stories to illustrate his points, making the book relatable and interesting.

The Infinite Game is a thought-provoking read that challenges much of the traditional, Wall Street centric business thinking.  

After all, business, like life, is about more than just making the quarters.

“A business that makes nothing but money is a poor business.” - Henry Ford

While repetitive at times, I feel that Sinek’s book offers valuable insights, many ahas and needed inspiration for anyone interested in building a purpose-driven and adaptable mindset.

“The Toyota Way to Lean Leadership” by Jeffrey K. Liker and Gary L. Convis goes deep into the heart of Toyota's success: its unwavering commitment to Kaizen. 

Liker and Convis illuminate how Toyota's leaders, at every level, embrace Kaizen as a lifestyle. 

It's not about sporadic bursts of improvement but a relentless pursuit of perfection, ingrained in the company culture. At Toyota, Kaizen is not a temporary fad but a permanent mindset. 

”Kaizen is not just about improving processes; it's about improving people." 

”The journey to excellence is never-ending. It's a daily commitment to Kaizen."

”Kaizen is not just a tool, it's a philosophy, a way of life."

These quotes encapsulate the book's core message: Kaizen is the lifeblood of Toyota's success, and it's a principle that any organization can adopt to achieve sustained excellence. 

The authors convincingly argue that without a deep-rooted Kaizen culture, any lean transformation is bound to be short-lived. 

The book also illustrates how Toyota's philosophy has acted as a bulwark against economic downturns, natural disasters, and industry disruptions.

Resilience through Flexibility: 

The book emphasizes that Kaizen, the cornerstone of the Toyota Way, fosters a culture of adaptability. By continuously improving processes, Toyota can swiftly respond to changing market conditions or unforeseen challenges.

Strong Financial Position: 

A byproduct of lean principles is a lean balance sheet. Toyota's focus on efficiency and waste elimination has allowed it to maintain a strong financial foundation, providing a cushion during economic downturns.

Employee Engagement and Morale:

The Toyota Way places a premium on employee development and involvement. It’s engaged workforce is more likely to go the extra mile during tough times, finding innovative solutions to problems.

Going from a traditional IT environment to a mature Cloud native one can be quite mind boggling, particularly if you’re used to a fairly flat network topology, where most resources are only an IP address away. 

In our cloud environments we practice a very strict micro-segmentation architecture, between deployment stages, between teams and within teams, all in an effort to create a very secure and tightly controlled public cloud setup. 

We use cloud native tools provided by each cloud supplier, to create micro-segmentation. In GCP projects, in Azure subscriptions and in AWS accounts. We also make sure that thus separated environments only create needful interactions with other environments, and actively sustain from creating and maintaining too many commonly shared IP address spaces. 

Micro-segmentation in general offers several benefits, in enhancing security, improving network efficiency, and providing better control over data and applications. 

Here are just some benefits:

1. Enhanced Security: 
- Minimized Attack Surface: By segmenting the network into smaller, isolated zones, micro-segmentation reduces the potential impact of a security breach. Even if an attacker gains access to one segment, they are prevented from moving laterally across 
the network.

- Granular Security Policies: Allows for more precise and detailed security policies tailored to specific segments, applications, or workloads, reducing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches.

2. Improved Compliance:
- Regulatory Adherence: Helps organizations meet compliance requirements by isolating sensitive data and systems, ensuring that regulatory standards for data protection and access control are met.
   
- Audit Trails: Facilitates detailed logging and monitoring within each segment, making it easier to track and audit access and activity.

3. Operational Efficiency: 
- Simplified Management: Easier to manage security policies and configurations at a granular level without impacting the entire network.

- Reduced Complexity: By isolating workloads and applications, micro-segmentation simplifies troubleshooting and reduces the complexity of managing network security.

4. Enhanced Performance:
- Optimized Traffic: Reduces unnecessary east-west traffic, improving overall network performance.

Resource Allocation: Enables better allocation of resources by ensuring that specific applications or workloads receive the necessary bandwidth and security.

5. Increased Agility and Flexibility:
- Adaptability: Quickly adjust security policies in response to changing business needs or emerging threats.

- DevOps and Cloud Integration: Supports modern DevOps practices and cloud environments by providing consistent security policies across dynamic and distributed infrastructures.

6. Cost Efficiency: 
- Efficient Use of Resources: Reduces the overall cost of managing and securing the network by optimizing resource use and reducing the likelihood of widespread breaches.

"Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism" by Yanis Varoufakis is an interesting and thought provoking book.

Yanis Varoufakis, a renowned economist and former Greek finance minister, presents a provocative thesis: 

capitalism is dead, replaced by a new economic system called "technofeudalism."

Varoufakis argues that the rise of Big Tech, with its control over vast amounts of data and online platforms, has created a new form of economic power. 

In this system, individuals are not so much employees as they are "serfs," offering their data and attention as a form of rent to the tech giants.

He draws parallels between this system and medieval feudalism, where serfs worked the land owned by their lords in exchange for protection and a share of the produce.

Varoufakis has an engaging and provocative narrative, as he blends economic theory with personal anecdotes and cultural references to make complex ideas more accessible .

At the same time, Varoufakis oversimplifies the complexities of the current economic system, reducing it to a simplistic dichotomy between capitalism and technofeudalism.

Be it as it may, "Technofeudalism" is a thought-provoking perspective on the evolving nature of capitalism and the influence of Big Tech.

The book challenges us to think critically about the power of Big Tech and its impact on our lives. 

Whether or not you agree with Varoufakis's conclusions, the book is a must-read for anyone interested in understanding the forces shaping the world.

I’ll leave off with two rememberable quotes about entertaining alternative viewpoints.

“It is the mark of an educated mind to be able to entertain a thought without accepting it." — Aristotle

"Your assumptions are your windows on the world. Scrub them off every once in a while, or the light won't come in." — Isaac Asimov

#bookreview #technofeudalism #yanisvaroufakis #bigtech

Creating a managed platform on top of a public cloud is not easy.

There are oftentimes expectations from the platform users that there will be little difference between the platform controlled and configured via our management layer and what they would get on their own if they’d go out and swipe a credit card. 

As the users start using our managed platform, a majority of them come to grips that the additional layers on top are for their own benefit, ease of use, security, compliance and general peace of mind. 

Some though still don’t fully understand and ask for more freedom, less restrictions and new additions to the platform in conflict with some set principles. 

That is, until something goes south due to their own actions and that some additional restrictions could have potentially prevented. 

Then the narrative rapidly changes and additional restrictions are asked for by those who normally advocate for fewer. 

It’s here it’s important not to get carried away with the passion of the moment, and start imposing additional restrictions. 

Rather, one should assess the whole situation, draw learnings and determine sound next steps, that may be additional restrictions or something else entirely.

Striking a sound balance between control and freedom that stands the test of circumstances is all but easy but well worth a try.

"The Five Most Important Questions You Will Ever Ask About Your Organization" by Peter F. Drucker is a short guide that encourages leaders and organizations to reflect deeply on their core principles and practices. 

This intuitive and powerful framework helps organisations evaluate their effectiveness and strategic direction through five essential questions:

1. What is our Mission?
2. Who is our Customer?
3. What does the Customer Value?
4. What are our Results?
5. What is our Plan?

The questions serve as a diagnostic tool, prompting leaders to critically assess their organization's purpose, target audience, value proposition, performance, and strategic planning.

1. Mission Clarity: Drucker stresses the importance of a clear and concise mission statement. The mission should guide all organizational activities and decisions, ensuring alignment and purpose. Organizations with a strong sense of mission are more likely to achieve long-term success.

2. Customer Focus: Understanding who the customer is and what they value is crucial. Drucker argues that organizations often assume they know their customers without truly engaging with them. Effective organizations invest time in listening to and understanding their customers' needs and preferences.

3. Value Proposition: Drucker challenges organizations to identify what their customers truly value, which may differ from what the organization believes. This requires regular feedback and a willingness to adapt and innovate based on customer insights.

4. Measuring Results: Results should be measured not just in financial terms but also in how well the organization fulfills its mission and meets customer needs. Drucker advocates for a balanced scorecard approach, incorporating various performance metrics.

5. Strategic Planning: A robust plan is essential for translating the mission into action. Drucker encourages organizations to develop flexible and dynamic plans that can adapt to changing circumstances and continuous learning.

Although the book was first published in 1993, it’s relevance is as great today as thirty years ago and one can notice it’s impact on the thinkers of our time.

The book's core questions encourage deep reflection and strategic thinking, promoting a customer-centric and mission-driven approach.

While the guidance is broad, the principles are timeless and provide a solid foundation for continuous improvement and innovation.
