I’ve begun wondering recently if observability and in particular logging isn’t about to go through a similar metamorphosis as we’ve seen with enterprise data journeys over the past decade. 

If you recall, for long, Big Data was all the rage and everyone had to have a lake, where they’d dump all their application data from all various sources, hoping that one day they’d figure out what good to do with it all.

Recently, that trend has shifted towards multiple fewer-purpose data warehouses where data aggregation can happen through data meshes, ie multiple connected data warehouses. (explained in simplific terms, if you want to read more about data mesh, you can look at the response I got from Bard about it in the comments)

Now, over to logging. 

Still today, there is sometimes this notion that logging should be centrally organised, as that would significantly simplify incident triaging or security response. The log vendors would have you (just like big data vendors of before) think that “dump it, and we’ll make sense of it”.

Nothing could be farther from the truth. To be usable, application and systems log need to be well understood by their owners, their data well structured and parsed and ultimately well linked between chained systems and applications. 

My own experience from searching in such central log stores, has often been along the lines of searching for a “needle in a haystack” and not seeing the “forrest for allt the trees”. And not to mention the performance aspect, which often has been excruciatingly slow. 

The notion “the more, the merrier” is ultimately wrong when it comes to both log and big data. 

If the log output is producing multiple stack traces which stem from the same error, then you’ve generated unneeded data. 

If the log output is unnecessarily verbose, then you’re logging more than you’ll need most of the time, if ever. 

Too much of the good stuff will ofcourse also have a performance impact on your logging system, making it slower on both search queries, alerting and dashboards, and in turn making your incident response slower.

Just like with data mesh, I am hopeful that we’ll start seeing more thoughtful logging practices, with only the most needful logs and alerts being selectively sent to a central logging place and the rest of the logs remaining in the Cloud where they were generated (should they need to be used for further triaging or deep dives).

What do you think? Am I on to something or is the discourse still fully controlled by the logging companies, advocating for the one-size-fits-all approach.

#observability #bigdata #logdata #datamesh

I recall how I in 2008 as a newly baked Product Manager for Nokia’s smartphone lineup Nseries, gradually shifted role to Business Manager Software and Services. 

From one year to another my role shifted from high-end hardware to software and services that would run on top of the same hardware.

Although in retrospect things went as they did for Nokia’s mobile phone hardware and software sales, back in 2008 Nokia’s ignited focus on software and services was more than well timed. 

In fact, I dare to say that for a number of years the additional focus on software and services helped Nokia maintain dominant market share, even as both Apple and Google were rapidly entering into, for them, new markets and attacking new price points.

Nowadays, attempts to turn paying customers into subscribers (ownership to usership) are gathering momentum across every industry. 

Apple is probably one of the role models in this aspect. It’s services business now has more than 1B subscribers (Aug 2023), ranging across App Store, iCloud, Music, Fitness+, Pay, Apple Card, Apple TV+).

What is the appeal of the services business? 

Well, it comes with higher margins and higher predictibility (because of recurring revenue) which is why it’s logical that’s where the trend has been going. 

In fact, subscription businesses have grown six times faster than the S&P 500 over the last nine years (as per Zuora’s Subscription Economy Index).

In the case of Apple, services is the most profitable line of business. In fact, it’s the business line that in the last earnings quarter made up for much of the struggles in the hardware divisions. 

And as the installed Apple user base continues to grow (now reaching over 2 billion devices), there is a large yet unaddressed portion of the user base. 

It will be interesting to watch how Apple manages to upsell paid-for services to the other half of it’s user base, and whether the juggernaut growth of the services division (user base doubled in three years) will carry on.

Also in the enterprise world it’s easy to fall prey for unrealistic expectations as to where your company should be on some transformation scale.

This Thoughtworks commissioned study comes therefore as a welcome reality benchmark for all those deep involved in various types of transformations.

The study (on 400 diverse enterprises) finds that less than 50% of organizations have adopted fundamental engineering best practices like DevOps, test-driven development, and cloud-native technologies. 

And less than a third have adopted basic processes like formal code reviews and continuous delivery.

In case you’re not consistently improving your engineering chops, how can you then expect to achieve business agility, or remain relevant in the long term?

Unsurprisingly, 73% of respondents said their engineers spend significant amounts of time addressing technical debt and other business-as-usual (BAU) issues.

On the positive side however, all respondents mentioned some practices they’ve engaged in that brought about positive outcomes on their engineering effectiveness.

Practices such as improving developer flow metrics, enforcing development guardrails, implementing developer portals and improving observability. 

Key conclusions:

- Align engineering teams with business results. Establish KPIs that reflect success or failure. 

- Let engineering teams own both the problems and the solutions.

- Accept that there’s no magic bullet. Start small, build from there. 

- Evaluate and understand your organization’s maturity and its tools, talent, and business needs.

Just as vacation was ending, I picked up "The Hard Thing About Hard Things" by Ben Horowitz. 

Horowitz, the co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz and one of Silicon Valley's most respected and well known venture capitalists, draws on his own experiences to offer uncensored and practical advice on how to deal with the tough challenges that one meets in any business.

Horowitz's writing is clear, concise, and humorous. He doesn't sugarcoat the challenges, but he also offers hope and encouragement. 

Here are some of the key takeaways from the book:

- The hard thing about hard things is that there are no easy answers. There is no magic formula for success, and every situation is different.

- The best way to deal with hard things is to face them head-on. Don't avoid them or hope they will go away.

- It's important to have a strong team of people around you who you can trust. Surround yourself with people who are smarter than you and who will challenge you.

- Be willing to make tough decisions, even if they are unpopular. Sometimes the best decision is to let go of something that is no longer working.

- Don't be afraid to fail. Failure is a part of the learning process.

Some of the specific topics that Horowitz covers in the book are following:

- Hiring and firing
- Product development
- Fundraising
- Marketing and sales
- Customer service
- Managing growth
- Dealing with failure
- Building a strong company culture

Related to all topics, Horowitz weaves in a number of personal anecdotes from his own experiences as an entrepreneur and venture capitalist. The anecdotes illustrate the insights that he is teaching, and they make the book more engaging and relatable.

The Hard Thing About Hard Things is a well-written and engaging book packed with valuable insights. It is a valuable resource for anyone who wants to build a successful company.

During the summer I finished listening to the audiobook “Ikigai: The Japanese Secret to a Long and Happy Life” by Héctor García and Francesc Miralles.

The book is an interesting mishmash of good ideas, useful takeaways and valuable concepts. 

There are 4 pillars of ikigai: 

- What you are good at, 
- what you love, 
- what the world needs, and 
- what you can be paid for.

To find your ikigai, you need to reflect on these 4 pillars and find where they intersect. This may take some time and soul-searching, but it is worth it to find your ikigai.

Once you have found your ikigai, you can start to live a more fulfilling and meaningful life. 

You will be more motivated and passionate about your work, and you will have a greater sense of purpose.

Ikigai can help you live a longer and healthier life. When you are doing something that you are passionate about, it reduces stress and increases happiness, both of which have been linked to longevity.

Ikigai can also help you to connect with others. When you are passionate about something, you are more likely to find others who share your interests. This can lead to strong friendships and relationships.

Ikigai is not about perfection. It is about finding something that you are good at and that you enjoy doing. 

It is about making a difference in the world, even if it is in a small way.

Ikigai is a journey, not a destination. 

It is something that you will continue to explore and refine throughout your life.

Although the book can seem unstructured and messy at times, I still feel it’s well worth the read and subsequent reflection. 

In fact, a number of rememberable takeaways from the book can be found on my own cloudcloud.dev site.

This is a major milestone for #personalprivacy, #techinnovation and #transatlanticcooperation.

The EU-U.S. Data Privacy adequacy decision concludes that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection – comparable to that of the European Union – for personal data transferred from the EU to US companies under the new framework. 

On the basis of the new adequacy decision, personal data can flow safely from the EU to US companies participating in the Framework, without having to put in place additional data protection safeguards.

The adequacy decision comes into force already today.

Key Principles:

• Based on the adequacy decision, personal data will be able to flow freely and safely between the EU and participating US companies.

• A new set of rules and binding safeguards to limit access to data by US intelligence authorities to what is necessary and proportionate to protect national security; US intelligence agencies will adopt procedures to ensure effective oversight of new privacy and civil liberties standards.

• A new two-tier redress system to investigate and resolve complaints of Europeans on access of data by US Intelligence authorities, which includes a Data Protection Review Court.

• Strong obligations for companies processing data transferred from the EU, which includes the requirement to self-certify that they adhere to the standards through the US Department of Commerce.

• Specific monitoring and review mechanisms.

Having shouldered roles as Product Owner, Engineering Manager, Scrum Master and Solution Architect (briefly), sometimes two or three roles at the same time, I have a few simple rules of thumb as to who does what.

- Product Owner takes care of WHY, WHAT and WHEN. 

- Team together with Solution Architect takes care of HOW. 

- Engineering Manager takes care of WHO.

- Scrum Master connects the dots, by helping the Team including PO, SA and EM continuously improve on HOW, WHO, WHAT, WHY and WHEN.

Maybe overly simplistic, and doesn’t really take into account that in an agile team it’s the entire team (including ofcourse PO, SA, EM, SM) that’s ultimately responsible for all aspects of HOW, WHO, WHAT, WHY and WHEN.

Drawing on my insights from working nearly 9 years in the online gaming industry and more than 2 years in financial services, here’s a comparison of the two industries along a few dimensions.

- Transactions, Transactions, Transactions - 

Underpinning both industries are transactions.

While real money gaming is about many “small” transactions (on average 1EUR worth), banks process both “small” and large transactions (salary payments, loan payments, company payrolls, invoices etc). 

In gaming the bulk of transactions happen in real-time while in banking the transactions happen both synchronously and asynchronously, where a transaction can be settled from in an instant to several days later. 

As gaming relies on real time settlements, the number of transactions flowing through the systems is huge. As an example my previous employer used to process upwards 70 billion transactions yearly. 

In comparison, in the Swedish payment system in 2021 there were 6 billion transactions made (per Riksbanken’s statistics on payments). 

- 50+ vs 20+ years of tech debt - 

Banks were early to adopt use of computer systems five decades ago and in many banks this is visible still today. Buying a system is easy enough, but replacing a bought system that you’ve embedded into your business with something else, is an entirely different story. Consequently there is a large number of tools, systems and integrations most banks need for their day to day, leading to significant complexity and high IT costs. 

As gaming companies have fewer decades of technical debt to maintain and support, the technology stacks with these are both smaller and more standardised than in the case of incumbent banks, consequently leading to better operability and significantly lower IT run costs.

- Regulations, Regulations, Regulations -

Both industries are heavily regulated and as a company expands geographically, the more regulations it needs to adhere to. In financial services there are a few cross-country regulations such as those coming from EBA (European Banking Authority), while in gaming regulatory frameworks are on an individual, per country basis. 

In real money gaming, the detail of regulatory scrutiny often goes systems deep. As an example, the Italian gaming regulator is involved in every single game session, from start to finish, and has it’s records updated in real time about the status of any game. In Denmark, there is a similar system in place. In other regulations, such as UK, Spain etc there are various types of games constraints imposed forcing game suppliers to constantly adapt to changing regulatory requirements. In some jurisdictions extensive external certification programmes are mandated for all games to go through, before being released to the market. In some jurisdictions, certified games checksums that are running in production are accessed by regulators in real-time and checked against their cerfication records.

16 years since the inception of the DevOps movement, regardless of the industry, continent or country, it’s no longer a question of whether companies should adopt it but rather how to adopt, and how to adjust over time. 

In a 2021 survey, 74% of 3200 enterprises said that they had adopted DevOps in some form.  

I personally recall very well the world before and after DevOps adoption at my previous employer.

Before DevOps, there was waterfall, a number of testing gates, slow progression through the gates, and then a few months after developers had forgotten all about what they wrote in the code, black box deployment of the application by an application engineer who had no clue what was changed in the application, how to troubleshoot in case something went south and who blindly followed a set of deployment instructions written by a developer who in turn was working in an entirely different environment than the one that was running in production. 

Of course things didn’t go as planned. 

Developers had to be pulled in to help troubleshoot and as the resolution appeared someone had to duck tape the app through infrastructure hacks or middleware fixes or database stored procedures as deploying a new version of the application would best case take a few more months. All of which was piling up on top of the already great mountain of technical debt.

After DevOps, developers became accountable for the state of their applications running in production. They got to learn the operational context, constraints and possibilities much better than before and consequently produced more performant and reliable applications. The applications made it to the production more frequently too, and while there still were bugs, they were fixed faster.

And, as important as it is that developers work according to the Verner Vogels mantra “You build it, you run it, you maintain it”, it’s equally important that they receive both tooling and support regarding various operational aspects. The cognitive load on developers as a consequence of additional responsibilities and expectations has been increasing worryingly in the past decade. 

The support should happen as much as possible through self service, scaffolding, forking, APIs and other developer friendly infrastructure consumption methods.

Many years ago I either heard or read a quote supposedly originating from Netflix along these lines:

“An accessed machine is a spoiled machine.”

The gist of the quote being that any machine in production accessed by a human should instantly be considered tampered with and thus need to be cycled out from the machine fleet. 

I had this notion that the Conformity Monkeys of the Netflix Simian Army (https://lnkd.in/dfsgCc8B) would get to work and make such machines their targets.

Quickly googling the internet yesterday gave away that Netflix seemingly allows sshing into production machines although quite neatly secured through several layers of security including usage of bastion hosts, short lived certificates as well as extensive logging of all actions through SSH as well as alert triggering in case of anomalies. More about that here: https://lnkd.in/d3jMK2u6.

Googling didn’t quite give away whether sshing is a common practice or something sparingly used.

Here’s why I still appreciate the idea of having a hands off policy for production machines.

- Machines should be treated as cattle rather than pets meaning that for each new deployment, a new machine should be spun up with the latest patches rather than the old one reused as is. The old machine’s resources should be returned to the virtual pool. 

- All deployments to machines including machine provisioning itself should be done via code and CI/CD pipelines, rather than manual actions or home brewed, unversioned and locally kept scripts.

- Keeping track of and monitoring who has what access to production machines and what they’re using the access for, is a fairly time and energy consuming endeavour. Only allowing deployment pipelines to have production machine access lowers the required effort significantly as well as increases the security posture, as malicious actors become less likely to gain foothold in production. 

- I still recall the many hours I personally spent on incident resolutions where there would be one or two or three ‘doers’ and half of a dozen of onlookers from mainly support and NOC, all of whom would be logged on to the machines where there were issues and by doing so placing further strain on an already strained system. 

Ofcourse going from pet hugging to cattle farming, or in IT terms, from little or limited to full automation, is no small feat, especially when your operations and development teams are busy fire fighting methanol flames on top of the technical debt mountain that you’re standing on.

However, keeping in mind the mantra of zero production access for anything but deployment tools, is a good North Star to guide your future improvement efforts. 

“The message of the Kaizen strategy is that not a day should go by without some kind of improvement being made somewhere in the company.” - Masaaki Imai

Earlier this week, in our management team’s full day workshop, all of us had a go at the #pechakucha presentation format. 

PechaKucha (Japanese: ぺちゃくちゃ, IPA: [petɕa kɯ̥tɕa],[1] chit-chat) is a storytelling format in which a presenter shows 20 slides for 20 seconds of commentary each.

The slides can be about anything really but for the workshop I chose them to be about places, people and things I hold dear. 

So, without any further ado here are my 20 slides and their 20s commentary.

Slide 1: Uppsala - the city where I grew up, studied all the way to the university and where I still have my parents and friends, is of course very special and dear to me. 

Slide 2: Royal mounds in Old Uppsala - an ancient burial site for Viking kings, where the place’s special atmosphere is preserved to this day. A place of calm and serenity, long walks and inspired runs. 

Slide 3: Yearly Light Festival in Uppsala - an established yearly tradition for me and my wife where we check in at a hotel, go for a nice dinner and walk around in the city, taking in all the amazing light creations in the middle of the darkest month of the year.

Slide 4: Hagaparken-Brunnsviken - the closest major green area to where we live. Place of many runs for me, pick-nicks and forest strolls with the family. Truly blessed to have something as beautiful so close by.

Slide 5: Stockholm Olympic Stadion - another place for peace of mind. There are few things in life as soothing as running around in 400m circles over and over again and listening to some upbeat music, while all the time pushing one’s legs to go faster. 

Slide 6: Skokloster - the place where we bought our country house just as the pandemic started. Amazing nature on the Sko peninsula topped off with one of world's best preserved baroque castles.

Slide 7: The eternal city - It’s not for nothing I used to say a couple of years back, that I only prefer my mother’s and Italian food. I might have added some more taste buds since, but Italian and Roman cousine are still my favourites.

Slide 8: Nokia - growing up from a junior product manager to developer evangelist over the course of seven years. Experiencing first hand the journey from working at the world’s largest mobile brand, to near oblivion, while maintaining morale and pushing on, was character building. 

Slide 9: NetEnt - where I got to manage external integration projects, learnt a lot about both technology & business and how to influence both. Also where I started my engineering management path and discovered my passion for building teams and helping people grow.

Slide 10: Gym - is the place I normally spend two evenings a week. Lifting weights, building muscle while listening to an audio book is my way to maintain strength and agility of both body and mind. Image is from the pandemic times when there was a limited number of spots available at the gyms. 

Due to the post length limitation on LinkedIn, the next 10 slides will be described in a follow up post.

I just went through 90 plus pending LinkedIn connection requests. 

I generally accept a request pretty fast when it comes from someone I know or have interacted with professionally. 

When I’m not as certain I leave the requests to marinate and then do them in a bulk.

The benefit of giving this sort of thing some time is that sales persons don’t have the patience to wait for a request to go through and have probably already been spamming me for weeks after they sent their LinkedIn connection request, so I know already very well what angle they are coming from and whether having the connection accepted makes any sense at all. 

Looking through these 90 profiles, it’s easy to see some common traits.

Profiles belonging to people selling something are basically billboards of whatever they are selling at the moment. 

Company logos and branding are the norm and there is zero to little own personality or signs there of.

Posts are corporate megaphones of the latest sales pitch deck, but sometimes they take on the shape of more elaborate schemes of generated content such as podcasts. Such content however is more often than not imbued with the same sales messaging.

While I very well understand the role LinkedIn plays for all who work in sales, I’d still appreciate a bit more own personality and a bit less mechanical marketing.

"The ultimate test of your knowledge is your capacity to convey it to another."

I’m a fan of calling things what they are.

No point in obfuscating fancy buzzwords, obsvuring what’s obvious to anyone with a little bit of know-how or more colloquially putting lipstick on a pig. 

That’s why I like the “Lift and Shift Landing Zone” concept in the Cloud Foundations model by meshcloud.io.

This particular type of landing zone is basically what you’d create in case you want to migrate your applications to the cloud but don’t want to (yet) refactor the applications, don’t want to (yet) change your operational model or previously established responsibilities.

This is the type of environment where cloud native tooling rather than being the default is the exception. 

As you are bringing along your on premise applications without spending the needed time to assess what sort of on premise middleware and customisations you should do away with in the new cloud environment, you’re bound to be bringing along a number of chained dependencies with your applications. 

Some of these dependencies can be middleware tools that you once acquired to solve a particular problem on premise but that over time started to be used for other less appropriate use cases, and became so ingrained and coupled with your applications that calling it tech debt is an understatement.

Other dependencies can be tools and systems that you acquired thinking they would run across multiple Clouds and on premise environments, providing a “single pane of glass” experience and “control”. 

These tools are rarely as magical or as great as the marketing would have you believe but rather better in some areas and on some clouds than others and sometimes with gaps that you’ll need to find some other ways to cover. 

So rather than having a neat and clean starting point in the cloud with cloud optimised code and low operational burden by using managed services, you’re bringing along an entourage of dependencies, practices and operational overhead by having to manage both your applications and your dependencies all on your own. 

Truth to be told, this is how many companies initially approach cloud migrations. Hey, even Spotify migrated to cloud more or less like this. 

What is important to keep in the back of your head is that the lift and shift landing zone is merely a stepping stone to other more mature and more appropriate landing zone types, as your and your team’s cloud chops evolve and get better.

Sometime in 2019 as we were setting up the cloud foundations at my previous work place, it struck me how useful it would be to provide each team going to Cloud with their own set of resources, mutually independent and isolated from those of other teams, except when explicitly needed and agreed between the teams.

How this approach improves #security and #reliability and generally bootstraps #DevOps is self evident. 

There would no longer be workloads connecting to one another over flat networks with shared IP plans. 

There would no longer be any (virtual) resource dependencies between resources in different environments, effectively removing chain effects in case resources in use by one workload would go south, taking with them any ‘bystanders’.

Achieving zero trust through a #microsegmentation approach like this is done fairly easy, particularly in case workload authorisations are deliberately connected to one single environment and not shared (or even worse reused).

All of these resources, configurations and states would ideally be written as code, stored in a git repository and always reflect what was running in ‘real life’.

At the time, I was pretty new to #cloudcomputing and probably didn’t voice my thoughts and ideas with these exact words.

Maybe that’s why my highly able and capable cross-functional teams didn’t quite align with the underlying meaning of what I felt we should do and why we should do it.

Maybe it’s because the concepts and capabilities of #publiccloud were quite new to them too, they didn’t know how to realise this vision or whether it was at all achievable.

Or most probably because there was a big pressure to start migrating to cloud quickly, doing things the right but longer way, wasn’t really an option on the table.

Fast forward a few years into future, coming into my current work place, I was more than thrilled seeing a Cloud foundations setup very much aligned with my ideas from 2019.

An automated, via use of CI/CD and #IaC (Infrastructure-as-Code), through self-service consumable public cloud platform, with micro segmentation and zero trust between cloud environments or tenants* (as per definition in Cloud Foundation Maturity Model: https://lnkd.in/dbP6Q2ra).

The team of less than ten cloud engineers built it gradually over a few years and the platform has over time scaled to just under a thousand tenants and more than that number of developers. 

More about it can be read on the #SEBTechBlog here: https://lnkd.in/dNxmyRdb. 

A quote by Lao Tzu springs to mind:

“Muddy water, let stand, becomes clear.”

The sound ideas and principles that I outlined initially are thankfully nowadays common practice and approach for many companies migrating to cloud. The muddy cloud migration waters from a few years back are hopefully now replaced by doing the Cloud the right but longer way.

Walpurgis Night, Valborg or Sista April (Last of April) as it goes by in Uppsala, marks the beginning of the spring, all over Sweden. 

While celebrations vary in different parts of the country and between different cities, they normally include lightning of a bonfire, choral singing and a speech to honour the arrival of the spring. 

Having both grown up and studied in Uppsala, I personally feel that is where Valborg festivities are the greatest fun, especially for students but also for alumni and all others.

Many traditions and celebrations are centuries old such as the choral song at the sunset. As it happens, this year marks 200 years since the tradition was started. 

Some are fairly recent. 

In 1975, students started rafting on Fyris river through the center of town on rickety, homemade, wreckable, and often humorously decorated rafts. This tradition, called Forsränningen (https://lnkd.in/dR7BnepT) is drawing huge crowds and great laughs.

A somewhat older tradition is putting on of the student cap. The student cap itself goes back to the 1830s but an organised tradition of putting them on together started in 1955 when rector magnificus (vice-chancellor) of Uppsala University stepped out on the balcony of Carolina Rediviva (university library) and waved his cap to the gathered crowd at exactly 15:00. Nowadays the crowd draws 50,000 people and the sea of waving, white caps is simply breath taking. 

There are many more traditions one can take part of when celebrating arrival of the spring in Uppsala, such as champagnefrukost (champagne breakfast), sillunch (herring lunch), Walpurgis Ball at the Uppsala castle and so on. 

A common theme with all these traditions though is that they’ve been evolving, changing and improving with the society itself, which in essence is what all traditions are about. 

“Tradition is not the worship of ashes, but the preservation of fire.” - Gustav Mahler

#FinOps can have many looks and feels depending on where you are on your Cloud adoption and maturity journey. 

My own first encounter was with a flavour of FinOps I’d like to call knee-jerk-FinOps. 

It was basically my direct manager at the time contacting me on Slack at 7 o’clock in the mornings, looking at the previous day’s Cloud spend and trends in the billing dashboard and asking why this or that team were spending this or that amount of money running certain Cloud services, and what we could do to lower the spend.

I was heading up our SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) teams at the time and he was Head of Infrastructure and Operations. 

As SREs were responsible for the Cloud setup and operations, we had of course some tools at hand to try keeping our development teams’ costs at bay.

He on the other hand, was ultimately responsible for the company’s IT spend and tried doing what he could to keep the costs within control (and of course within budget).

For the lack of a better word, I call it knee-jerk as while intentions were for sound reasons, there was an inflated view of how much SREs could and should do about the spend vs how much responsibility was with the developers creating the applications that were driving the spend.

Still quite a few interesting cost optimisation efforts came out of this, such as putting into use kubecost.com, or achieving ephemeral usage of test environments, or an aggregate company view of Recommendations API complete with information about individual resource owners, workloads and potential savings, or using Liens objects to protect production workloads while a script would go over all unused, zombified resources and remove them. Well, we didn’t implement the last one. People thought it would cause more harm than do any good.

Needless to say, all of these efforts received developer buy-in and eventually we starting seeing costs keep within control.

I recently finished the novel “Investments Unlimited”. The book takes on where it’s predecessors “The Phoenix Project” and “The Unicorn Project” leave off.

The book takes off with the company in the book, Investments Unlimited Inc. (IUI), receiving an MRIA ("Matter Requiring Immediate Attention") a regulatory finding issued by the Federal Reserve. 

While the company’s DevOps transformation has finally started to bear fruit, there hasn’t been enough “shifting left” on Risk, Compliance, Governance and Security which is basically what the MRIA findings are about. 

As it normally goes, a task force is rapidly essembled to find a way forward and keep Investments Unlimited in business.

This cross-functional team of executives and engineers focus on developing a modern automated governance process without slowing the company's ability to meet customer demands and compete in the market.

Needless to say, in spite of various obstacles, difference of opinions and perspectives, and occasional setbacks, the task force manages to pull through and deliver an automated governance including both Risk, Compliance and Security imbued into DevOps ways of working and operating. 

While the book is written as a fictional novel, in the style of The Phoenix and Unicorn Project books, it’s not quite there literally.

Inspite of that, its a really good book packed with further references about achieving compliance in an efficient way without just ticking boxes. 

Further, it shows in an inspiring way how engineering, security, risk and audit are able to work together on achieving common goals.

The ideas, implementations and discussions from the book will without a doubt be well known to anyone who’s worked in a regulated industry and been trying to implement DevOps thinking and practises.

Recommended to anyone in Software Engineering within a financial services company but even more to people engaged with Compliance, Risk, Security and Audit questions in financial services.

I’ve recently started thinking that developing, running and maintaining one’s own data centres (or at least being part in a colo) is a better idea than running one’s apps on a cloud.

Hear me out. I’ve worked long enough to experience first hand the best and worst of both worlds.

- You get to buy different types of hardware from different vendors, while suboptimising for something in particular in any given moment such as price, performance or reliability. 

- You get to think of redundancy and observability for these components so that if any one fails, you’ll be able to continue operations uninterrupted.

- You get to periodise the costs and plan for HW replacements long in advance (even if the components may live long beyond the CAPEX lifetime).

- You get to take into account delivery times of components and the possibility that they may come faulty on delivery. 

- Even HW needs updating and patching from time to time, so you’ll need to take that into consideration, so that your operations can run uninterrupted, while your HW is up to date, performant and secure. 

- You get to fit those pieces of HW so that they play well together and make a solid base to build your virtualisation layer on top. 

- Once you have your virtualisation layer, you need to make sure that you have virtual (and sometimes maybe logical) separation between different types of environments (think dev/acc/prd), that the environments within same type are networking wise separated (think micro vs macro segmentation), that you make the virtualisation abstraction layer and thus the underlying hardware consumable-as-code, through self-service and APIs, to cater for fast, iterative, repeatable, secure and reliable flow of work, from idea to production.

I don’t know about you, but I see so many ways where things can go sideways in the above scenario or at least don’t go fully as intended, contributing to the proverbial pile of technical debt, any company regardless of size or age has to carry around and deal with.

But hey, on the positive side, you get to solve really complex hardware, software and integration problems and isn’t that what engineering is all about!?

After the presentations is time for short mingle, food and drinks and then some lightening talks where certain topics of high interest are selected and attendees are free to choose amongst the topics that draw their interest and talk to each other about. 

At the end is an engaging quiz that raises the attention levels once more, followed by a thank you to sponsors, attendees and organisers.

After that was mingle with food and drinks followed by a talk by Amir Rahafrouz on how Avro is used at SEB Embedded. 

The meet-up was finished off with a CI/CD trivia Menti quiz with almost 40 participants and 10 or so questions, where I ended up 6th.

Special mentions and thanks to Matilda Nordquist, Alexia Bohm, Ella Weintraub for making this event come true!

I have been fascinated by the Lean (process) thinking for many years now.

While I try to take in as many as possible human schools of thought, I often return to Lean as one of the purest and most sensible.  

A key concept in Lean is Waste or Muda in Japanese. Waste is basically anything that inhibits value delivery to customers.

Although Lean was originally developed for the manufacturing industry, I’ve found that it equally well is applicable to IT, across both software development and operations.

Defects - easily translatable to application errors, system failures, performance degradation etc.

Overproduction - delivering features, and functionality that the customers haven’t asked for or have a need of. 

Waiting - batching and queuing up software releases, waiting for pro forma approvals, waiting for deliveries from other teams etc.

Non-value processing - any activity that doesn’t add value to the end product, such as extra process steps that are not needed. An example would be creating unnecessary documents that are not used. 

Transport - handovers between teams, dev and QA etc. The more transportation steps the bigger overhead and Waiting time.

Inventory - partially done work that doesn’t carry any customer value until completed.

Motion - constantly changing customer requirements, disturbances in the team such as task switching, rework etc. 

Employee knowledge unused - assigning  team members to the wrong tasks, requiring wasteful or unneeded administration tasks, inadequate training etc. 

While many companies proud themselves to have adopted an Agile way of working, I don’t know of many companies that consistently work to make their processes efficient and value flow to customers both fast and secure.

Recently I picked up “Fundamentals of Software Architecture, an engineering approach” by Mark Richards and Neal Ford. 

While I’m barely halfway through, an interesting way to visualise technical depth and technical breadth caught my interest. 

On the top layer, there is the stuff we know: our knowledge, experience and expertise. 

In the mid-layer, we have the things we know that we don't know: the things we know exist, that we've heard of or even used, but without any deep expertise. 

The last but the most significant portion of our knowledge is the stuff we don't even know, that we don’t know. 

Neal Ford outlines in this article https://lnkd.in/d2WmNybA why breadth is more important than depth for architects than developers and how it’s important for both to maintain expertise as to not make technological decisions using ancient criteria (also referred to as Frozen Caveman Antipattern).

Head over to the article or better yet pick up the book!

The father of modernity, Baruch Spinoza, is to have said in the 1700s:  

”The highest activity a human being can attain is learning for understanding, because to understand is to be free.”

Often I take to this quite literally as I try to get to the root of many things I encounter in my day to day. 

Most often than not, other things get in the way though and I have to settle for less than full understanding and move over to the next priority on the list.

Still, the ambition to understand is always there which is why I’m quite puzzled when people rather than seek understanding, seek shortcuts.

Shortcuts are, well, shortsighted, bring little value beyond potential initial wins and there is no compounding of positive effects over time.

When life gets in the way and when the lure of shortcuts is strong, it’s clever to remember that there are no shortcuts to any place worth going.

I recently asked DALL-E to create an image for me with the following prompt: 

“Frankenstein Cloud consisting of more or less together fitting technical pieces”.

I guess inspired by a recent meet-up I’d been to, where a highly technology driven company gave a good talk on their journey from on-premise VMs to a cloud native, managed Kubernetes stack. 

So far so good, but on top of that stack they had also put a bunch of self-managed tools and middleware layers, more or less well integrated with the underlying cloud native Kubernetes runtime.

I asked why they had chosen that path, rather than using as much as possible of the cloud provider’s native, provider managed stack. After all, they were starting afresh. Why then lift-and-shift their “old” tools into the new?

The reasons were varying but stretched from external (out of team) requirements to use a particular system or a tool, to cloud native tools missing a particular set of features that their migrated applications required. 

While all perfectly understandable reasons from their point of view, I felt that they kind of had only gone halfway through in their migration effort. 

They had done a good replatforming, as their Kubernetes stack was scaling up and down better with the load and was more cost efficient. 

But they hadn’t done a refactoring of the application code base to better utilise the true benefits of the Cloud.

This is far from unusual and more often than not this is a viable migration path to the cloud, provided that the “Frankenstein Cloud” is not seen as your end station, but rather an evaluation stage you’re passing by on your way to a better place (that one visualised by the other cloud image, prompt: “Cloud made of perfectly well connected Lego pieces”).

Yesterday my daughter went with her class to the Vasa museum, holding the unique and well preserved warship Vasa from 1628. 

She came back home with a number of stories and anecdotes about this fascinating ship. 

In the 1620s, Sweden and Poland were at war. The king of Sweden, Gustavus Adolphus commissioned a new warship the likes of which had never been seen before. 

Vasa was to be the world's most formidable war and transport ship: 70 meters long, carrying 300 soldiers, with 64 heavy guns mounted on two gun decks, stretching Vasa's armaments beyond the limits of the day.

Her shipbuilder, Henrik Hybertsson, was well experienced with an impeccable reputation, but this task was far outside his capability. 

Two-gun-deck ships were rare, and none had been built of Vasa's size and armament.

Hybertsson had to balance many conflicting concerns. 

Fast time to deployment was critical, but so were performance, functionality, safety, reliability, and cost. 

He was also responsible to a variety of stakeholders. The primary sponsor was the king, who frequently changed his requirements and priorities.

On Sunday morning, August 10, 1628, the ship was ready. She set her sails, wobbled out into Stockholm's deep-water harbor, fired her guns in salute, and promptly rolled over. 

Water poured in through the open gun ports, and Vasa sunk. A few minutes later her first and only voyage ended 30 meters beneath the surface. Dozens among her 150-man crew drowned.

Inquiries concluded that the ship was well built but "badly proportioned." 

Today we know that Hybertsson did a dismal job of balancing all the conflicting constraints. In particular, he did a poor job with the stakeholder management. He acquiesced in the face of impossible requirements.

There is an important lesson here to be learnt for any product leader. 

Trying to fulfil each and every requirement (as with Vasa) creates an unstable end product, that provably doesn’t accomplish anything well.

No product can have it all, at least not in the first version!

By focusing on only a few core features in the first version, you are forced to find the true essence and value of the product.

In the case of Vasa, the focus should have been on picking a few key attributes and getting those very right. 

Thankfully for us however, this sensibility wasn’t there in the 1600s, leaving us with an amazing cultural treasure to cherish and learn from. 

Head over to this blogpost by Paul Buchheit, one of the original product managers of Gmail called “If your product is great, it doesn’t have to be good” if you’re interested to learn the right approach to new products. https://lnkd.in/d--hgiTb

It’s said that cloud transformation is far more about people, and far less about technology. 

I couldn’t agree more. 

Cloud transformation is about creating a broad movement with broad support and with returns to all involved.

When seeing Richard Seroter’s 2022 reading list posted a while back here on LinkedIn, a particular book stood out. 

It was John Doerr’s “Measure What Matters”.

I quickly figured out it was because I had previously returned the book to Audible after just a few chapters. I decided to give it another go and I’m quite happy I did.

Doerr started working at Intel in 1974, and got to work with the legendary Intel CEO, Andy Grove. 

By 1975 Grove had fully developed his system of Objective and Key Results, OKRs, inspired by ideas from MBO, Management by Objectives and Peter Drucker in the 1950s.

In 1979, the system was put to test when Motorola released its 68000 chip, a 16-bit microprocessor superior to Intel’s 8086. However, in the end, Intel came out winning by strictly following Grove’s OKR technique. 

Doerr starts with these first steps for OKRs and then the story unfolds of how the system is used in a variety of different industries and contexts. 

From big Tech, such as Google, to global movements, such as Bono’s ONE campaign to end extreme poverty and preventable disease by 2030. 

The case studies such as these take up a good part of the book, many times read out by the main personas themselves. 

What are then OKRs? Doerr himself explains it like this:

- An objective is simply WHAT is to be achieved. 

- Key Results benchmark and monitor HOW to get to the objective. 

It’s however not an immediate recipe for success. Defining, using and following up on OKRs takes perseverance and patience. 

It’s easy however to understand the appeal of OKRS. They have four ingredients: focus, transparency, accountability and ambition (the BHAG – Big Hairy Audacious Goal). 

All ingredients that any company needs in order to survive.

My personal experience from OKRs come from a few quarters trying to and only partially succeeding to implement them at NetEnt, and than doing the same at Evolution where OKRs had already but slowly begun to work their magic. 

The book is mostly relevant and interesting for the many case studies but if you’re more on the lookout for how to:s, I’d suggest to start off by checking out the website www.whatmatters.com that has a number of different resources and examples.

In a recent presentation I talked about the 5 essential characteristics of #cloudcomputing as defined by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology). 

Below an excerpt from that presentation.

While all five are important and at the core of what Cloud is about, in my view there are two that stand out.

It’s on demand self service and rapid elasticity.

Some companies can achieve reasonably central and dynamic resource pooling and fewer still can achieve broad network access and measured service in their own data centre setups.

But not many companies at all are able to achieve on demand self service and rapid elasticity in data centres run and managed by themselves.

Rapid elasticity means a surplus of resources idling and waiting to be put in use. And equally so, released back to the resource pool when no longer needed. 

Most companies don’t have that surplus of compute and storage, but must procure it, install it, configure it and then run it. This process takes months and not seconds like in the case of Cloud.

In the case of on demand self service, a Cloud user is able to provision, configure and operate Cloud services without any need for human interaction. User accesses what he/she needs via the UI (user interface), API (application programming interface) or CLI (command line interface). 

Putting the Cloud self service behind a ticket tracking system is only OK, in case the output is instantaneous. 

If there are additional human approvals in the process to be had, then the self service characteristic of cloud computing is not fulfilled.

Personally, I really like this key differentiator of Cloud. It allows for both great autonomy and accountability. It allows for full traceability as well as faster innovation. It is basically the special ingredient in the Cloud sauce.

Various studies agree that most organizations and businesses suffer from too many meetings and not enough time to get work done. 

There is this notion that endless meetings help clarify, unify and accomplish results. 

When meetings are done well, they are purposeful, planned, structured and facilitated. They add value to participants and generate impact for the organisation.

Ideally most meetings would be done well, but truth to be told, in most companies there are both good and bad meetings.

Steve Jobs is told to have had a 3-point formula for effective meetings. 


- Steve Job’s “Meeting Rule of 3’s”

1) Keep the participation list small. 

3-5 people is ideal. The more people you have in a meeting, the less productive it is. 

Too many voices become a sea of noise and it’s less likely you will get anything accomplished. 

Also, as you consider your invitation list know exactly what each person’ stake and role in the meeting will be and what they may contribute. If they cannot contribute, then they don’t make the list. 

Anyone else that needs to know can receive  a copy of the minutes.

2) Keep the agenda short. 

Agendas should be kept to no more than 3 items. This number allows for concentrated focus. 

With more than 3 items on an agenda, you’re likely to experience side conversations. 

Prioritize and ensure that all 3 agenda items are clearly connected to the purpose of the meeting.

3) Keep the length to no more than 30 minutes. 

The key to effective meetings is to keep them short. 

You may think that the topic of a given meeting demands a longer time slot, but research tells that isn’t so. 

Our attention span is short and we’re unable to sustain in-depth or analytical discussion for very long. 


As a final guideline, research shows that leaders should aim to schedule no more than 1 minute of meeting time for every 3 minutes of work. 

This means that no more than a quarter of anyone’s day should be spent in meetings.

A reasonable benchmark figure that I guess most companies don’t meet today.

How do you test your process quality? 

How do you know that a process is meeting its designed objectives? 

How do you know it’s void of inefficiencies, partisanships and other flaws? 

A couple of years back one of my Network Engineers told me a trick he’d apply whenever he would start a new job, to get a feel for the quality of internal processes.

His trick was rather simple. 

He’d write a fairly simple but well explained change about a reasonably common network task. 

It would be a well written body of text with very few language errors. He would attach a script to be executed as part of the change that to inattentive eyes would pass as a harmless script to execute. 

However, anyone paying attention and knowing the details of the craft, would spot the script for what it in fact was. A kill switch to shut down production in the environment where it’d be used.

If the process and the approvers within it would let such execution take place, then both the process and the selection of approvers were flawed.

Depending on the outcome of the process, he’d either correct the script in case the actual effects of the change were discovered, or run a harmless version of the script in production in case the change would be approved as originally submitted. 

While quite a lot of work, I still today think it was a really refreshing take on how to test a process for what it’s worth.

Is the “single pane of glass” the new black? 

If you somehow haven’t met the concept yet, single pane of glass (SPOG) is a term used in IT and management fields referring to a tool that unifies data or interfaces across several different sources and presents them in a single view.

The lure of the concept is easy to understand. 

Who wouldn’t like to have one single tool to go to and immediately see or control whatever it is that needs seeing or controlling?

The concept is so attractive, maybe in particular with centralised, functionally organised teams, that it more often than not leads to premature sub optimisation around individual silver bullet tools, that rarely deliver on all their promises.

Lowering your team’s cognitive load, while delivering on all external expectations is a difficult proposition to say no to.

In a situation like this, it’s wise to consider whom else you’re expecting to use your SPOG tool, and how it fits their ways of working and operating. 

Do you need your users to do some work based upon the findings in your SPOG tool? 

What additional cognitive load will that mean for their team?

Is there a way to meet your users halfway? 

Send relevant signals or data that you expect actions on to where they normally operate, rather than have them log onto yet another tool?

This is probably one of the reasons I really appreciate the idea behind Spotify’s Backstage. With developers being one of any company’s greatest assets, it’s foolish not to optimise for their best flow of work and throughput.

Below Daniel Bryant’s excellent visualisation from #kubecon on the increasing level of cognitive load experienced during his developer career. 

Anyways, key point of this post: 

if you’re in a team either already having or about to have a SPOG tool to lower your own cognitive load, please consider the cognitive load effect of your tool on your development teams. 

Try at least to make it cognitive load neutral, if you can’t help to lower overall cognitive load.

I’ve long been a proponent of the #fourkeys DORA metrics as both the simplest, and most comprehensive way to measure a team’s performance in software development and operations.

The four key metrics are: 

- Deployment Frequency
How often an organization successfully releases to production. 

- Lead Time for Changes
The amount of time it takes a commit to get into production.

- Change Failure Rate
The percentage of deployments causing a failure in production.

- Time to Restore Service
How long it takes an organization to recover from a failure in production. 

Following these consistently over time should give any organisation a good idea if they’re improving or not, and where to focus if metrics are not meeting set goals.

Here’s a 30 min video on how the insurance company Liberty Mutual is using the #fourkeys to help the teams identify bottlenecks, move towards a test-driven development approach, and realize improvements in their overall performance.

Sometimes I hear when talking to folks across industries but with the same cloud goals: “No, we’re not planning to lift and shift anything when we move to Cloud. We will build everything from scratch.” 

While I intuitively appreciate the ambition, I personally see a few problematic factors with the strategy:

1) it will take long(er) to get immediate value delivery as everything is being rebuilt and rethought.

2) building in the now, with the current knowledge, constraints and context, for tomorrow, is building future tech debt. By the time you’re cloud native and have gone live, you’ve probably made a few new bad choices, that will do well with some refactoring. (Still, much better tech debt wise than with the old application/system.)

3) getting the product out to real customers to validate previous (and new) functionality may be challenging but without it, how do you know that you’re building something your customers will appreciate, once you start shipping it?

Having grown old with either wisedom or experience, or both, I know that sometimes (semi) lift and shifting is a fairly ok strategy.

I say “semi” because actively and transparently acknowledging that certain technical choices, tools and ways (of working) have become obsolete and will need to be replaced (sooner rather than later), is the only honest option on the table for any technical leader. 

Keeping that to oneself, is selfish, inconsiderate and doesn’t do any good to the leader or his/her team. 

With clarity and transparency on the table, initially going down a suboptimal path may very well be a good strategy, as long as one’s learning from going to cloud is practically validated and tech debt shown in the open, with the ambition to be addressed, sooner rather than later.

There were two events in 2007 that set in motion powers that today define many aspects of our online lives. 

One is given to most. It’s the unveiling of iPhone in January 2007 and sales start in the US in June the same year. 

The second is the establishment of the Open Handset Alliance in November the same year, the organisation behind Google’s Android smartphone platform.

For me personally, none of them seemed overly significant at the time.

After all, I was working as a product manager at the world’s largest mobile manufacturer that in 2007 held a global mobile device market share of more than 50%, and upwards 70% in smartphones. I was also working with the absolute high end of Nokia’s offering: Nokia Nseries. Ofcourse I was biased.

Nokia phones were found in more than 1 billion pockets around the world and were in many countries the very first contact with the Internet. Nokia had at the time reached more people than any other tech brand. Only Coca-Cola and Colgate were more known.

Our market dominance was total in 2007. 

We had just launched the most tech packed mobile device to date, Nokia N95, with a GPS, 5MP camera and a bunch of other features not previously seen in mobile phones. 

The tagline read: “It’s what computers have become.”

There are many books as to why things went sideways in the following years, so I’ll leave that discussion aside.

I can say it’s not because we didn’t clearly see in which direction the market was going. Early on, we recognised that the future was about ecosystems and that those controlling ecosystems, would be calling the shots. 

Facebook stands as an excellent example as to what can happen when ecosystem owners decide to shut one out. Mark Zuckerberg’s fortunes have more then halved following the privacy changes implemented on both iOS and Android.

That’s why the Android option wasn’t really an option for Nokia. Playing on Google’s terms alongside Samsung, HTC, LG and others wasn’t an appealing prospect at all for a company that had been the biggest player of all for nearly two decades in a highly competitive and dynamic market.

At Nokia, we recognised that the future would be equally about sticky and emersive services as features and specs of mobile devices. Many acquisitions in this space were made; maps and navigation, music, messaging, and so on. 

But going from stand-alone services to an intuitive and seamless experience between service, device and the user, took far too long. And the market doesn’t wait for too long, not even on the most beloved brands.

So, here is a case where both the vision and strategy were right, but where failures in execution ultimately took down the world’s largest mobile manufacturer.

Recently I finished Eliyahu Goldratt’s audiobook “Beyond The Goal”. 

The audiobook is a series of lectures held by Dr. Goldratt giving an overview of the Theory of Constraints and it’s different applications. This includes production management from "The Goal", selling reliability from "It's not luck" and project management from "Critical Chain". 

If you haven't read the books, it can give you and overview/introduction and if you have read the books it can give a refresher.

Lots of great takeaways, but my personal favourite: 

- What benefits will any technology bring if we neglect to change the “rules”?

Here, Dr. Goldratt uses the example of ERP system introductions into enterprises. 

Before ERP, data aggregation, validation, report generation, checking and cross-checking were highly manual tasks that took weeks and months to complete. 

As ERP systems were introduced, tasks that before took weeks and months to complete, just took minutes and hours. 

However, only a handful of enterprises changed their ways of working, processes and practices to reap the business benefits of the much faster turnaround time by the ERP systems. 

Others carried on as before, with monthly reporting cycles, rather than more frequently as was possible, failing to reap benefits of the new systems.

This is an unabridged and unfiltered Goldratt in a lecture series. Lots of candor and passion in every line delivered.

The theories are powerful and solidly anchored in Dr. Goldratt’s experiences. 

The audiobook and Dr. Goldratt’s deliverance makes one understand and appreciate the lasting impact Goldratt has had on the DevOps movement.

A question that anyone who’s been working with public cloud platforms long enough is bound to get is “how do we ensure application portability between different cloud vendors?”

It’s almost as if all applications up until that Cloud point in time have been highly movable, hosting/OS/middleware agnostic and remarkably flexible.

Hate to come with the spoiler, but the amount of lock-ins on premise are sometimes the very reason companies go down the cloud path.

Regardless of how the things may be in the on premise land, the question of portability (or simply a plan B) is relevant to ask in any responsible company, even if the plan may never need to be put into action. 

My answer to the question is rather self explanatory.

The only way to ensure portability between clouds, VMs, containers, serverless options or whatever other compute options may be relevant, is by ensuring deep knowledge and ownership of one’s code base as a first. 

As a second, decent enough understanding of one’s dependencies, both upstream and downstream ones. 

That’s it! Boring and simple (to say, not do) for sure, but an application not fullfilling the two criteria above, is a security, operational and business liability, regardless where it’s hosted, on premise or in cloud.

Breaking down a business strategy to individual team contributions is hard as a first.

Making sure that the various teams understand the overarching strategy, their own roles in realising it and how they should play together is even harder.

And to top it off, from own experience, I’ve seen that ‘culture eats strategy for breakfast’. 

What Peter Drucker meant with the quote wasn’t that strategy is unimportant, but rather that an empowering and trustful culture is a far more given indicator of future success. 

So, when setting a strategy consider and note down where you’re coming from so that future progress or lack thereof is crystal clear, engage your teams to figure out how they best contribute to the strategy in the short, mid and long run and then compare how your teams’ individual contributions play together with those of other teams. 

And most important of all, continuously invest in your culture. 

In business like in life, making tough choices, pivoting on the direction and generally responding fast enough to changing conditions, is much easier when there is trust around!

First time I personally learnt the importance of monitoring (and observability in general) was in 2013, when I production launched my first integration project to an external website hosting our games and connecting to our platform in real-time over SSL for transaction settlements. 

At NetEnt we had a proactive approach of constantly monitoring number of logged on players and reacting when the trend went southwards. The tools were not particularly pretty (I recall Hobbit and Nagios) but they did what they were supposed to do. 

Constantly monitoring hundreds of external integrations and alerting when the trends dipped for whatever reason, ensured that we could rectify issues on our end faster, notify customers of issues on their end, sometimes before they even knew about them themselves and overall ensure a minimal downtime for our games (and in extension ensure earnings).

Fast forward a decade later and while the observability tooling has matured immensely, it’s still far from given that teams see it as a given ingredient of their day-to-day, as it deserves to be.

Below image from one of the #googlecloud online course materials, depicts well the importance of monitoring as the foundation of product reliability. 

Monitoring reveals what needs urgent attention and provides trends and application usage patterns which can help with better capacity planning and improve an user’s experience of our products.

With monitoring, we can ensure continued system operations, uncover trend analysis over time, build dashboards, alert our team members when systems violate predefined objectives, and provide data for improved incident response, just to name a few benefits. 

To be truly reliable, the very best products must be deployed into environments with enough capacity to handle the load. 

Great products also need automated testing, in a CI/CD pipeline. 

Postmortems and root cause analysis are the team's way of letting the stakeholders know why an incident happened and why it's unlikely to happen again. 

We need our products to improve continually, and we need data we receive from monitoring to make sure that happens. 

We need dashboards to provide business intelligence so our teams have the data they need to do their jobs. 

We need automated alerts because humans tend to look at things only when there's something sufficiently important to look at. 

Also, we need monitoring tools that help provide data crucial to debugging an application’s functional and performance issues.

Finally, observability to me, has a natural place in any team’s Definition of Done. If it isn’t already, you should definitely look to include it!

The quote “Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM” has been around since the 70s. 

What it really means is that nobody ever got fired for buying the Incumbent Mega Brand. 

It’s perfectly on point to replace IBM with any “safe”  brand of your choice. 

Who coined it remains unknown, but it remains as indicative as ever of how plenty of companies (still) approach their tech procurement decisions.

The question springs to mind. 

Why have the Incumbent Mega Brands been so successful? 

Why have companies consistently bought more expensive, but less functional technology?

For one, because the incumbent mega brands broadly met the functional requirements set out by the company. 

And probably because the same technology was also used by the company’s competitors. 

As a result, competitive technology differentiation was off the table, but at least there were no “failures” due to the “wrong” procurement decision. 

Does it still work to play it safe and rely solely on incumbent mega brands in today’s highly volatile and disruptive world?

No. Not if your company is in it for the long run.

One big driving force at play here is the incredible innovation speed of consumer technology, which in turn is driving, influencing and challenging how we work in our companies and what sort of products our companies are offering to our consumers.

With technology as the engine of innovation, choosing the incumbent mega brand is no longer the safe career option. It’s probably the easiest one, but more often than not, the wrong one.

#innovation #technology

Earlier today I finished "Clean Agile - Back to Basics" by Robert C Martin, colloquially known as "Uncle Bob". 

Released in 2020, the book reintroduces Agile values and principles for a new generation of developers. 

At it's core, Agile is simple but over the years, a number of misconceptions, distractions and superfluous additions have made it harder to use Agile, than was originally intended. 

Uncle Bob, was one of the 17 people who met at the Snowbird ski resort in Utah, in February 2001. They were all leading experts in extreme programming, scrum, and adaptive software development, who all wanted to make software development easier. 

It's wrong to say that they "invented" Agile right there and then. 

Rather, they collectively formulated the Agile Manifesto based on a large body of previous, battle-tested work as well as own and others' experiences.

The profound effect of the manifesto on the world (Yes! On the world, as the software is eating the world!) is unquestionable and has since led to even the traditional enterprises seeking to become "agile". 

In "Clean Agile - Back to Basics", Uncle Bob, deservedly puts the focus back on the often forgotten technical practices of Agile: TDD (Test Driven Development), Refactoring, Simple Design, Pair Programming, Coding Standards, Collective Ownership, Continuous Integration, Sustainable Pace etc. 

In the case of some topics, where Uncle Bob's opinions are not aligned with the general mainstream views, he has intentionally invited others to contribute and add additional perspective. This goes for the topics of agile coaches and (large) scaling of agile teams.

It is ofcourse an opinionated book and Uncle Bob gives a fair warning about that already in the opening paragraphs. However, I personally, have found that many of  the opinions and thoughts resonate well with my own.

I'd definitely recommend the book to anyone who's interested in understanding what more Agile could be and what additional value it could bring developers, companies and our communities.

One-two weeks back, I finished “Empowed - ordinary people, extraordinary products” by Marty Cagan and Chris Jones of Silicon Walley Product Group.

Here’s my review, while the book is still fresh in my memory.

Marty’s previous book “Inspired” puts focus on the role of the product manager, while “Empowered” centres around how to create a good product culture, capable of creating extraordinary products. 

The authors reveal the “secrets” of world class product organisations, in an easily digestible and relatable way. 

The book covers:

- How empowered product teams are different from "feature teams" used by most companies to build technology products.

Multi tenant or multi cluster?

Yesterday I read an inspirational piece on Mercedes Benz and the scale of their Kubernetes operations. They manage more than 900 Kubernetes clusters used by hundreds of standalone development teams. 

The development teams simply order their brand new Kubernetes clusters, be that for dev, staging or prod, through an automated process and receive it within minutes after making the request. 

While there are some choices made that I have problems understanding the logic behind, I find it really refreshing to hear of the multi cluster approach to Kubernetes at this scale.

A few years back I was hoping to do a similar (albeit smaller) thing, but the idea was shot down rationalised by increased complexity, harder operability and a number of other reasons up the same alley.

Still, the benefits of multi cluster over multi tenant approach are many more than drawbacks.

Multi cluster creates a natural and self given isolation between applications not being owned or managed by the same team. (In case many clusters per team sounds like overdoing it, you can isolate higher up in the abstraction chain, ie per department, or per domain.)

It also helps in workload decoupling as any between-service connections need to be explicitly defined and configured rather than just inherited through cluster sharing.

It decreases the blast radius in case of cluster issues. In case a cluster goes down it no longer takes all your applications along with it, but only those residing in that cluster. And if there is a high availability setup in place for a given application, the worst that could happen, is service degradation. 

If cluster creation is “easy” (or at least easy to consumers of the same) and everything is done as code, then there is no pointing in patching and pampering aging clusters. 

Whenever it’s appropriate, redeploying all workloads in a new, freshly patched and updated cluster should be the preferred method. This alone further underlines that infrastructure should be viewed as cattle, rather than pets. Ephemeral, transient, easily consumable, reliable (while it exists) and measurable.

And lastly, the multi cluster approach empowers team autonomy, through a clear(er) responsibility and accountability division between consumer (product development) teams and producer (platform DevOps) teams.

Can you think of any other benefits or drawbacks of multi cluster vs multi tenant approach? Would love to hear it in the comments field (or in a DM if you don’t want to share sensitive details).

FOMO in the workplace. Friend or foe?

First, what is FOMO, or Fear Of Missing Out? 

Simply put, it’s fear of not being included in something. 

In a workplace context, it can be a new, interesting project, a decision/discussion/collaboration forum of any kind, or anything else that the person experiencing FOMO feels that he/she should take part in.

Like most things in life, FOMO is neither just good or bad.

It can lead to employees becoming too distracted with projects that their coworkers are involved in, instead of focusing on their own priorities and tasks.

It can also lead to employees wishing they were part of a different department or team, causing them to feel disengaged in their current position and tasks. 

If FOMO is producing inefficient employees, you must address the issue. 

At the same time, FOMO helps make employees feel engaged, wanting to take part and contribute which leads to increased employee productivity. 

There are some simple strategies to employ to keep FOMO a friend and not a foe.

1. Limit the nr of messages sent.
2. Target how messages are sent.
3. Be strategic about who sends the information.
4. Be exclusive about who receives the information.
5. Pay attention how the message is crafted.

If you’d like to read more about why FOMO matters in the corporate sector, there is this excellent, short article by Deloitte: https://lnkd.in/eSm5j4Sq.

The word has it that Jeff Bezos issued his API Mandate in 2002. And although 20 years have since passed, it's importance for Amazon's success (and other companies that were wise to follow suite) can not be understated. Copied below the short but concise API Mandate that helped transform both Amazon and change the entire industry. 

1. All teams will henceforth expose their data and functionality through service interfaces.

2. Teams must communicate with each other through these interfaces.

3. There will be no other form of inter-process communication allowed: no direct linking, no direct reads of another team’s data store, no shared-memory model, no back-doors whatsoever. The only communication allowed is via service interface calls over the network.

4. It doesn’t matter what technology you use.

5. All service interfaces, without exception, must be designed from the ground up to be externalize-able. That is to say, the team must plan and design to be able to expose the interface to developers in the outside world. No exceptions.

6. (The mandate closed with:) Anyone who doesn’t do this will be fired. Thank you; have a nice day!
