I recently finished listening to the excellent “Building Microservices” 2nd Edition by Sam Newman. The 2nd edition that came out in August 2021 is a complete rewrite of the previous best selling edition from 2015.

The audiobook which is more than 21h long at 1x speed (still haven’t learnt to listen faster I’m afraid) gives a broad overview of all aspects related to microservices. 

Setting off with a firm foundation in the basic concepts, it goes further, and covers all aspects of the software delivery process, and how they are impacted by adopting a microservice architecture.

Sam’s breakdown of the microservices architecture model is insightful, honest and well written. He discusses the trade offs openly and without much bias, and does a great job of comparing different models and techniques.

Sam states three key reasons for microservices. 

First one is independent replayability and taken to the extreme, zero downtime independent deployability. In other words, the ability to make a change to a piece of functionality, deploy that functionality, and do so in a way that the rest of the system doesn't need to change, which in turn limits the scope of each release, but also implements that deployment in such a way that one gets zero downtime deployment.

Second one is isolation of data and isolation of processing around data. With a microservice, you can isolate the data and the processing that acts on that data. You can clearly delineate the services that touch personally identifiable information, and therefore require more oversight, a higher degree of governance, and need to be audited. And the services that never touch sensitive data and don't talk to the services that touch sensitive data can therefore be separated out.

The third reason is when you're looking to achieve a higher degree of organizational autonomy. It’s when you want teams to be able to make sound decisions faster, shoulder due responsibilities, roll out better software more often, and reduce the amount of coordination those teams need with other parts of your organization.

While the audiobook was great and convenient, I’ll probably be looking to buy an e-book or hard copy as I’m certain I’ll be using it as a reference piece with pointers to further deep dives, for years to come.

Do you treat observability as an afterthought or a first class citizen? While many won’t admit to the former, it’s how unfortunately many teams and companies deal with observability. As a necessary evil rather than a source of information for future improvements.

I recall how we in my Delivery Platform team had set up a dashboard with all the systems we were maintaining and simple red/amber/green traffic lights to indicate health of each service. There were also indicators on continuously scheduled CI/CD pipeline runs indicating health of our delivery platform and it’s components. The dashboard hang over our desks and as soon as anything went amber or red, there’d be someone in the team looking further into the cause.

While seemingly pretty simplistic, this dashboard gave us both the confidence and knowledge to be able to respond to any query coming to the team regarding uptime, stability or other operational aspects of our services offering.

Here and now, we’d also spend time to update the dashboard with new or removed services as well as tweak settings to ensure relevant alerting and remove false positives. 

The benefits of staying on top of one’s services, platforms and systems can not be overstated. 

This is why I really think each (feature or platform alike) team should at least engage in daytime observability (if they are not on-call responsible during off work). By having someone dedicated (and rotating) in the team to respond in case health metrics start to deteriorate, fosters a culture of ownership, well needed familiarity with troubleshooting and last but not least ensures that the issues are dealt with as soon as they appear and that future improvements are never too far away.

What’s is the best approach for Brents in any organisation?

For context, Brent is the character from “The Phoenix Project” by Gene Kim, George Spafford and Kevin Behr. 

Brent is the most knowledgeable engineer at the fictional Parts Unlimited. He has a monopoly on knowledge of the company's IT systems and therefore must be present for anything to get done.

Brent is basically indispensable and as such something of a bottleneck, as his time, like everyone else’s is limited, although he probably will and most often goes to extreme lengths to fix things.

How heroic it very well may sound, in the longer run it’s rather a disservice to the company as well as Brent himself. 

To the company, as it intentionally puts all its eggs (ie dependencies) into one basket. And to Brent himself, as he can never really have any time off.

I remember well taking over after a Brent in a previous role. He himself had been in that role for a couple a years and basically had defined most of what the role was about. He had also worked with some of the company’s biggest customers and given them technical solutions that were pretty nonstandard, and frequently risked being forgotten and not reimplemented (by others). Ofcourse as soon as something like that would happen, Brent would rush in to save the day and restore production.

Filling out such big shoes and expectations was anything but simple, and all I could do was to be honest about what I knew and didn’t, and consistently document and share further any integration particulars and gradually, with customer’s good will and buy-in align any particulars with our company’s set standards.

As I too changed the role, many nonstandards had been removed, but not all. 

Still, I must say that I am happy that the next person in line didn’t have nearly as much work or effort continuing standardisation and that the customer continued to be happy with provided services, with fewer errors and SPoFs overall.

How much (in %)  of your (Cloud) infrastructure code is in version source control? 

How many of your (Cloud) infrastructure deployments are 4-eyed reviewed, tested and automatically deployed to their respective environments?

While many companies go all-in on various kinds of KPIs, metrics and OKRs, I haven’t really seen enough companies put sufficient focus on having most of their infrastructure changes done via Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC).

I recall back in 2018, as we were taking our first steps into public Cloud at NetEnt, how new and even frightening IaC felt to many in our infrastructure engineering teams. 

Gradually we moved the needle over and got a decent IaC coverage for our Cloud and on premise infrastructure but it was far from given back in the day, when we initially started talking about it.

To my surprise, as I was coming to SEB, I was expecting a similar situation, but it turned out things were quite the opposite. 

Nearly all of our acceptance and production infrastructure in Cloud is in version source control and highly automated, with all the benefits of that approach, such as visibility, repeatability, traceability, resilience, control and governance. 

By having IaC as a first class citizen for all working in Cloud, and maintaining the discipline throughout, many other benefits realise as well such as: decreased overall risk, stable & consistent environments for faster product and infrastructure iterations, easier cost optimisation, self documenting and simpler onboarding. 

As I mentioned, achieving solid Infrastructure-as-Code practices is no small investment time or people wise. 

It has its own learning curve and the steepness of the curve varies across different IaC tools and ofcourse the maturity of your (infrastructure) developers.

However, it’s the only feasible solution if you’re going for scale in public Cloud. 

Not having IaC is not a problem if you are running a single web application on an compute instance behind a load balancer. But it’s an entirely different matter when you are running a web application, a database, a Kubernetes cluster, and some serverless functions to support all the services of your application.

That problem exacerbates when you need to run many environments (hundreds and thousands). Consider your development, acceptance, and production environments. You have to provision and maintain all that infrastructure. 

Doing that manually is a massive burden and time commitment (and of course highly prone for human error). 

However, doing it as-code, gives almost immediate benefits. 

This investment into a more sound infrastructure process using infrastructure as code will pay dividends for the entire life of the product or company.

This is what I think. What do you think?

You don’t need a dedicated CI tool to do CI (Continuous Integration). Equally, you may not be doing CI, only because you have a CI tool.

Jez Humble has a simple test to determine if a team is really practicing CI. 

1) Are all the engineers pushing their code into trunk / master (not feature branches) on a daily basis? 

2) Does every commit trigger a run of the unit tests? 

3) When the build is broken, is it typically fixed within 10 minutes? 

If the answer is yes to all three questions, congratulations! You are practicing Continuous Integration.

A while back I heard a phrase regarding Kubernetes that since has stuck with me.

It basically said that the “Kubernetes is the only multi cloud API”.

It’s true, on so many levels. Kubernetes is at the heart of many of public cloud providers’ own services, from Gmail, Netflix to Youtube and many other services used at a billion plus people scale, being available 24/7. 

Initially developed by a group of Google engineers, the first Kubernetes commit on GitHub was made on June 6, 2014, paving the way for the release of Kubernetes v1.0 on July 10, 2015.

Today, Kubernetes is the leading container-orchestration platform, with countless companies building on and migrating to this popular open-source technology.

As popular as Kubernetes is, it’s not necessarily the easiest runtime platform to develop on, manage or deploy to. 

Which is why it’s great that many public cloud providers go to great lengths to ensure that the operational and development burden as well as adoption is made both easier and smoother.

Which is why I’m surprised sometimes by folks asking for plain, vanilla Kubernetes. 

Putting together bits and pieces to make a full product offering on top of a Kubernetes runtime, when there are bigger fish that do that exact thing at a much larger scale, feels very much like a total waste of good engineers’ time and efforts. 

The focus of your Kubernetes engineers should be on making further adaptions to your own business and development context and ensuring that development teams’ onboarding onto your Kubernetes runtime is as smooth, fast, secure and reliable as possible. 

You should ensure that your Kubernetes engineers very well understand the inner workings of Kubernetes and take all possible advantage of the operational scale and learnings public cloud providers put in their managed Kubernetes offerings.

And should you at some point need to move from one cloud to another, then you can bet the cloud providers will have created appropriate migration tools.

Many aspects of Lean have become commonplace in the Western world such as the concept of Kaizen (continuous improvement to create more value with less waste) but true implementation often comes short of the original intention.

In the linked post, the author, Tracey Richardson, describes how at Toyota no one was ever happy or complacent with just maintaining something. 

While creating standards (or processes) to achieve certain business or other types of objectives, was an essential first step, it wasn’t the end of line.

Far from it. In the DAMI thinking process, Define is just the first step. 

The second one, Achieve is about reaching the defined objectives, whilst constantly measuring your progress. 

Although reaching an objective once or twice may be perfectly doable, an unsubstainable and unrepeatable process won’t cut it for long.

Hence why the third step in the thinking process, Maintain, is really important. 

And finally the last step, Improve, which tends to be the most misunderstood one. 

Continuous Improvement is not easy, particularly when you are asked to measure it and prove it. 

You may change something every day to make it appear like you are improving, but improvement without measures is waste. 

Kaizen without value isn’t Kaizen. 

You must measure value. 

Without clear standards this is impossible.

Gil Broza delivers an excellent elevator pitch (for a bit longer elevator rides) as to what constitutes true agile (senior) management. Quoted below:

“The key premise is to have the company’s systems of work mostly operate themselves, instead of being controlled by management and powerful stakeholders. In each system, people have a high level of autonomy and they collaborate toward outcomes. Everybody sees the work and follows the same criteria for choosing what to do next. They clear blockages to the best of their abilities.

You and the other senior leaders ensure that each system ‘points in the right direction’ in terms of the organization’s priorities and constraints. For that purpose, you work as a team on vision, strategy, capabilities, and alignment; you review them frequently and adjust as needed.

This system is the result of the humans that create and operate it. Therefore, you also help them grow, increase their independence, and operate from a place of greater responsibility. You do that through frequent touchpoints with individuals and with entire groups. You make it safe to fail, to learn, and to collaborate, and you model these behaviours. You keep watching the systems for problems and opportunities, and lead organization-level changes to improve the systems.”

In many aspects, Nokia was a place of incredible innovation, fresh thinking and immensely forward looking.

But as iOS and Android market share grew, our arrogance diminished, eventually forcing Nokia into a total restructuring and refocusing and the mobile device business becoming a side note in the whole schema of things.

I’m very grateful for both the good and the bad years as they thought me the importance of being honest to myself and those around me (regardless where I or they are in the command chain), and that the most dangerous enemies come from places where you least expect them and they often seek to change and disregard established rules of play to their benefit.

Over the course of the years, from time to time, I meet this notion of software being as good as “done” once it’s code complete and running nicely and safely in production on some arbitrary hosting platform. 

As if it no longer needs to be changed, modified or adapted to cater for changes in its surroundings. 

As if it’s some kind of infinity machine, that just keeps on running flawlessly once deployed.

Nothing could be more wrong. Software is almost as living as the people writing it. It can’t be shelved and expected to age like a good wine. In fact it doesn’t age gracefully at all.

Maybe this notion stems from the fact that while it’s “easy” to estimate how many man hours a software delivery will take and very roughly when it might finish, it’s far more difficult to indicate how much the maintenance and upkeep of it will cost and for how long it will be needed.

One could liken developing and maintaining software to ￼raising and taking care of a ￼plant. 

A plant requires frequent watering, certain temperatures, and sufficient amounts of light to grow just like software needs having its dependencies frequently updated and it’s code modified in small increments, so that it continues to satisfy current needs of the business.

Now and then, a plant needs nutrition to grow and stay healthy. Equally so, software may need to adopt new libraries and new functionalities, to cater for changes in requirements or usage patterns. 

Throughout, the plant needs trimming, and doing away with dead leaves and branches, so that new ones can come in their place. In the case of software, this translates to doing away with no longer needed parts of the code or moving out functionalities that may be better suited residing elsewhere.

And if you’ve taken well care of the plant so far and if it has outgrown it’s current pot, it may be high time to change the pot to a bigger or otherwise more suitable one. ￼

In the world of software, this equals to changing the hosting platform, and more often than not, having to reevaluate parts or all of its architecture, and refactor accordingly so that the software can draw scaling, performance and other benefits in thus changed hosting environment.

The point I’m trying to make, beside that I’m the one with green fingers in our household, is that software easily zombifies, if it goes uncared and unattended for longer periods of time. 

And the further away from understanding how the software a team is responsible for, really works, the harder it gets to for the team to maintain, operate and develop it.

This is what I think. What do you think?

I’ve been spreading the word about the DORA DevOps Quick Check for a year or two now. 

The people I’ve been talking to about it generally fall into two categories; those who get it and who want to use it, or are already using it, and those who superficially get it, but counter with a number of reasons as to why the check is not relevant in their context, with their constraints.

Here’s a quick intro as to what the Quick Check is all about.

Basically it consists of five questions, takes less than 1 minute to answer and benchmarks your team against your industry as a whole. What’s there not to like, right!?

These are the questions:

- How long does it take to go from code committed to code successfully running in production?

- How often does your organization deploy code to production or release it to end users?

- How long does it generally take to restore service when a service incident or a defect that impacts users occurs?

- What percentage of changes to production or releases to users result in degraded service and subsequently require remediation?

- What is the principal industry of your organisation?

And that’s it! These figures is something I believe every team member should know by heart and strive to improve. And you don’t have to be a traditional feature dev team to measure these metrics. You can just as well be an engineering team releasing code changes to your infrastructure and systems. 

I truly believe that frequently releasing code to production, with as short lead time as possible from code commit to production deploy, is a North Star any team should be setting for themselves. 

Restoration of service and percentage of faulty changes puts the spotlight on operational practices and quality gates, which are as crucial as the ability to release often and fast.

Most companies on a public Cloud adoption path tend to agree that doing an application “lift and shift” is generally a poor idea. That is, if you don’t have committed and viable plans what to do about such workloads in short, mid and long term. 

What I haven’t read or heard equally much about from companies adopting public Cloud is that “lift and shifting” on premise ways of working and collaborating within and across teams is an equally bad idea as lift and shifting applications.

While it’s possible to do both types of “lift and shift” and still reap benefits of a public Cloud migration, sticking to any of them is not advisable in the long run. 

Public cloud should be seen as a blank canvas, a blank sheet full of opportunities to do away with all previous toil and focus one’s energy on true value adding activities. 

If your job on premise is about maintaining, upgrading and generally making sure a particular service is running, and meeting consumer requests delivered in order tickets, then it may seem reasonable to set up a similar service in a public cloud context and carry on as before. 

But by doing that you’d be 1) making yourself blind for all new faster, better and more secure ways of running a similar service in a public cloud context, 2) making yourself blind for all new (self-service, APIs etc) ways your consumers could be using and further enriching your services.

It’s in the very nature of a public cloud architectural setup to allow for both greater feature team autonomy within set boundaries and highly controlled centralised platform governance across all of company’s public cloud resources. 

In other words, achieving true DevSecOps while many times troublesome on premise is definitely more within reach in public cloud due to the very nature of the hyperscaler platforms where everything is programmable, auditable and built for massive scale, extensibility and operability. 

The 2021 State of DevOps Report further underlines that observation.

“Teams continue to move workloads to the cloud and those that leverage all five capabilities of cloud* see increases in software delivery as well as in organizational performance.” (See link below for full report)

Embracing new ways of working doesn’t come easy or without a cost but it’s guaranteed to pay dividends in the long run to those who are willing to broaden their perspectives and combine their extensive on premise know-how with the Cloud ditto. 

And not only that, it’s also guaranteed to pay dividends to any company making this type of commitment and investment in their employees. 


* 5 capabilities of Cloud: On demand self-service. Broad network access. Resource pooling. Rapid elasticity. Measured service.

- Team culture makes a large difference to a team’s ability to deliver software and meet or exceed their organizational goals. Inclusive teams with a positive culture experienced less burnout during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Quite a few years ago now, I was in charge of an integration project between my at time employer’s web games platform (better known to the industry as CasinoModule) and a up and  coming turnkey casino platform with both a B2B and B2C offering. 

Up until then I had done a great number of integrations, most standard and a few bespoke. Most of them were done with me in direct contact with customer’s developers, who’d be gradually iterating their code, releasing it and then us jointly testing the release and figuring out what still needed fixing, until at the end of project, I’d sign off on the integration and we’d go live.

However, I wasn’t quite prepared for what this particular integration effort would entail. It started off with an extraordinarily thourogh deep dive into our integration manuals, handbooks, API reference docs and whatever other integration documention that had been produced. Any possible ambiguity in the documentation, big or small, was brought up and further queried about. Anything just briefly covered in documentation was particularly asked about and explored at length. While I knew our products really well, I can honestly admit getting this amount of questions, only to get additional follow up questions, was both stressful and rewarding at the same time, as it forced me to learn our product at an incredible depth, at an amazing speed. 

Only when all questions had been answered did the customer start architecting the integration between the two platforms. And after that, the architecture was handed off to a development team that didn’t get the chance to iterate on their assumptions and improve the integration incrementally until fully complete. Instead they simply had to deliver according to the architectural blueprint. 

Given the time and energy spent on requirements gathering, analysis, architecture etc, one could think this would have been one of the best and most stable integrations ever made. However, it was quite the opposite.

The first integration attempt was full of bugs and was rejected. False assumptions had been drawn, so new architectural blueprints had to be made and handed off to the dev team. Gradually the integration became satisfactory enough, so it went live. However, every once in a while, something in the integration would break, and the customer would come blaming us for the issue. In a vast majority of cases though, the issue would be on customer’s side, probably due to some other new integration project ongoing at the time and the vast discrepancy between architectural blueprints and visions and the reality on the ground.

The main point of the story is that while its necessary to do due requirements gathering, create architectural blue prints, and come up with initial product visions, it's equally important just to get going, to learn, allow oneself to pivot and (continuously) make the end product better.

Having worked in IT for many years I’ve seen my share and filled out a good number of assessments, be that DevSecOps, ISO-27001, SDLC Due Dilligence or as in this particular case a Cloud Maturity Assessment.

First, the assessment analyzes where your business sits on the path to transformational cloud maturity. Then, it generates a personalized interactive report to help you plan your cloud adoption roadmap.

Definitely recommended to take the assessment if you want to put your own transformation efforts in a bigger context!

The deeper I go into Uncle Bob’s book on “Clean Architecture”, the more I nod in agreement with both how fundamentally sound and purely logical software architecture really is and yet how difficult it seems to get that right. 

Here a good piece on screaming architecture. 

- Software architectures are structures that support the use cases of the system. Just as the plans for a house or a library scream about the use cases of those buildings, so should the architecture of a software application scream about the use cases of the application.

- Architectures are not (or should not) be about frameworks. Architectures should not be supplied by frameworks. Frameworks are tools to be used, not architectures to be conformed to. If your architecture is based on frameworks, then it cannot be based on your use cases.

- Good architectures are centered around use-cases is so that architects can safely describe the structures that support those use-cases without committing to frameworks, tools, and environment.

- Good software architecture allows decisions about frameworks, databases, web-servers, and other environmental issues and tools, to be deferred and delayed. 

- If your system architecture is all about the use cases, and if you have kept your frameworks at arms-length, then you should be able to unit-test all those use cases without any of the frameworks in place.

Insightful reflections on what a service- and subscription-centric world might look like in 2030, when more or less nothing will be really “owned”. 

Makes me look back at the ambitions and aspirations we put into the Ovi brand back in 2007-2008. Ovi was the brand name for Nokia's Internet services in five areas: Games, Maps, Media, Messaging and Music. 

There was a nagging realisation throughout Nokia, and primarily the Multimedia business unit that I belonged to, that services rather than hardware was to rule the world and that the only way to remain relevant was to try becoming big in the services space. 

Nokia made a number of strategic acquisitions to support this platform building mission, but by the 2009 time frame when most service areas had been launched and an ecosystem began forming, both Apple and Google (through Samsung) had managed to cut Nokia’s global smartphone market share from 50% in Q1 07 to 39% in Q1 09. 

The rest is, as they say, history. 

Anyways, the core idea behind creation of a services ecosystem where both Nokia and partners would offer their services to consumers was sound and well in line with the time. What it fell on, in my view, is some key things. 

- Way too long time-to-market for key services such as Music and Store and by the time they launched, the competitors had already managed to push our similar services with comparable or better feature sets.

- Both services, updates and improvements were released in a Big Bang style too far apart rather than incrementally and frequently. 

- External ecosystem partners (for Store, Maps etc) were looped in far too late in the process, to give needed and candid feedback and to commit already early on. 

- Hardware itself that Nokia was always known for, had been put on a BOM (bill of materials) diet, so that the devices were sporting previous generation chipsets, directly working against the UX and all services running on top of the system. 

Fast forward a decade and a few years more, hardware is still relevant, but now more than ever as a vessel for services. ￼

With IoT more and more beyond the doorstep and inside the house, the 2030 prospects may very well be in line with the article.

”You don’t know what you don’t know.” - Socrates 

I find this statement both humbling and energising. Humbling in that common sense validates it must be true. Energising in that there are oceans of untapped knowledge yet to take on and make one’s own.

It’s also what I’ve witnessed over the years to be the case with Cloud adoption across different technology stacks, and engineers working within these stacks. 

While the basic principles are naturally the same versus traditional on-premise IT, for networks, storage, compute, data processing and analytics etc, there are more or less subtle differences. 

Things are done slightly differently in public Cloud and for a good reason. This is where the rate and speed of innovation is all the greater and some previous limitations and drawbacks removed.

Of course many tasks in public Cloud can be dealt with more or less similar fashion as on-premise, through similar/same tools and systems. 

But by following this path, one may very well be missing on the finer, smarter and better details of what dealing with and solving the same tasks can look like in public Cloud.

That’s why my recommendation to any engineer taking the leap from on-premise to public Cloud (be that a Network, Data, CI/CD etc engineer, DBA or a software developer), is to boldly, experimentally and objectively learn the differentiators and improvements public Cloud brings to his/her work domain(s), take these learnings into practical use and over time make them one’s own.

Your customers (be that internal or external), your company and most importantly you, will thank you for embracing and owning the change!

Today I finished listening to Sam Newman’s recent book “Monolith to Microservices: Evolutionary Patterns to Transform Your Monolith.” 

Sam is far from a newcomer to this area. In 2015, he wrote the extremely popular book “Building Microservices”. In this new companion book, the focus is on decomposition side of things. 

Rather than glorifying Microservices over Monoliths, Sam gives an honest account of the challenges and benefits associated with a microservice architecture, and helps you understand whether starting the journey is even right for you.

For many companies with existing (non-microservice-oriented) systems, the challenge is about how to adopt microservice architectures. How do you take an existing system and rearchitect it without having to stop all other work?

These are the main topics in the book:

- Should you migrate to microservices, and if you should, where do you start?

- How do you incrementally decompose an application?

- Detailed outlines of multiple migration patterns and where they apply.

- Details of database decomposition, including the impact of breaking referential and transactional integrity.

- And last but not least, the growing pains you'll experience as your microservice architecture grows. 

Some of my main take outs from the book. 

- It’s not about this or that architectural method. It’s about creating systems, services and architectures that are highly decoupled, have high deployment frequency (releases to production and end users) and have low mean lead time for changes (time from code commit to production release). 

When satisfactorily met, all of these key (DORA - DevOps Research Agency) metrics lead to companies at a higher degree meeting and anticipating their customers’ wishes and demands. 

So if you can release a monolith frequently enough (here we’re talking hours/days and as a maximum single digit weeks), without being impacted by or impacting other services and dependencies in the process, and do so with no or limited end user impact, than the monolith architecture in that particular SDLC may be the right fit for you. 

- Monoliths are for scale-ups, not start-ups. Sam has a valid point that when you’re looking for a business break-through and probably having to pivot technologically and business wise a couple of times from your original idea, then a micro services architecture may not be the right choice for you. When you’ve later on created a solid enough business for yourself in a scale-up rearchitecting the current monolithic architecture into a microservices one should be fairly easy, and help you scale for the future.

- Whenever you can, go serverless. With the public Cloud vendors releasing more and more Function-as-a-Service functionality, there is no added benefit of voluntarily choosing the operational burden of managing Kubernetes clusters, when you absolutely don’t have to. 

I picked up a few new thoughts from the book and quite liked it, so it’s definitely a recommended read!

"Reliability is any system’s most important feature."

From Google's SRE Workbook. If a system isn't reliable, users won't trust it. If users don't trust a system, when given a choice, they won't use it. Since all software systems are governed by network effects, if a system has no users, it's worth nothing.


"SRE is what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations function."

Benjamin Treynor Sloss - the originator of the term “Site Reliability Engineering” - explaining how SRE emerged at Google.


"Move decision making close to where the information is."

Inspired by David L. Marquet. "Don't move information to authority, move authority to the information. Eventually we turned everything upside down. Instead of one captain giving orders to 134 men, we would have 135 independent, energetic, emotionally committed and engaged men thinking about what we needed to do and ways to do it right. "If you can’t help, don’t be a bottleneck."

In his 2016 letter to shareholders Jeff Bezos writes how a company, of any size, of any age, must be wary not to fall in the trap of Day 2. 

While Jeff Bezos’ letters to shareholders are a goldmine to any business or tech leader, this particular one resonates too well with me personally.

Why should one avoid Day 2, one may ask. As that’s where most companies aspire to be after their initial success and breakthrough. Here’s why. 

“Day 2 is stasis. Followed by irrelevance. Followed by excruciating, painful decline. Followed by death. And that is why it is always Day 1.”

Jeff gives a starter pack of essentials for Day 1 defense: 

“customer obsession”, 
“a skeptical view of proxies”, 
“the eager adoption of external trends”, and 
“high-velocity decision making”.

I’ll deep dive into one of these essentials particularly close to my heart. 

“Good process serves you so you can serve customers. But if you’re not watchful, the process can become the thing. 

This can happen very easily in large organizations. The process becomes the proxy for the result you want. 

You stop looking at outcomes and just make sure you’re doing the process right.”

Over the years, I’ve first hand witnessed how processes start living lives of their own, letting go of the anchors of the original why and gradually growing bigger than was ever intended. 

Those working with the processes are generally too busy ensuring that all things have been crossed off to have any significant time to spend on much needed process improvements, and those who are working in the processes, have generally stopped asking questions and accepted the processes as they are, hoping to pass them through in the smoothest and least bruised way possible.

I’ve discovered that putting both perspectives in the same room, repeatedly, with a mutually shared realisation that things need to change, for the sake of all affected teams and company itself, has consistently given lasting results. It takes time ofcourse, but dividends when continuos process improvements become the norm, are well worth the time spent.

Over the years, I’ve often encountered the argument that a given product is better released through an infrequent, single large batch release than a series of more frequent, small ones. 

The reason has been that batching up a release would give the responsible team(s) more time to “properly” test and validate the release, thus making it more suitable for and less error prone when in production. Another stated reason was that it was time better spent as releasing more often, also would mean needing to spend more time on red tape. 

I personally believe that batching up any application in bigger, infrequent releases, has a direct correlation with the amount of bugs discovered when released in production and gradual, unwarranted build-up of technical debt, as issues are discovered late in the process and corners cut to make the impending release window.

The ideal state in my view is building, testing and releasing upon each code commit, once due review, policy, testing and security requirements have been checked off.

Releasing should happen to a limited but representative subset of users and if error count within that subset would increase, an automated rollback to previous functioning version of the release should occur. 

This feedback loop should ideally be quite fast so that the developers can act upon any issues encountered and apply learnings straight away.

As the number of changes to any small release is limited and easily comprehensible, accessing what (if anything) caused the issue(s) should be a matter of minutes, rather than days or weeks as can be the case in a bigger release gone berserk. 

Jez Humble famously stated: “If it hurts, do it more often, and bring the pain forward”. 

The same heuristic applies to working in smaller release batches. Do it more often, automate the red tape as much as possible and as the Southpark saying goes: Profit!

Great 10 reflections on what it takes to pull through major change. 

While all the points bear their own weight, I particularly appreciate numbers 3, 4, 5 and 7 having first hand experienced major transformations initiated without broad enough people anchoring. 

And while the transformations produced initial successes, they also surfaced new dysfunctions which in turn led to waivering and flickery sponsor support.

Already 2600 years ago Heraclitus coined the term “The only constant in life is change.” And we’ve all in our life time witnessed the mind blowing accelerating rate of technological change. 

So fact of the matter remains. The software is eating the world. Any company is only as good and future proof as it’s ability to adapt and respond to the fast changing software disrupted landscape it operates in.


1. Change is great. It’s changing that’s hard. Looking back, we will appreciate it was worth it. But now, in the middle, is tough.

2. Change is disruptive. Expect disruption, plan for it, and manage it.￼

3. Organizations don’t change, ￼people do. Invest money, time, energy, and thought in your people. Change is successful when it is accepted and adopted by people.

4. All change should happen as fast as possible, but no faster. All change is disruptive, but you must watch for warning signs that it has crossed into dysfunction.

5. In change, both success and failure can become habits. If you are unwilling to do whatever it takes to succeed, don’t start. You will only make the next change harder.

6. What will be different this time? To shift expectations, change your behavior.

7. Sponsors give permission, and they provide protection. Change is risky. It’s important that your people know someone has their back.

8. You cannot change others without changing yourself. Leaders should start by changing themselves before asking others to.

9. Change is social. It’s easier together. The need for connection is strongest when we’re under stress or feel threatened.

10. Cut ties to the present. We are creatures of habit. Leaders must explain why we absolutely can’t stay where we are.

I just finished “Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship” by Robert C. Martin.

Clean Code consists of three parts. The 1st describes the principles, patterns, and practices of writing clean code. The 2nd consists of case studies of increasing complexity. Each case study is an exercise in cleaning up code, ie transforming a code base that has problems into a sound and efficient one. The third part comes with the payoff: a list of heuristics and “smells”. The result is a knowledge base that describes the way we (should) think when we write, read, and clean code.

While the case studies are pretty Java heavy and outdated (2009-ish), one should choose to see the book as a solid basis to use within one’s own programming style and language of choice.

The main lesson is to create code that is small, has a specific purpose and does that one thing.
When functions or methods start to stray into doing multiple things, pull aside those code pieces off on their own and repeat.

I enjoyed the audio book a great deal and got away with a renewed interest in the finer details of the craftsmanship that is good and maintainable programming. When advice from the book is taken to practice, I believe it helps one refactor when possible and write new, better, smaller and tighter code.

I liked the most the segment on how to think of monitoring, with a quote pasted below. 

It’s puzzling to me that many still view logs (rather than metrics) as the single source of truth for anything monitoring related. 

The real truth is more nuanced. 

A log is an event that happened and a metric is a measurement of the health of a system. A metric can have a value, timestamp, and identifier of what that value applies to. Metrics are typically collected at fixed-time intervals. The metric is a fraction of the size of an entire log entry. 

“So there are, in my view, only three kinds of valid monitoring output. 

There are alerts, which say a human must take action right now. Something that is happening or about to happen, that a human needs to take action immediately to improve the situation.

The second category is tickets. A human needs to take action, but not immediately. You have maybe hours, typically, days, but some human action is required.

The third category is logging. No one ever needs to look at this information, but it is available for diagnostic or forensic purposes. The expectation is that no one reads it.”

Although already 3,5 years old, I still feel that this research piece by Gartner covers well the main considerations on how to in an organised and structured way manage, track and optimise Public Cloud costs. 

This particular framework for cost management consists of five main steps:

Plan: Create a forecast to set spending expectations.

Track: Observe your actual cloud spend and compare it with your budget to detect anomalies before they become a surprise.

Reduce: Quickly eliminate resources that waste cloud spending.

Optimize: Leverage the provider’s discount models and optimize your workload for cost.

Mature: Improve and expand your cost management processes on a continual basis.

Having worked with public cloud a while, I often get the question how to accurately predict the cloud costs say a year from now.

In a public cloud setup this math takes a bit more effort than on-premise, and for good reasons.

One major advantage of cloud computing is the usage based pricing. You simply pay for what you consume (or store, or query). While in the on-premise world, you could allocate far more compute and storage than you (ever) would need without anyone raising eyebrows (until you would run out of resources and had to acutely buy more hardware or begin to life cycle), in the public cloud setup such wastefulness has a direct impact on your company’s spend.

Cloud cost management requires you to be disciplined enough to only allocate what you consume, to scale your resource allocation with your growing or decreasing load, auto shut down not used resources during particular hours, performance tweak your applications to do more with less resources and proactively lifecycle any resources that no longer are needed.

Plus, there are also a number of discount and cost cap programs offered by Cloud providers to enroll in that help with cost predictability.

With Cloud adoption exponentially growing for each year, it’s no wonder that also FinOps is becoming more relevant.

Episode 5 tells the story when and how Spotify Operations team realised that own data centers no longer were a leverage but a liability.

If you had asked me 3-4 years ago when I was heading the CI/CD effort at NetEnt whether I might consider a cross-functional setup, I would have probably said no.

At the time we thought we were in a perfect spot. We were in continuous dialogue with our users. We were on top of our backlog. We were delivering product increments as they were coming in, often directly from our users. Plus, we had our systems and tools well monitored, probably better than most other teams.

On the flip side however were the negatives of any single function setup. Most out of team dependencies could and would have an adverse effect on our own deliveries, due to frequent misalignments in priorities and perspectives. 

Gradually though, a cross functional setup emerged as a viable path and we were not late to try it out for size. 

Looking back, I’m pretty proud of what that setup turned into and churned out.

Priorities aligned as the cross functional team became more self-sufficient and autonomous, deliveries became easier, more frequent, and more in line both with what users wanted and what was feasible from different angles of the tech stack, simplicity replaced complexity and in turn increased maintainability. 

And most importantly, the team members came to love and thrive in the new setup!

First time I got a feel for Cloud Computing was in 2013, as I was working on an integration project at NetEnt. 

Normally, integration projects would go on for a few months, with the customer extending their platform according to our definition file, helped along by yours truly, followed by some weeks of testing, bug fixing, configuring and tweaking on both ends and finally releasing the completed integration. 

Back then, it took us a bit more than a week to setup and deliver a dedicated test environment to the customer. Given all the paperwork that had to be done and the inter-team coordination between various single-function teams, we took pride in what we perceived were really fast turnaround times.

While it took us weeks to deliver a test environment, I quickly learned it took the lead developer on the customer side just under 2 hours.

If the latency between AWS and our data centre showed to be too high, he would spin a new instance closer by in matter of minutes. 

And as soon as we discovered a bug, he would push the code changes, restart machines and we’d run another test and have it sorted in no time.

This particular integration went live in record time of 1 month, and half of that time was due to the wait for our environment setups.

That was truly an eye opener!

One of my absolute favourite agile ceremonies is the retrospective. 

While I appreciate the need of stand-ups for frequent alignment, the importance of planning sessions for setting the focus and the joy of demo sessions to show off progress and gather feedback, I like retros for their versatility.

The retros can be exercised in a number of different ways, all with different outcomes and benefits. 

Two formats I’ve learned a lot from, are the timeline and competence mapping exercises.

The first one is about placing a team on a timeline, and listing achievements, issues solved, people joining/leaving and other noteworthy events. It leads to many good discussions within the team and serves as a great morale booster when looking back at all good stuff delivered and all problems sorted. 

The second one is about listing individual team members’ hard and soft competences in a safe, open and non-judgemental environment through the team members themselves doing the rating of their various skills and giving an explanation if they feel the need to motivate further. This exercise puts the finger on team’s overall competence gaps visavi future needs and helps facilitate a much needed discussion within the team how to move the needle forward when it comes to joint competence upskilling.

While kubecost that I touched upon in one of my previous LinkedIn posts is great for increasing awareness, visibility and calling for action, it was the work with Kube Downscaler that brought about the biggest cost savings, particularly when used in Kubernetes clusters that don’t need to be running all the time, such as test, stage etc.

Kube Downscaler scales down / “pauses” Kubernetes workloads (Deployments, StatefulSets, Horisontal Pod Autoscalers and CronJobs) during by the user specified non-work hours. 

It also has an exclusion possibility for those deployments that the user may not want to be down scaled at any time.  

While confusing for many dev teams at first, gradually the teams got used to the Kube Downscaler doing it’s magic while they were asleep. And even better using Kube Downscaler lead to a cost decrease of 35% month on month for the GKE test clusters, with zero or minimal impact on dev teams’ daily work.

So definitely a recommended path, if you have workloads that don’t need to be running all the time but that are not appropriate to be made serverless (yet). 

Here some kudos is due to the guys that did the heavy (code) lifting leading up to these impressive results: Ankur Gupta, Pramod Kumar, Victor Castillo!

In “Think Again: The Power of Knowing What You Don’t Know”, Adam Grant asks us to be humble in our opinions, curious about the alternatives and unafraid of discovery and experimentation.

The last year’s pandemic induced shift to remote work across continents, countries and companies is this year bringing a move to hybrid work, a blended model where some employees return to the workplace and others continue to work from home. Naturally in a vaccination enabled post pandemic world. 

To help through this transition and to reflect on the year gone by, the “2021 Work Trend Index” gathers findings from a study of more than 30,000 people in 31 countries and an analysis of trillions of productivity and labor data points across Microsoft 365 and LinkedIn. 

It also provides perspectives from experts who have spent decades studying collaboration, social capital, and space design at work for decades.

Here are some trends and findings I’ve appreciated in the report. 

- Flexible and hybrid work is here to stay.
- High productivity is masking an exhausted workforce.
- Digital overload is real and still climbing.
- Shrinking networks outside of one’s immediate team is a danger to innovation.

As we venture into the hybrid ways of working, we will need to keep in mind that remote work makes for more siloed teams. Leaders must look for ways to foster the social capital, cross-team collaboration, and spontaneous idea-sharing that’s been driving workplace innovation for decades.

This weekend I successfully completed the course "Site Reliability Engineering: Measuring and Managing Reliability". 

The chapter 19 of SRE Book* starts with an important principle: "Reliability Is the Most Important Feature of Any System". Why this is the case is rather self-evident:

- If a system isn’t reliable, users won’t trust it. 
- If users don’t trust a system, when given a choice, they won’t use it.
- Since all software systems are governed by network effects, if a system has no users, it’s worth nothing.
- You are what you measure, so choose your metrics carefully.

This intermediate level course helps a lot with the last point above, ie with choosing good error budgets, SLIs and SLOs. On a high level it covers following topics: "How to make systems reliable", "Understanding SLIs, SLOs and SLAs" and "Quantifying risks to and consequences of SLOs". 

What I appreciated a lot was seeing concrete, real-life examples of good SLIs and SLOs, figuring out my own SLIs and SLOs and having them reviewed by other course participants. I also enjoyed greatly the whole section on managing risk and both seeing and practicing how the risk spreadsheet quantifies and models various types of reliability risks.

3+ years back as our CI/CD efforts started bearing fruit, we saw our delivery capabilities increasing, but still couldn’t for some reason deliver features faster to our customers. 

We realised one of the speed bumps was the highly manual and time consuming CMP (Change Management Process) that had been built over the course of many years, and probably never revisited or streamlined.

Realising that some degree of process automation was inevitable if we were to achieve anywhere near delivery speeds we aspired to, I took on the role as the manager for the CM team, when the opportunity presented itself. 

It was a team of six senior individuals, with various backgrounds, competences, throughput, motivations and aspirations (just like any other team really).

Motivating the team to change their ITSM tooling, their predispositions, ways of working, and to effectively and continuously streamline and optimise CMP for their end-users’, stakeholders’, company’s and their own sake, is probably one of the toughest leadership learnings I’ve had so far.

Nonetheless, I’m quite happy that both the team, I and our senior management sponsors persisted in driving through this change, as it’s led to far less manual work, faster turnaround times for production changes and happier stakeholder teams!

Already when we created our first SRE teams in 2019, our thinking went beyond a simple rebranding and glorifying of traditional Operations functions, which is an unfortunate dilution of the SRE concept I sometimes see happen.

We set the bar high, really high. We made sure it was clear to team members, other teams and stakeholders that SREs are mainly software craftsmen with propensity for systems engineering. Git is where they make the magic happen, and Operations they treat as a software problem.

We also made sure to establish an “internal consultancy” rather than “support function” mindset with SREs. The distinction is a key one. 

The former prefers interactions between SREs and other teams via mobbing, pairing, pull requests, all of which lead to better feedback loops and end products, rather than in the case of a support function just having to shuffle tickets, provision resources or grant permissions.

Looking back, I can say I’m proud by the change we introduced, by the adoption rate and by the success it’s gradually led to.

This approach enabled a great share of dev teams to assume end to end responsibility, while relying on SRE self-services and platforms on top of commonly shared infrastructure.

Timeline is one of my favourite retrospective formats. I’ve only used it sparingly but each time I’ve come away wondering why I don’t use it more often.

It’s pretty simple too. As the name gives away, at the core is the timeline of team’s major and minor successes and fails taken over a set period of time. 

Start off by deciding on how far back in time you want to go, mark the time stamps clearly and ask the team to think of their major and minor successes and fails, write them down and place them on the timeline. 

Successes on the upper half and fails on the lower half. Set aside at least 10-15 mins for the team members to get into the reflection zone, collect their thoughts, and write them down.

After that go jointly over individual post-it’s by having the team members give a brief account of each and group duplicates or similar ones.

What one pretty fast notices, as most of us like telling about our accomplishments, the timeline retro also gets to serve as an incredible morale and ego booster.

As it happens, we did this retro format earlier today, and it led us to a number of good and important discussions and an adrenaline boost thinking of past successes!

In the SRE team we’ve been big proponents of offering as much as possible of our services through dedicated self service or by inviting others to do pull requests to our shared infrastructure libs. 

One of the self services I’m most proud of is called the “GCP Inventory”. 

While GCP offers a really good UX, for an enterprise looking to get an aggregate view of the entire organisation’s resources, there is little help to be found. 

That’s why we sometime in mid 2020 decided to create our own, table view of provisioned Google Cloud instances, with information such as place in folder structure, project, zones, machine types, network interfaces, network tags, allocated disk space, whether preemptible or not, run status, cost recommendations (by scraping Recommender API) and finally owners.

We also added firewall configurations for the instances in a dedicated tab and another tab for security findings by using data from the Security Command Center API.

The reason why we could pull this off is thanks to the scanning data we are continuously aggregating using Forseti and by having our own Victor Castillo visualise all this data using TypeScript with a table view in the web app now known as “GCP Inventory”, further enriched by usage of Recommender and Security Command Center APIs.

Earlier today the team and I tried a simple, yet effective and powerful retrospective format that may be interesting to share.

After setting the stage for a few mins, just two distinct questions are asked.

- What makes you happy at work? 

- What makes you sad at work?

Time box the data gathering for both of these questions to 10-15 mins.

After data gathering has been done, group jointly similarly themed notes and discuss as appropriate. 

Pick one or two items on the sad side and discuss what actions you as a team can take to change things for the better. 

Please be wary to only choose such items that you as a team can directly influence through your own actions.

I’ve surely written about the TPS (Toyota Production System) reference chart on my desk. Nowadays when I’m not nearly as often in the office as I used to be, I’m missing throwing a glance or two at the chart and reflecting a bit on the meaning of individual concepts. A central one I try to practice often is “Hansei”.

Hansei (反省, "self-reflection") is a central idea in Japanese culture, meaning to acknowledge one's own mistake and to pledge improvement.

While the term Hansei is related to the concept of shame in Japanese, it doesn’t have the negative connotation we associate with it in the Western world. 

Hansei is about making one aware there is room for improvement and humility. It is an objective criticism of oneself so that one understands the gap in one’s performance and thus corrects this in the future. 

In Japanese schools, the children are trained to perform Hansei on a regular basis. Hansei is scheduled at the end of the school day as an opportunity to think about areas of self improvement. 

In the adult life, Hansei also includes an introspection of “what went right” along with “what went wrong / what could be improved”.

Practicing Hansei regularly promotes humility and helps establish a sound path of a life-long learning. Stay humble, stay hungry, move mountains!

A colleague of mine shared recently a somewhat provocative article titled “Let’s stop fooling ourselves. What we call CI/CD is actually only CI.”

Having personally worked in the field for a number of years, I had to nod semi-agreeingly. I know very well that many of us have the capability of doing CD or even continuous deployment, but most of the time we “choose” not to. 

The reasons often stated for choosing not to are everything from organisational (processes, hand-offs etc), technical, contractual (like SLAs written ages ago), regulatory (literal interpretations of regulations). 

What all of these poor excuses lead up to in the end, are poor software success metrics in all four areas (Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, Time to Restore Service) and naturally in the long run for the company itself end customer dissatisfaction and decreased competitiveness.

Being an avid runner, I have a running analogy that I feel works well in this context. 

The faster one runs, the more one needs to be in full control of one’s gait, pace, breathing, focus etc. 

Ergo, one can only achieve control and increased quality of software by increasing speed of delivery, enhancing observability and ensuring automated recovery, rather than through obstruction thereof.

“Research at The Standish Group also indicates that smaller time frames, with delivery of software components early and often, will increase the success rate. 

Shorter time frames result in an iterative process of design, prototype, develop, test, and deploy small elements. 

This process is known as "growing" software, as opposed to the old concept of "developing" software. 

Growing software engages the user earlier, each component has an owner or a small set of owners, and expectations are realistically set. 

In addition, each software component has a clear and precise statement and set of objectives. Software components and small projects tend to be less complex. 

Making the projects simpler is a worthwhile endeavor because complexity causes only confusion and increased cost.”

Sounds familiar right? One could think it’s a quote from a recent publication but in fact it’s from a 26 year old paper.

In January 1994, the Standish Group published a research paper analysing why so many software projects resulted in failure, what factors were the cause and how to reduce failures.

Some how-to:s have been quoted above. Some others are also familiar to any modern day agile practitioner; user involvement, executive management support, realistic expectations etc.

How do you keep your Cloud tidy and clean?

In 2019 as our teams started working with GCP, one of the epics I wrote on our Kanban board, was about defining cleaning policies for our Cloud resources and putting in place automation around these policies. 

While everyone liked the idea, it soon got forgotten due to other priorities.

Fast forward to now, with a growing number of GCP resources in use and therefore a bigger need to clean up unused or unowned resources, we dusted off the epic.

As we asked our Google contacts if they had any best practice sharing, we soon realised we had covered most of the ground Google was proposing and beyond already. 

It’d be interesting though to hear whether anyone here has any additional advice or suggestions.

Here is what we’re currently doing / about to do as goes for GCP resource cleaning:

- Billing data exports into BQ used for Data Studio dashboards and further sent to Grafana for additional graphing and alerting, giving visibility.

- Labelling of all GCP projects per a set norm.

- Automated (supervised) jobs gathering unlabelled/incorrectly labelled projects, emailing owners with due warnings and eventually deleting them if no action is taken. 

- Using Liens objects to further protect production critical resources from deletion.

Gil Broza’s latest newsletter touches a topic well recognisable by any business, product and team leader. 

“By saying ‘yes’ to X, what am I saying ‘no’ to?”

Gil is telling about a company that’s been working hard on a digital transformation project, whose deadline is approaching fast. 

However, recently business stakeholders have gotten the PO to add a few new features. 

Gil is asking by saying “yes” to these new features, what is the company saying “no” to? What is the trade off?

The business is adamant the new features need to make the deadline as well as the old features. 

So what’s then being sacrificed? Team’s morale, increase in technical debt, retention? Or could it be product’s quality? With scope creep and feature cramming, the probability is high is that more defects will make it to the customer.

Gil ends by saying that it’s one thing not to be explicit about consequences to the team, the product, the business but a quite bad idea not to be intentional about the consequences to oneself. 

He has a good practice to share to anyone facing a decision about doing more. 

“Say out loud, and write down, a full sentence describing what you’re trading off. Being explicit this way will force you to be honest with yourself so you’re intentional about your choices.”

An idea that stuck with me from “Leadership is the Language” is about “Sue stuck in blue”. 

Sue is prone to rumination & debate, hesitant to make a decision, a commitment to start doing. She is scared what comes after the thinking & discussion phase, ie proving something, that the taken decision was right, that the job can be done. That’s daunting. It’s holding her back.

Many technology leaders will probably nod and recall someone in their own team. 

Here Mr Marquet has some good tips how to get out of stalemate.

Commit to Learn, not (just) Do - View work as a learning cycle; make a prediction, then test the prediction by observing what happens, then reflect upon the observations with respect to the prediction. This idea of work on the basis of a hypothesis puts us in a learning and improving mindset.  

Commit Actions, Not Beliefs - For every significant decision you’ll have people who would have chosen a different path. There is little point in trying to convince outliers. Focus on committing action straight after the decision is made from all involved, to pursue a learning and evolving path forward. 

Chunk it Small, but Do it All - split up work in chunks but ensure that reflection happens throughout so that the sum of decisions taken leads up to a better whole.

Recently I finished listening to “Leadership Is Language” by David L. Marquet, former US Navy captain and the writer of the now classic “Turn The Ship Around!”. 

In his first book, Mr. Marquet used his counterintuitive model of leadership to turn the worst-performing submarine crew into the best-performing one in the fleet.

In his second book, he draws on a wide range of examples, to show exactly how the words you use (and don't use) impact how your people and teams feel, contribute and evolve.

Here he introduces six new leadership responses, quite different from the old responses, based on an old paradigm of leadership back from the Industrial Revolution. They are, in order:

1. Control the clock, instead of obeying the clock
2. Collaborate, instead of coercing
3. Aim for commitment rather than compliance
4. Complete defined goals instead of continuing work indefinitely
5. Improve outcomes, rather than proving ability
6. Connect with your people, instead of conforming to your role

If you want actionable tips on how to motivate team and individuals to do their best and be their best, then look no further! 

This is a well narrated account on the importance of the intersection of communication and leadership, with simple steps to transform your thinking, doing and influence.

Do you struggle finding the 1-2-1 time slots for your team members and yourself? 

Nearly a year back, Andreas Rehn and I started dedicating the second half of our Wednesdays to a set number of 1-2-1 slots, that our team members could book themselves into.

What we noticed was that while initially the booking rate was really high, it gradually declined over time. Reminding the team of the time slot, once in while, will help bump up the rate. And also, in the case of the team members who never themselves would book the 1-2-1, the traditional method of scheduling a dedicated time slot now and then, has to be applied. ;-)

Overall, I would say that the approach works well for the two of us, as we both see 1-2-1s as crucial for team and personal development, but don't really have much more time to dedicate to 1-2-1s, given that we are also trying to help our teams navigate through shifting product requirements as well as both new and old tech challenges. 

Recently, we have "automated" time booking from Confluence to somewhat more of a "self service" approach via appoint.ly.

During my lunch run last Friday, I was witness to an incident that shook me up and had me thinking about fragility, preciousness and priorities of life.

As I was running underneath the bridge across Ålkistan (sv: ’The Eel Hatch’) I saw an elderly lady rolling down the rocky and steep sides and stopping just before she would hit the dark and deep waters of the canal.

Seeing that, I hurried to her, sliding down the sides of the canal.

Even as streams of blood were covering parts of her face, arms and legs, she was collected and quite calm. She said she felt fine and that the blood was merely superficial.

In the meanwhile, two other runners had also come to assist. I found her slip-on shoes laying scattered around that happily hadn’t fallen in, and after Barbro, as was the 86-year old lady’s name, had gathered some strength, the three of us, as gently as possible pushed her up the steep sides of the canal, back on to the road. 

We ordered a taxi and one of the other runners followed along to the ER.

All’s well that ends well and in this case Barbro got away with some bruising and scrubs. 

I got away an experience and a few good reflections richer, particularly about what life’s true priorities are and how fickle and fleeting life is for all of us. 

Take care of each other!

During my uni years I got to work as election official for a few general and EU parliament elections.

While a great learning experience overall, what I appreciated the most is probably not what one would first guess.

As it happens, these were the last elections in which one didn’t have to ID oneself to vote. 

The voter would approach the election officials, state their name (and if several people with the same name their civic number), the official would pass on voting envelopes, the voter would go behind the privacy screens, cast their vote, seal the envelopes and return to the official with the envelopes to be inserted into the voting box, upon which the official would mark that the person had voted.

Underpinning everything was mutual trust. 

Trust that the voter would not give a false name. Trust that the respect for elections and democratic process was commonly shared between all.

I appreciated this small but telling expression of mutual trust in our society, especially as many in between elections had forgotten they didn’t need IDs, but always got happy hearing they didn’t need them to vote. 

It also gave a shared sense of familiarity and belonging even as the voting circuits were a few thousand voters in size.
Although written in 2016, just as relevant today!

Nowadays there is talk of data-driven organisations, data-driven marketing, data-driven decision-making, data-driven product management, and so on.

The adjective data-driven means that progress in an activity is compelled by data, rather than by intuition or by personal experience.

My first touchpoint with “data-driven” was back in 2007. I was working with services sales and marketing at Nokia Nordic, and we had just gotten a shiny new tool to use. It was QlikView, and it was connected amongst other things to our factories’ SAP systems, giving device sales numbers in almost real time. 

At the time, the mobile services adoption was at it’s infancy and we were doing our best to understand the correlation between our marketing efforts, digital, analog, bought, earned and owned, and our services adoption rates. 

Using data flooding into QlikView from different sources, massaging it a bit and presenting it in a dashboard, we were able to successfully boost our services activation rates. In fact we were so successful that our activation rates were double digit every single month, much to envy of our European colleagues.

That mindset that “data is power” has since remained. I try to tackle almost every problem by first gathering all required data rather than guessing on a whim.

“A little progress each day adds up to big results.”

Every year, on August the 15th, I recall the same day in 1993. 

This was the day I came to Sweden from the (at the time) war struck Sarajevo. I was 12, my syster 8, mum and dad 37. 

Dad was being air lifted out with other heavily wounded to Sweden for further treatment. Naturally he wanted us to come along. We on the other hand were far from convinced. 

My granddad who for many years had lived and worked in Vienna was advising against us going, although the war was raging on at full strength. He knew, from own experience no doubt, how difficult it’d be to return once the war was over. 

Mum and dad decided to leave together, hoping that the dad would get well and we, the kids, would once again have a chance for a normal life, without shells, shots and death being key elements of our everyday. 

This was the last time I saw my granddad. He died of cancer towards the end of the war. 

Today, a lifetime later almost, I’m thinking how right he was in that we probably wouldn’t return for good again. 

Although starting all over again, at an age of 37, was not easy at all, my parents did their outmost to give my sister and me, a solid ground to build our own lives on, in our new home country.

That persistence and perseverance has been a key source of inspiration in my life.

I simply love the user story format! 

To me, the user stories are the epitome of agility. They explain “who”, “what” and “why”, but leave out “how”. They are as customer centric as can be, as the starting point is the customer for whom the change is performed. They are also purpose centric, which is almost as important as customer centric, as they explain “why” the requested change will bring customer value. 

If you happen to be unfamiliar with the format, user stories are short, simple descriptions of a feature told from the perspective of the person who wants the new capability, normally a user or a customer. They follow a simple pattern:

As a <type of user>, I want <some goal> so that <some reason>.

Even if they may seem simple enough, mastering the art of writing good user stories is something that takes many years to acquire.

Some people write them too generic, others lay out long text chucks around the user story and bury it within. Others write one liners about what they plan to do, and forget the key elements of why and for whom. 

In fact, over the course of the years, I’ve only read one or two dozen really, really good user stories. The rest have fallen in one of the three categories above. 

This is what I think. What do you think?

I for one love the Greek legend of Sisyphus. He was a mischief maker and for that Zeus punished him with something worse than death. 

Sisyphus was given a boulder. The boulder had to be pushed up a mountain. When the boulder reached the top of the mountain, it would roll back down and he had to push it up again... it would roll back down and he had to push it up... for the rest of eternity!

I use this image as a reminder to always look for the “why” in established processes, procedures and ways of working. 

Only by asking why something is done in a certain way by someone for someone, we can hope to find new, better ways and introduce much needed change and improvements in our teams and companies.

But by blindly just accepting the current ways, we can hardly hope on a change for the better. We’ll just continue rolling the boulder up the hill until it roles back down again, and then we’ll just have to have yet another go at it.

Recently I finished listening to “Ego is the Enemy” by Ryan Holiday.

The author does a good job of tying together some note worthy anecdotes from literature, philosophy and history, with the book’s title message that the enemy lies within ourselves: the ego. 

Early in our careers, it impedes learning. With success, it blinds us to our faults and sows future problems. In failure, it magnifies each blow and makes recovery more difficult. At every stage, ego holds us back.

The fact that Ryan Holiday is personally invested in the message shines through and makes the book both more and less enjoyable at the same time. 

More because his personal stories make the book come alive. Less because he at times uses ego as a substitute for human vice in general, as he’s trying to underline his point. 

Overall he’s pretty successful in the effort though. He uses the term ego to describe the part of you that is always striving for recognition. The part of you that always has an excuse. It decreases your perspective. It makes you see what you want to see. Ego is the default choice, because it's soothing. That is precisely why we must be cognizant of it, and counter-balance it.

To sum it up, the book is a good manual how to counter egocentricity through stoicism, and usable for most people.

What we had at the time was a highly functional and reasonably extensible CI/CD toolchain catering for both a monolithic and microservices based architecture.

I love the concept of dogfooding, or “eating one’s own dog food”. 

I believe it can and must be applied broadly, not just in engineering teams but also in teams working in other parts of the business. 

The term is traced back to Microsoft manager Paul Maritz, who, in 1988, challenged Microsoft's employees to increase their use of company's products.

The practice of using your own products provides a number of advantages, both marketing and technology wise.

From a marketing standpoint, it definitely looks much better if you use your own products over those of a competitor. 

It’s also a great way to receive valuable feedback early and be able to demonstrate to your customers firsthand your product’s capabilities.

Technology wise, there is nothing more eye opening than personally experiencing what the user experience of your product in fact is like. 

Using your own product, alone and with other end users, is a great way to determine not only if you’re building the thing right, but also whether you’re building the right thing. 

A famous case of dogfooding is Jeff Bezos’ mandate to Amazon in 2002 requiring all teams to expose their internal APIs publicly, which made the same APIs usable and paved the way for Amazon’s journey into cloud computing.

Do you practice dogfooding?
