”Permission Paralysis” - not sure if it’s a concept or just something I’ve coined. Either way, to me it’s one of the main killers of innovation and productivity in a team. 

Permission paralysis is what happens when your team or individual team members are keen to explore some new tooling or a new approach to an old problem, but due to the inflexibilities of the permission model of what they are allowed to and not to, have to request such permissions from another team(s) (or even a board - TEP-LARB anyone!?!). 

Instead of spending time and energy pursuing the original line of thought to see whether it brings the intended business value, the team and/or team members go into idle mode, waiting for someone else, not equally invested or interested, to make the unblocking decision.

This brings frustration about with all involved, as generally the receiving team also has things to do and deliver, and such a request from the requesting team is breaking the receiving team’s flow of work.

One solution is allowing temporary elevation of privilege so that the requesting team may continue their exploration with no interruption, by doing it themselves, at their risk and peril. The receiving team should show a helpful, trusting mindset and of course a fault tolerant permission model!

For some years now, I’ve been an advocate of T-shaped skills and how important it is having people with both broad, general skills as well as deep skills in one area within one’s teams. 

Here are some benefits of a T-shaped skill set:

- Better collaboration with others.
With the broad range of knowledge, one knows enough to communicate with specialists in different fields, which makes collaboration smoother and faster.

- More likely to stay interested.
When one’s focus is on a single area, it can get monotonous. After all, the variety is the spice of life. No matter how fascinating the topic, variety is key to keeping one’s mind engaged. As a T-shaped person, one always has other areas to go to when one needs a break from one’s specialty.

- Satisfaction of depth. 
Even as one gets to move around to different areas, one also gets to experience the satisfaction that comes from diving deep in one subject area. The deeper one goes, the bigger the realisation how vast one’s area of knowledge is and how there’s a lifetime of learning ahead. 

- Increasing creativity.
The greatest ideas normally happen at the intersection of disciplines. When one has a broad base of knowledge, there is a small risk of one’s specialist knowledge in one field clouding one’s ability to see new ideas.

I’m at times surprised by how people in general just accept and assume things, without trying to look at the underlying why. 

Why something is being done, by certain people, in a certain way? 

What puzzles me even more is when people in fact dare to ask the question why, and they receive a simple “because XYZ” (replace XYZ with some arbitrary big word such as legal, tradition, security, best practice, regulations, you name it), and then they stop right there. 

Even as they’ve taken a great leap forward in asking the why, they are being scuffed back into the cupboard, just by receiving some capital letter word(s) as “valid” explanation.

I for one like digging further into the why. 

I guess it’s partially due to my background in physics and engineering and (maybe naive) assumption that most things are logical and rational. 

I also like surrounding myself with people who equally discerningly dare to continue asking the question why from their peers, managers and other functions. 

It’s only by unravelling why we’re doing things in a certain way today, while taking into account the relevant aspects, that we can change, improve and do better tomorrow. 

In my view, blind acceptance without further exploratory whys leads at best to mediocrity and at worst complacency.

It may come as a surprise that what many consider the most famous of all wartime motivational posters “Keep calm and carry on” had in fact a very limited distribution before and during the WW2. 

It’s siblings “Your courage...” and “Freedom is...” on the other hand enjoyed a much longer time in public eye.  

The “Keep Calm...” poster was designed by the British Ministry of Information in 1939. It was produced as part of a series of three posters. Each poster showed a slogan under a representation of a "Tudor Crown" (a symbol of the state). Their intended use was wide distribution to strengthen morale in the event of major wartime disasters. 

And while it’s siblings came to use straight after coming off the presses, the “Keep calm...” poster wasn’t sanctioned for immediate public display and distribution. By April 1940, 2,5 million copies of the poster were pulped as part of a nationwide paper salvage campaign.

It wasn’t until 2000 when the poster got rediscovered in a small bookshop off the beaten track, that it’s resurrection and popularity came to be. 

In today’s turbulent times, the words off the poster ring as true as ever. It’s the calm, and all the daily tasks that we carry on doing in spite of Corona, that will bring us victory and help us retain the course!

Time and again, whenever pondering a given situation, I circle back to the Toyota Way. 

The Toyota Way rests on two pillars: Continuous Improvement, with concepts of Challenge, Kaizen (“change for the better”) and Genchi Genbutsu (“going to the source”), and Respect for People, which embraces Respect and Teamwork.

While I draw lots of inspiration from the Toyota Way, at times I find some concepts harder to fully use. 

One is “Nemawashi” which is the first step in the decision making process. It is sharing of information about the decisions that will be made, in order to involve all employees in the process. During the nemawashi, the company is seeking for the opinion of the employees about the decision. 

So far, all fine and good. I highly value and endorse transparency and openness as well as open dialogue and contradictory opinions. 

I also appreciate and embrace giving due heads-up early so that all affected will have their say and possibility to change, modify and eventually implement a better decision than was originally thought of and suggested. 

My experience though is that in bigger companies the case is often that many feel they have a say although not necessarily their skin in the game. Which makes the process of identifying whose consensus is truly needed harder!

“Svakoga dana, u svakom pogledu, sve više napredujem.” Or “Every day, in every way, I’m getting better and better.”

I think I was 6 or 7 when my aunt first introduced me to these great words of wisdom that stuck ever since.

What I didn’t understand then was that she was quoting them from Kusturica’s first film “Do you remember Dolly Bell?”, a bittersweet comedy set in Yugoslavia during the 1960s.

The words rang all the more true because of her personal example. She was a law student at the time, studying hard, day and night, and passing her exams with flying colours.

One can say that this is Kaizen or continuous improvement at its core. Pursuing an objective relentlessly, while examining and improving oneself and one’s surroundings.

This pursuit for always better has in many ways shaped both my personal, academic and professional life. 

While I very well understand that I may not be technically most skilled person in the room, or the fastest runner in a competition, I always strive to listen and learn more or to keep the other’s pace for as long as I can, intentionally pushing myself out of the comfort zone. 

It’s been a most humbling and rewarding experience and each day I try my best to get people around me to also seek out their Kaizen, “the change for the better.”

I first started working in a ticketing system in 2006 as 2nd line NOC/Support Engineer at Ongame Network. I recall taking great pride in ensuring high quality in the responses back to poker operators, and the language I used. And also I wanted to respond to as many tickets as possible, so I aspired both to speed and quality.

Fast forward 13-14 years, the ticketing systems are all over. Everything is tracked in some ticketing system, be that a request for phone repair or a user story defining a team’s or a individual’s development work. Equally so, tickets are used for cross-team requests and communication. 

While I recognise the need for tickets (hey, I still love writing impressive tickets!), I also see them as problematic as the primary mean of communication between technical teams.

The execution and resolution speed becomes greatly stifled by bouncing back and forth of a word, code and jargon potpourri. The frustration between individuals in the ticket thread grows incrementally as the resolution of reporter’s problem is delayed. 

In these situations I advocate less tickets and more face time. More interactions between teams via mobbing, pairing, pull requests and/or dedicated Slack channels, all of which lead to better feedback loops and superior products.

”Managers should not be operational.” 

Of all statements regarding the manager role, this is probably the one that fastest hits a nerve with me.

As you probably gather, I disagree with the statement. 

I for one love seeing my teams and team members act autonomously, in harmony with stakeholder requirements and feedback as well as the bigger company and industry context. 

As that Nirvana state is never fully achieved across all teams, me as a manager having a certain degree of hands-on knowledge of the teams’ work, technical, organisational or contextual, is something that over the years have been appreciated by a majority of my team members and teams, and useful in our deliveries to our customers. 

I know that my team members are more capable than myself making tough technical (or non-technical) decisions. I also trust them to make good on made decisions and execute in value increments. 

In my view a good manager is like a light house, assisting teams and individuals with contextual awareness and staying clear of dangerous paths, whilst helping to light up possible ways to the target.

I can’t quite put the finger on when I started viewing myself as a runner. 

It probably wasn’t in the summer of 2013 when it felt as if a turtle could do those long 4,9km runs faster (not far from the truth as my average speed at the time was just under 6km/h and a turtle does 5,4km/h). 

In 2014, I was at home for a few months with our second born and started running with him in the baby jogger. My speed improved from 10-9min/km at the beginning of the year down to 7-6min/km and finally 5min/km over the course of a few months. 

With the speed, also the mileage increased, from just a few kilometres to 10-15km per run. As well as the frequency, from 16 runs in 2013 to 104 in 2014. 

Neither the speed, mileage or frequency increase came without injuries, far from it, but by then, I had already fallen in love with the sport. The injuries healed and I returned for more; faster speed and longer runs. 

In November 2014, I run my first race, the Stockholm Tunnel Run, 10km in 45m 25s. I totally loved the atmosphere, the adrenaline, and the comradery. 

I guess it could very well be at this race that I fully assumed my runner’s identity.  

I’ve kept this identity ever since and it’s given me so much. Balance and perspective in life paired with relentless focus on things that matter.

Taiichi Ohno, father of the Toyota Production System (TPS), defined three categories of waste: Muda, Mura, and Muri. 

Muda refers to processes or activities that consume resources but bring no value to the end customer. They increase costs and make tasks take much longer than they should. Finding and eliminating Muda is essential if you wish to reduce costs, improve efficiency, and increase profits. 

Mura is caused by unevenness (both high and low) in production and services. It is also caused when standards are nonexistent or not followed. 

Mura creates either overproduction and over-processing (Muda) when the load is low, or Muri (overburden) when the load is high, which in turn undermines efforts to eliminate the seven wastes of Muda.

Muri is the result of tasks or processes that are overly difficult, or ones that overburden employees.

In the real world, reducing Muda can lead to Muri. The existence of Mura can be seen as a waste in Muda. And finally Muri may lead to a breakdown in the system that will result in a large amount of Muda and Mura. 

To summarise, any efforts spent on removing Muda may very well be wasteful, if you don’t also address Mura and Muri.

In the past few months I’ve started all the more appreciating and applying the concept of Last Responsible Moment in weekly work planning.

The concept is simple. Rather than doing everything you need to do all at once, you do something either at the point in time at which you in fact need it, or the point at which it would be irresponsible not to do it. 

All you need to do is ask: “Do we need to do this now?” 

If the answer is no, then you can focus on something immediately more important. 

If the answer is yes, then you should ask: “Do we need to do all of this now?” 

If the answer is no, then you have managed to better prioritise and reduce your immediate workload. Doing this also helps you break down bigger tasks into smaller ones.  

Benefits of following LRM are many. 

- You focus much better on the task at hand. 
- You get more (right) things done.
- By delaying, you may very well discover a better way of doing the task. 

Risks are a few but good to be aware of.

- You need to have a feeling for when the Last Responsible Moment is, as being late with the delivery may lead to issues you were trying to avoid in the first place.
- You need to ensure all stakeholders understand and respect the process. Just because something hasn’t been done, it hasn’t been forgotten.

I just finished listening to the marvellous “Never Split The Difference” written by the former top FBI hostage negotiator, Chris Voss and co-authored by Tahl Raz. 

Everything you’ve been previously taught about negotiation is simply wrong: you are not rational and neither is the person you’re negotiating with; there is no such thing as ‘fair’; compromise is the worst thing you can do; the real art of negotiation lies in mastering the intricacies of No, not Yes. 

These surprising tactics are the field-tested tools FBI agents use to talk criminals and hostage-takers around the world into (or out of) just about any scenario you can imagine.

Throughout the book, Voss draws on his experiences to bring to life these techniques and how they apply to situations in our daily lives, at work, at home and elsewhere. 

It’s a really immersive book and one I’ll definitely reference and come back to!

There is something special about first time experiences. First love, first car, first day in school, you name it. Phone in the image below, Nokia N78, code name Merlin, was my first solo Go To Market project as semi fresh Product Manager at Nokia Scandinavia.

It was the successor to the popular N73 and it launched in May 2008. Nokia N78 packed numerous features such as A-GPS, HSDPA and Wi-Fi. It had a touch-sensitive Navi wheel, and was the first phone to feature an FM transmitter.

While N78 was far from my first or last Go To Market project, it was the first one where I was solely responsible for all aspects of its launch in Scandinavian countries, including its sales performance. 

Even as I already from the offset knew that N78 wouldn’t break many sales records given its cumbersome (but innovative) keyboard, and (often) unruly Navi wheel and in light of the market landscape at the time, I still gave both my heart and soul in making this device launch as good as it possibly could be.

Although I don’t remember many details on how N78 did in the market, I still fondly recall how I gave this launch all I had and then some more. And this continues to be the way I tackle most challenges in life. It’s not always painless or without cost, but it gets things done and is great fun!

Today was my 5th year in a row running Stockholm half marathon. This time placing 460 out of 6459 men, at 1:29:15.

This is one of my favourite quotes in Swedish and one I often return to. 

Roughly it translates as “What is dimly said, is dimly thought.” 

First voiced back in 1820 by the author and professor Esaias Tegnér, the words ring equally strong 200 years later. 

If you don’t really think through what you’re saying or writing, there is a high probability your unconnected thoughts shine through to the recipient(s) of the message, and in turn fail to make intended impact. 

I for one am at times too fast saying and writing thoughts that would have been better off processing in my head for a few seconds longer. 

And here is the key. A few seconds longer pause that brings additional clarity to one’s thoughts is always to prefer over something speedier but more dimmed. 

(Photo credit: myself, Stockholm City Hall from München Brewery).

“Lijepa riječ i gvozdena vrata otvara.” 

Literally: “A kind word opens even the iron door.”

Leaving aside why irons doors would be more difficult to open than doors made of other materials, this is probably one of my favourite South Slavic proverbs. 

My grandmother who never had a bad word for anyone, instilled this saying in me since young age. 

Coming home angered over some injustice done to me, she would say these words and gradually turn my childish anger into more positive feelings.

Even today, I often return to this saying, as a guiding light. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t. But it always makes me remember my grandmother, and puts a smile on my face.

“If I’ve seen further, it’s by standing upon the shoulders of giants.” - Isaac Newton 

First time I encountered this quote, was during my university days as an Engineering Physics student in Uppsala.

For some reason, I immediately identified with the idea, not because my scholarly achievements were surpassing those of Newton (far from it) but because I saw beyond the scholarly context in which the quote was formulated.

I saw that it meant that one should share one’s knowledge, learnings, ideas and resources with those around, as to achieve more than just the sum of the parts. 

Consequently, I’ve always been wary of people deliberately withholding knowledge and information from others, shying away from transparency and hogging resources when given opportunity.

At times, this openness and positivity has worked against me but in the grander schema of things, I’m pretty confident this mindset has served me and people around me well. 

I’d really like to hear what thoughts this quote evokes in you.

Earlier today, I went with my family to a McDonalds place just south of Stockholm. Imagine our surprise when we saw that the order taking had been fully digitalised, meaning that there was no longer a cashier taking orders. 

While this transformation has been long coming and the pros are quite self evident, such as more staff available to work in the kitchen with food preparation, more food being made to order and much less food being thrown away, I was still quite amazed at how fast it had gone. 

While standing there and placing our order on the giant touchscreen, I became witness to an elderly couple in their early seventies not even being able to get past the initial welcome screen. 

Passing by, I gave them some cues on how to take on the touchscreen, and from distance, I proudly observed that they even got halfway through, but then, for some reason they decided not to follow through and left the premises, looking for another place to eat. 

This short real life episode left a somewhat sour aftertaste. While digitalisation most of the time is democratic, empowering, and liberating, for some groups in the society, it’s quite the opposite. 

The question that inevitably springs to mind is what we can do to make the technology gap as narrow to as many as possible?

“Individuals and interactions over processes and tools”.

To me this 1st core value of the Agile Manifesto is the most central of the 4 core values, as it sets the scene for the values as well as the 12 principles of Agile Software.

But, and here’s a big but, I find that for many this very principle is the hardest one to adopt and live by. 

I see people entrenched in the process trenches, overly eager to defend the process (it can be any process) and equally eager not to understand any individuals, in their view, not conforming to the process. 

Valuing people and interactions more highly than processes or tools should be easy to understand because it is the people and interactions between people that deliver value by responding to (changing) business needs. 

I for one consider myself very much to be a process driven person, both aspiring to formalise new processes as well as follow processes as set out by others, when and where it makes sense. 

And here lies the culprit, the process needs to make sense and be subject to constant improvements, to remain relevant and alongside tools continue to support individuals and interactions in the pursuit of incremental customer value. 

Can you think of at least one process that you engage in, that doesn’t really make sense?

Research shows that educational experiences that are active, social, contextual, engaging, and student-owned lead to deeper learning. The benefits of collaborative learning include:

- Development of higher-level thinking, oral communication, self-management, and leadership skills.

- Increase in student retention, self-esteem, and responsibility.

- Exposure to and an increase in understanding of diverse perspectives.

- Preparation for real life social and employment situations.

While I see a number of collaborative learning formats actively being used (such as mob or pair programming), I still think that we as grownups need to do even more collaborative learning (regardless of job type), so that we can faster disseminate knowledge, experience and fresh ideas between team members.

“I’m just a manager.” 

This evening I went to a really good Continuous Delivery meet-up and during the mingle, I took part in a not too unusual conversation with some of the meet-up participants. 

As the conversation went a bit deeper into the tech-stack used at some company, a person working at this company exclaimed the quoted words above. It’s by far not the first time I’ve heard these words spoken by a manager colleague.

I for one am humble enough to know that my team members are more skilled than myself at both their current and whatever future tech stack that we may explore. Hey, I would be really, really worried if they weren’t! ;-)

But at the same time, I think that a manager must invest both time and effort understanding 1) human, 2) business and 3) technical context of his/her team, in that order. 

The human context as in individuals and interactions is a given one. The people are the secret sauce to all successful results and they’re a manager’s first priority. 

The business context is key for team’s target setting and provides the necessary framework for team’s value delivery.

And the third one (the technical context) I’m afraid is often the most neglected one, although quite crucial particularly in tech driven teams. 

This is what I think. What do you think?

I recently finished listening to 
“Lean Thinking: Banish Waste and Create Wealth in Your Corporation” (Revised and Updated) by James P. Womack and Daniel T. Jones. The core of the lean model is the same in the new edition. All businesses must define the real "value" that they produce as the product that best suits customer needs. Then the "value stream” is identified and clarified, the set of actions required to bring the product through problems solving, information management, and transformation tasks. Next, "lean enterprise" lines up its suppliers and teams with the value stream. "Flow" traces the product across teams. "Pull" then activates the flow as the business re-orients towards the pull of the customer's needs. Finally, with the company reengineered towards its core value in a flow process, the business re-orients towards "perfection," constantly removing the remaining muda (Japanese for "waste") in the system. While I found the book by these two legendary authors quite entertaining and worthwhile, I don’t think that the lean model is clearly demonstrated with applications in the IT or service industries, so if you’re on the hunt for a practical guide for your IT business, I’m afraid this is not the book.

This framework aims to help managers build better relationships at work, and fulfill the three key responsibilities of a leader: creating a culture of feedback (praise and criticism), building a cohesive team, and achieving results you’re all proud of. All in all, I found a number of thought worthy ideas and practical tips, and I’ll be probably be returning to the book for the same.

I just finished listening to “The Toyota Way: 14 Management Principles from the World's Greatest Manufacturer” by Dr. Jeffrey K. Liker. The two focal points of the Toyota Way are: “Continuous Improvement” and “Respect for People”. The principles for ”continuous improvement” (Kaizen) include establishing a long-term vision, working on challenges, continual innovation, and going to the source of the issue or problem (5 whys). I found the book quite educational with certain themes and ideas fairly easily transferable to my own work, and will probably be returning to the book over time for reference.

In one of my teams, we’ve kept recurring meetings to an absolute minimum. We do our weekly planning of tasks every Monday for no more than 1h, daily stand-ups Tue-Fri for no more than 15 mins and biweekly retros in 1h sharp. That’s it. Beyond that we do a lot of pair and mob programming if and where it makes sense, and call for focused, agenda-driven meetings only on an absolute need-to-basis and with the most relevant attendees. In fact, we take pride in cutting meetings short, and we generally have complex technical discussions in a smaller task force, rather than the team as a whole. With these practices firmly set, I gather that we are far more productive, task focused, aligned and content than ever before.
